# Unit 1: Basics of Communication
Communicative English · Semester 1

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the lesson, students should be able to explain a basic communication process, distinguish verbal from non-verbal communication, identify barriers and suggest ways to overcome them.

## What is communication?
Communication is the process of creating and sharing meaning. It can inform, request, persuade, build relationships or coordinate action. It is more than producing words: the receiver must interpret the message, and shared understanding should be checked rather than assumed. Communication is important in classrooms, workplaces and daily life because it helps people learn, collaborate, resolve misunderstandings and make decisions.

## The communication process
A useful introductory model is: sender → message → channel → receiver → feedback. A person (sender) forms an idea and encodes it using words or other signs. The message travels through a channel, such as speech, a phone call or email. The receiver decodes or interprets it. Feedback is the receiver’s response, which lets the sender check understanding. Context includes the situation, relationship and expectations. Noise is anything that interferes with the message; it can be physical, linguistic or psychological.

Example: A teacher (sender) emails a changed deadline (message) to students (receivers). A student replies to confirm the new date (feedback). If the email goes to spam, the channel has failed; if “next Friday” is ambiguous, the wording creates a barrier. Real conversations are often simultaneous and interactive, so this simple sequence is a model, not a complete picture of every exchange.

## Verbal and non-verbal communication
Verbal communication uses words, whether spoken or written. Spoken communication permits immediate clarification but may leave no permanent record. Written communication can be reread and shared, but tone may be unclear. Choose the form according to the purpose and audience.

Non-verbal communication includes facial expression, gesture, posture, use of space, eye behaviour and features of voice such as pace and volume. In a lecture, a pause may help a class process a difficult idea. Do not assume that one gesture has the same meaning everywhere: culture, disability, personality and context affect interpretation. Lack of eye contact, for example, is not proof of dishonesty or lack of attention.

## Barriers and responses
• Physical: noise, poor lighting or an unstable internet connection. Move, adjust equipment or provide written notes.
• Language/semantic: unfamiliar vocabulary, jargon or ambiguous instructions. Explain terms, use examples and ask for a paraphrase.
• Psychological: anxiety, frustration or assumptions. Create a respectful environment, listen and ask clarifying questions.
• Cultural and social: different expectations, stereotypes or unequal power. Avoid assumptions and invite questions without embarrassment.
• Organisational: unclear responsibilities or too many messages. State who must do what, by when, and use an appropriate channel.
• Access: inaccessible formats, hearing difficulties or language barriers. Offer captions, accessible documents or alternative ways to participate when needed.

## 50-minute lesson plan
0–5 min: Ask students to recall a misunderstanding. 5–15: Explain the model using the deadline example. 15–25: In pairs, identify sender, channel, noise and feedback in a classroom scenario. 25–35: Compare spoken, written and non-verbal signals. 35–45: Groups suggest solutions to one barrier. 45–50: Exit ticket: describe one barrier and one practical response.

## Practice with answers
1. A teacher says “submit it soon,” but students do not know the date. Barrier? Ambiguous wording. Improvement: give a specific date and time.
2. A student replies, “So the meeting is at 10 a.m. on Tuesday?” Which element is this? Feedback that checks the message.
3. Is a spoken instruction verbal or non-verbal? Verbal, because it uses words; its tone and gestures may add non-verbal information.

## Questions
Why is feedback essential? How do channel and context influence meaning? Give two barriers and explain a solution for each. Why must non-verbal cues be interpreted cautiously?

## Reading note
The linked open textbook provides further discussion of communication and perception. Match the terminology used in the department’s prescribed textbook.

## Teach the process through one complete example

Suppose a teacher needs students to bring a draft to the next class. The teacher is the sender. The intended meaning is the message: students should bring a draft on a specified day. The teacher encodes it in words, choosing a language and level of detail. A spoken announcement, email or printed notice is the channel. Students receive and decode it, relating the words to what they already know. A student who asks whether a handwritten draft is acceptable provides feedback; the teacher's reply can repair ambiguity.

Context affects every stage. Students may be in a noisy room, may have missed the date, or may understand the word “draft” differently. Communication is therefore not complete simply because words were spoken. In real conversations people can send and receive at the same time; the sequence is a teaching model, not a claim that every exchange follows a rigid one-way order.

## Verbal and non-verbal communication

Verbal communication uses words, whether spoken, signed or written. Non-verbal communication includes features such as facial expression, gesture, posture, spacing, timing and vocal tone. A sentence may be verbal while its tone supplies a non-verbal cue. A written message lacks some cues available in person, but punctuation and layout may influence interpretation. Do not assign a fixed emotion to one gesture: crossed arms can reflect cold, comfort, habit or discomfort, and eye contact norms vary.

## Barriers and responses

Physical barriers include poor acoustics, distance and an inaccessible room. A practical response might be a quieter space, a written copy or appropriate amplification. Semantic barriers arise when words are vague, unfamiliar or interpreted differently; explain terms and replace “soon” with a specific deadline. Psychological barriers include anxiety or preconceptions; invite questions without ridicule and check understanding. Organisational barriers can include messages passing through several people without an agreed record; confirm key decisions in writing. Accessibility and language barriers require accessible formats, interpretation or another suitable channel rather than blaming the listener.

Feedback should make correction possible. “Does everyone understand?” may produce silence without revealing a problem. A more useful check is: “What will you bring, and by when?” A student can answer in their own words, after which the teacher can clarify any difference.

## Model teaching explanation and practice

Explain: “Communication is a shared process of making meaning, not simply a person talking. The same message can be understood differently because people bring different experiences and work in different conditions.” Then ask pairs to improve this notice: “Bring it next week.” One possible revision is: “Please bring your first essay draft to our next class on [date].” The date is a placeholder, not a claimed timetable.

To assess the example, students should name the unclear word, rewrite the instruction and propose a feedback question. Accept other clear revisions that give the missing information. A strong answer connects a specific barrier to a practical remedy rather than only listing barrier names.

# Communication basics · activities with answers

## Goals and teaching
Students identify purpose, sender, receiver, message, channel, feedback and noise; they practise adjusting a message for an audience. Noise can be physical, semantic, emotional or technological. Feedback can be delayed or absent, so communication is not always a neat two-way loop.

## Model
A teacher emails students that a room has changed. Sender: teacher; message: new room and time; channel: email; receivers: students; feedback: replies or confirmation. If the time is unclear, that is a message-design barrier. If a student has no internet, access is a channel barrier. A quiet student is not automatically inattentive.

## Practice
1. A speaker gives directions while traffic makes the words hard to hear. Identify one barrier and one response. 2. Rewrite “Meet me there later” for a class group without inventing a venue: provide placeholders for place and time. 3. Give one example of non-verbal communication and two possible meanings. 4. What could confirm that the receiver understood?

## Suggested answers
1. Physical noise; move somewhere quieter or write the directions. 2. “Please meet at [place] at [time].” 3. Folded arms might indicate discomfort, cold or habit; context is needed. 4. Ask the person to summarise the instruction in their own words; do not assume a nod proves comprehension.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: discuss a misunderstood message. 10–20: map the email example. 20–30: rewrite vague instructions. 30–42: pairs practise accessible channels and feedback. 42–50: exit ticket names one barrier and a remedy.

## Worked classroom case: a misunderstood room change

A teacher announces that a discussion will meet in a different room. Several students hear the room number, but a student at the back hears only part of it because a fan is loud. Another student hears the number correctly but assumes the change is for every future week. A classmate posts “new room” in a group message without the date. These are distinct problems: physical noise, an assumption about duration and missing information in a written message.

Map the first announcement: sender, teacher; intended message, the changed room for a particular session; channel, spoken announcement; receiver, the students; physical noise, the fan. The student's request to repeat the number is feedback. The teacher can repeat it, write it where everyone can see, give the date and ask a student to state the information back. For an actual notice, insert the verified room and date rather than inventing them.

## Classroom activity with teacher guidance

Give each pair an original instruction that lacks one important detail: “Hand in the work later.” Ask one partner to act as receiver and list possible interpretations, without silently supplying a deadline. Ask the other to rewrite it using placeholders for the assignment, date and time. Partners then swap and check whether the message gives a clear action and whether the medium works for the intended reader.

A possible answer is: “Please submit [assignment] by [date] at [time] using [submission method].” Its strength is not the particular words; it identifies the action, deadline and channel. If the student cannot access that channel, the message is still incomplete as a practical communication strategy.

## Assessment with answers

1. A printed notice has tiny type. Identify a barrier and remedy. Suggested answer: an accessibility or physical barrier; provide readable type and an accessible digital or alternative format.
2. A person hears “next Friday” but is uncertain which week is meant. Suggested answer: semantic/contextual ambiguity; give the calendar date and invite confirmation.
3. A student nods but later performs a different task. Does the nod prove understanding? No. It is feedback, but its meaning is uncertain; ask for a brief explanation of the task.
4. Why can an email be useful after a spoken change? It supplies a record that people can revisit, provided recipients can access it and the wording is clear.

A short evaluation can award one mark for the named barrier, one for a suitable remedy and one for explaining why the remedy addresses that barrier.

course-2:1.text:
# Unit 2: Listening and Speaking Skills
Communicative English · Semester 1

## Learning outcomes
Students should be able to distinguish hearing from listening, recognise listening purposes and barriers, participate in a dialogue and discussion, and organise a short prepared or extempore speech.

## Listening and its importance
Hearing is the physical perception of sound. Listening involves attending to sound, interpreting meaning and, where appropriate, responding. A student can hear a lecture without following its argument. Effective listening supports learning, accurate instructions, empathy and respectful disagreement.

Active listening is a set of practices, not simply silence: focus on the speaker, allow them to finish, ask relevant questions, paraphrase important points and check whether your understanding is correct. A listener can disagree while still showing that they understand the other person’s position.

## Types of listening
• Informational/comprehensive: understand and remember an explanation or instruction, such as a teacher’s directions for an assignment.
• Critical: evaluate a claim, its evidence and assumptions, such as an advertisement’s promise.
• Empathetic: seek to understand another person’s experience or feelings without assuming what they mean.
• Appreciative: listen for enjoyment, as when hearing a poem or song.
These labels overlap: a person may listen to a speech for information and evaluate it critically at the same time.

## Barriers and solutions
External noise, uncomfortable seating, a poor connection and inaccessible audio can prevent reception. Prejudice, anxiety, distraction, mentally preparing a reply and unfamiliar terms can obstruct understanding. Choose a quieter environment, request accessible materials, take brief notes, ask the speaker to repeat or explain, and avoid interrupting. Never assume that silence, eye contact or accent alone proves whether someone is listening.

## Dialogue and conversation
A dialogue is an exchange of ideas between people. A useful sequence is to greet, establish the purpose, listen, ask a follow-up question and close politely. Example:
A: “Could you tell me when the assignment is due?”
B: “It is due on Friday at 4 p.m.”
A: “Thank you. Should we submit it online?”
B: “Yes, through the course portal.”
The final question checks a detail rather than making an assumption. Practise turn-taking, clear requests and clarification: “Could you explain what you mean by…?”

## Group discussion
A discussion has a purpose and several participants. Begin by defining the topic, invite different views, give reasons and examples, and summarise areas of agreement and disagreement. Useful language: “I agree with that point because…”, “May I add another perspective?” and “Could we return to the question?” A good participant makes space for quieter voices; volume or dominance alone is not effective leadership.

## Public speaking and extempore
A prepared speech benefits from a clear opening, a small number of organised points and a conclusion. Consider audience, time and purpose. Speak audibly and at a manageable pace, use examples, and rehearse. Extempore speaking means speaking with little preparation, not necessarily without any structure. Given a topic, take a brief moment to choose an opening, two points and an example, then close. Do not invent statistics to fill time.

## 50-minute lesson
0–8 min: Compare hearing and listening. 8–18: Read a short instruction aloud; students paraphrase it. 18–28: Pairs practise a dialogue with a clarification question. 28–40: Groups discuss a familiar campus issue with a facilitator. 40–47: Volunteers give a one-minute extempore response. 47–50: Each student identifies one listening improvement.

## Assessment and answers
1. A listener checks whether a speaker’s claim has good evidence. Type? Critical listening.
2. Give one useful response if an instruction is unclear. “Could you repeat the deadline, please?”
3. Outline a one-minute speech on reading: opening statement; two reasons; one example; conclusion. Multiple sensible outlines are possible.

## Questions
How does listening differ from hearing? What are two listening barriers? How can a group include quieter members? What structure helps an extempore speaker?

## Reading note
The linked Open University resource lists common barriers to active listening.

## A complete listening-and-speaking cycle

Listening is an active process: a listener attends to sound, identifies words and ideas, interprets them in context, remembers relevant information, and responds or checks meaning. These stages overlap in practice. Hearing sounds is not the same as understanding; a learner can hear every word and still miss an implied request or unfamiliar term.

Before listening, establish the purpose. Is the learner listening for a main idea, a particular date, the speaker's reasons or a response to a concern? During listening, taking a few key words can be more useful than trying to transcribe every sentence. Afterward, a listener can summarise and ask a focused question. Checking understanding is different from immediately agreeing: “If I understood, you need the draft on Monday. Is that right?” allows correction.

Effective speaking also begins with purpose and audience. Organise a short response around a clear opening, one or two relevant points and a conclusion or request. Use a pace and volume suitable to the setting, but avoid treating one accent or one style of eye contact as the measure of intelligence. Clarity can be developed without erasing a student's identity; accessibility may require a different format or communication aid.

In a discussion, turn-taking involves making space for others, listening without completing their sentences and entering politely when a turn is available. A useful disagreement identifies the idea and gives a reason: “I see the benefit, but could we also consider the cost?” It is possible to be clear and respectful without avoiding disagreement.

Worked example: a student hears “The seminar is on Thursday, but the draft must be sent on Tuesday.” A correct summary separates the event from the deadline. A useful check asks for the time or submission method if it was not stated. Assess listening by the accuracy of the summary and the relevance of the question, not by whether the learner maintains continuous eye contact.

course-2:1.text:
# Listening and speaking · practice and answer guide

## Key distinction
Hearing is perceiving sound; active listening includes attention, checking meaning and responding. Listening purposes include understanding instructions, appreciating a performance and evaluating a claim. Do not equate a single posture or eye-contact pattern with good listening: disability and culture affect communication.

## Listening task
Read aloud: “The reading club meets on Thursday at 4 p.m. in Room 12. Bring a notebook. If Room 12 is unavailable, meet outside the library.” Ask: day? time? room? contingency? Replay once and invite students to ask for clarification.

## Answers
Thursday; 4 p.m.; Room 12; outside the library if that room is unavailable. The passage does not say a fee or name a book; avoid guessing.

## Speaking tasks
Pairs: greet each other, ask for a repeat and summarise a message. Group discussion: “Should a college library stay open later?” Assign facilitator, timekeeper and note-taker; support claims with reasons rather than invented statistics. Extempore: allow one minute to plan and one minute to speak on “A useful learning habit,” with an opening, one example and closing.

## Feedback rubric
Give one point each for relevant content, understandable organisation, respectful turn-taking, a clarification strategy and a response to the listener. Accent is not a measure of intelligence. Allow alternatives to oral performance when needed.

## 50-minute lesson
0–8: discuss listening. 8–18: read and check the task. 18–28: pair conversation. 28–40: group discussion. 40–50: short extempore and supportive feedback.

## Worked listening exercise and answers

Read the following original announcement twice: “The reading group will meet on Friday at 3 p.m. in Room 6. Please bring a short passage you would like the group to discuss. If you cannot attend, tell the organiser by Thursday.” These details are invented for practice; they are not an actual timetable.

First listening: ask students for the main purpose. Suggested answer: to announce a reading-group meeting and what participants should do. Second listening: ask for day, time, place, item to bring and what an absent student should do. Answers: Friday; 3 p.m.; Room 6; a short passage for discussion; inform the organiser by Thursday. If a student confuses Thursday with the meeting day, replay the last sentence and compare the two functions.

## Speaking exercise

Ask each student to give a 30-second invitation using a topic, date, time and place. Use placeholders when real arrangements have not been confirmed. Partners listen and repeat the key information, then ask one question. Evaluate whether the speaker's purpose and details were clear, whether the listener's summary was accurate, and whether the pair repaired a misunderstanding respectfully.

## Distinguish fact, inference and response

If a speaker says “I could not finish the reading because my bus was delayed”, the delay is the speaker's stated reason. “The speaker is lazy” is an unsupported judgement. A constructive response could ask what support is needed or agree on the next step, without pretending to know the person's intentions. A good listener reports the statement accurately before evaluating it.

course-2:2.text:
# Unit 3: Reading Skills
Communicative English · Semester 1

## Learning outcomes
Students should be able to identify a main idea and supporting detail, choose an appropriate reading strategy, infer a word’s meaning from context and use common vocabulary relationships accurately.

## General and technical comprehension
Comprehension means constructing meaning from a text. For a general passage, identify the topic, main idea, supporting details, purpose and tone. Technical texts may contain specialised vocabulary, definitions, diagrams, procedures and qualifications. Read headings first; identify important terms; then check what a table, condition or warning actually says. An inference is a reasonable conclusion supported by the text, not a guess detached from evidence.

## Four reading strategies
• Skimming: reading rapidly for a broad idea or structure. Example: preview headings and opening sentences to decide whether an article addresses your topic.
• Scanning: searching for a specific item. Example: locate a date or room number in a timetable.
• Intensive reading: careful, detailed reading of a selected passage to understand its argument, language or evidence. Example: analyse a difficult paragraph in a literary essay.
• Extensive reading: reading larger amounts, often for overall understanding or pleasure, rather than analysing every item in detail. Example: regularly reading graded stories or longer articles.
Strategies can be combined: skim an article, scan for a definition and then read a relevant section intensively.

## Vocabulary in context
Before reaching for a dictionary, look for clues: a definition, example, contrast, synonym or explanation nearby. Then check whether your guess fits the sentence and verify it in a reliable dictionary. Word families also help: communicate, communication and communicative share a root but have different grammatical functions. Record a word with its meaning, pronunciation, example and relevant usage—not just a translation.

## Idioms and phrases
An idiom is an expression whose meaning is not always predictable from its individual words. “Once in a blue moon” means very rarely; “break the ice” means make an awkward social situation easier. Context and register matter: idioms can confuse a formal or international audience. A phrase is a group of words functioning together, such as “in the morning”; not every phrase is an idiom.

## Synonyms and antonyms
Synonyms have similar meanings in a particular context, but are not always interchangeable: “slim” and “thin” can carry different associations. Antonyms express contrast, such as “clear/unclear” or “early/late.” Check tone, grammar and context before substitution.

## Worked comprehension exercise
Passage: “The college library extended its evening hours during examination week. More students used the reading room, but the librarian reminded them that discussion rooms still needed to be booked in advance.”
1. Main idea? The library changed its hours during examination week and gave a reminder about room booking.
2. What must be booked? Discussion rooms.
3. Can we conclude every student used the library? No. The passage says more students used the reading room, not all students.
4. Which strategy finds the booking requirement quickly? Scanning; read the relevant sentence carefully to confirm it.

## Thirty idioms and phrases in context
These are informal unless context suggests otherwise; meanings depend on use.
1. Break the ice — ease an awkward beginning. A game helped break the ice.
2. Once in a blue moon — very rarely. We eat out once in a blue moon.
3. A piece of cake — very easy. After practice, the task was a piece of cake.
4. Under the weather — feeling unwell. Ravi stayed home because he felt under the weather.
5. In the same boat — in a similar difficulty. We are all in the same boat before exams.
6. On the right track — progressing correctly. Your outline is on the right track.
7. Hit the books — study hard. I must hit the books tonight.
8. A blessing in disguise — an apparent problem that proves beneficial. Missing the bus was a blessing in disguise when the later journey met an old friend.
9. Better late than never — a late action is preferable to none. She returned the book late, but better late than never.
10. Call it a day — stop working for now. We finished the draft and called it a day.
11. Get the ball rolling — begin an activity. The chair asked a question to get the ball rolling.
12. Give a hand — help. Could you give me a hand with these chairs?
13. In hot water — in trouble. He was in hot water for missing the deadline.
14. Keep an eye on — watch or monitor. Please keep an eye on the oven.
15. Learn the ropes — learn the basic procedures. New volunteers learn the ropes from experienced members.
16. Make ends meet — manage to pay essential expenses. Rising costs made it difficult to make ends meet.
17. On cloud nine — very happy. She was on cloud nine after hearing the good news.
18. Out of the blue — unexpectedly. An old friend called out of the blue.
19. See eye to eye — agree. The committee did not see eye to eye on the plan.
20. Speak of the devil — said when a person being discussed appears. Speak of the devil: here is Meena now.
21. Spill the beans — reveal a secret. Arun spilled the beans about the surprise.
22. Take something with a pinch of salt — treat it sceptically. Take that unverified rumour with a pinch of salt.
23. The ball is in your court — it is your turn to act. I have sent the proposal; the ball is in your court.
24. Time flies — time seems to pass quickly. Time flies when we are busy.
25. Turn over a new leaf — start behaving better or differently. He decided to turn over a new leaf and arrive on time.
26. Up in the air — undecided. The venue is still up in the air.
27. By and large — generally. By and large, the session went well.
28. At short notice — with little warning. The room was changed at short notice.
29. In advance — before the event. Please book the room in advance.
30. In the long run — over a longer period. Regular practice can help in the long run.

## Thirty synonym pairs
Meanings are approximate and context-sensitive: 1. begin/start; 2. end/finish; 3. quick/rapid; 4. small/little; 5. large/big; 6. silent/quiet; 7. happy/glad; 8. sad/unhappy; 9. brave/courageous; 10. reply/answer; 11. help/assist; 12. choose/select; 13. correct/accurate; 14. difficult/hard; 15. easy/simple; 16. honest/truthful; 17. idea/notion; 18. aim/purpose; 19. error/mistake; 20. gift/present; 21. safe/secure; 22. shut/close; 23. rich/wealthy; 24. tidy/neat; 25. vacant/empty; 26. angry/cross; 27. beautiful/lovely; 28. old/aged; 29. strange/unusual; 30. careful/cautious. Check grammar and connotation before substituting.

## Thirty antonym pairs
1. early/late; 2. open/closed; 3. hot/cold; 4. high/low; 5. near/far; 6. wide/narrow; 7. large/small; 8. fast/slow; 9. clean/dirty; 10. full/empty; 11. strong/weak; 12. rich/poor; 13. kind/cruel; 14. happy/sad; 15. begin/end; 16. accept/reject; 17. arrive/depart; 18. borrow/lend; 19. buy/sell; 20. build/demolish; 21. increase/decrease; 22. include/exclude; 23. legal/illegal; 24. possible/impossible; 25. visible/invisible; 26. noisy/quiet; 27. safe/dangerous; 28. true/false; 29. generous/stingy; 30. permanent/temporary. Some contrasts depend on context.

## General comprehension: fictional passage
“The River Lane reading group started a monthly book exchange. Members place books on a table in the community hall and take another book to read. The organiser asks each person to return borrowed books at the next meeting. The group is looking for a volunteer to maintain a list of titles.”
1. How often does the exchange take place? 2. Where are books placed? 3. When are borrowed books due? 4. What help is needed? 5. Does the passage prove that every book is a novel?
Answers: 1. Monthly. 2. On a table in the community hall. 3. At the next meeting. 4. A volunteer to maintain a list of titles. 5. No; genres are not specified.

## Technical comprehension: fictional passage
“A rainwater tank has a filter at the inlet. The filter catches leaves before water enters the tank. A sensor signals when the water reaches the marked maximum level; a valve then closes the inlet. The sensor does not measure whether the water is safe to drink. The filter should be checked every month.”
1. What does the filter catch? 2. What happens at maximum level? 3. Does the sensor test drinking safety? 4. How often should the filter be checked? 5. Why must a reader not infer that the water is drinkable?
Answers: 1. Leaves. 2. The sensor signals and the valve closes the inlet. 3. No. 4. Monthly. 5. The passage explicitly says the sensor does not measure drinking safety; no safety test is described.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10 min: Explain purpose and four strategies. 10–20: Skim the passage and state its main idea. 20–30: Scan for details and distinguish inference from unsupported assumption. 30–40: Practise context clues and synonyms. 40–47: Students use two idioms in suitable contexts. 47–50: Exit ticket: explain one difference between skimming and scanning.

## Questions
How is intensive reading different from extensive reading? What is the difference between a main idea and detail? Why are synonyms not always interchangeable? Explain one idiom and use it in a sentence.

## Reading note
The linked Curtin University guide explains skimming, scanning and intensive reading. Consult the course textbook for additional vocabulary exercises.

course-2:2.title: Reading, vocabulary and comprehension · worked exercises
course-2:2.text:
# Reading, vocabulary and comprehension · worked exercises

## Mini-passage
“The college garden collects rainwater in a small tank. Volunteers water the young plants in the morning. The club hopes to add more shade next year, but it has not yet chosen a design.”

## Questions
1. What does the tank collect? 2. When do volunteers water plants? 3. Has a shade design been selected? 4. Skim: state the passage’s topic in one sentence. 5. Scan: locate the time word. 6. Can we conclude every college student volunteers? 7. In “a clear explanation,” suggest a context-appropriate synonym for clear; give an antonym for “early” in a time context.

## Answers
1. Rainwater. 2. In the morning. 3. No. 4. A college garden’s present work and plans. 5. “Morning.” 6. No: the passage says only “volunteers.” 7. “Understandable”; “late.” Other appropriate answers are possible.

## Skills
Skimming establishes overall meaning; scanning searches for a specific detail. Intensive reading studies wording and reasoning closely; extensive reading builds experience through larger quantities of reading. A technical text may require attention to definitions, diagrams, units and claims. An idiom’s meaning is conventional and may not be literal; always consider context.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish skim and scan. 10–20: read the mini-passage. 20–30: answer and justify. 30–40: infer cautiously and compare synonyms. 40–50: write one factual and one inferential question.

course-2:3.title: Unit 4 · Writing Skills
course-2:3.text:
# Unit 4: Writing Skills
Communicative English · Semester 1

## Learning outcomes
Students should be able to write clear sentences and paragraphs, correct common errors, and choose a suitable structure for essays, reports, letters, emails, notices, agendas and minutes.

## Functional grammar and common errors
Functional grammar considers how grammatical choices help communicate a purpose. A subject and finite verb normally need agreement: “The student writes” but “The students write.” Articles depend on meaning: “a book” introduces one non-specific book; “the book” identifies a particular book in context. Tense should suit the time and situation: “The meeting starts at ten” may refer to a scheduled future event. Punctuation helps readers understand structure; it is not decoration.

Common errors: “She go to class” → “She goes to class” (agreement). “He discussed about the issue” → “He discussed the issue” (discuss takes an object without “about”). “I am here since Monday” → “I have been here since Monday” when the state began in the past and continues now. Explain the reason and context; language use can vary across dialects and situations.

## Paragraphs and essays
A paragraph develops a central idea, often introduced in a topic sentence, followed by explanation and evidence or examples. Use transitions where helpful. Example: “Regular reading improves vocabulary. Readers meet words in meaningful contexts and see how they are used. A reading journal can help them review new words.”

An essay develops a larger argument: introduction (topic and central claim), body paragraphs (one related point each, with support) and conclusion (synthesis, not an unrelated new argument). Plan for audience and purpose; revise for organisation before proofreading individual sentences.

## Report writing
A report presents findings for a purpose and audience. Depending on instructions, include title, date, purpose, method or background, findings, conclusion and recommendations. Separate observed facts from interpretations; do not invent data. Example: a report on a campus workshop could state attendance from the verified register, summarise activities and recommend future improvements. Institutions may require different formats.

## Letters and email
Formal letter: sender/contact details if needed, date, recipient, subject where appropriate, salutation, concise body, courteous close and name. State the request clearly. Informal letter: adapt address, greeting and tone to a friend or family member; it still needs clear organisation. Email: use a specific subject line, appropriate greeting, short paragraphs, clear action or deadline and a name.

Sample formal email:
Subject: Request for a classroom projector on 12 August
Dear Sir or Madam,
Please arrange a projector for the English workshop on 12 August, from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. in Room 204. Kindly confirm whether it is available.
Thank you,
Anita Rao

## Notice, agenda and minutes
A notice informs a defined audience about an event or instruction. Include organisation, heading, date, what, when, where, who is concerned and contact or signature as required. An agenda lists topics to be considered before a meeting. Minutes record what happened after it: meeting details, attendance where required, decisions, assigned actions and deadlines. Minutes are not a verbatim transcript unless specifically required. Formats vary by institution and examination.

## Model formats and samples
All names, institutions, events and dates below are fictional classroom examples. Real documents must use verified details and any required institutional layout.

### Formal letter
Format: sender and date; recipient; subject; salutation; purpose and details; courteous request; closing and signature.
12 Lake Road, Malgudi
12 August 2026
The Librarian, Malgudi College
Subject: Request for a reading room
Dear Sir or Madam,
Our reading group requests the use of a room on 20 August from 3 to 4 p.m. Please let us know whether it is available and how to book it.
Yours faithfully,
Anita Rao, Group Secretary

### Informal letter
12 Lake Road, Malgudi
12 August 2026
Dear Leela,
Our reading group is planning a book exchange next week. I hope you can visit and tell us about the stories you enjoy. Write soon and let me know how your course is going.
With love,
Anita

### Notice
MALGUDI COLLEGE READING GROUP
NOTICE | 12 August 2026
Book exchange: 20 August, 3 p.m., Community Hall. Members may bring a book to exchange. Contact Anita Rao, group secretary.

### Agenda
Reading group meeting, 20 August 2026, 3 p.m., Community Hall
1. Welcome and apologies. 2. Review of previous actions. 3. Book-exchange arrangements. 4. Next meeting. 5. Closing.

### Minutes
Reading group meeting, 20 August 2026, Community Hall
Present: Anita Rao and Leela Das.
Decision: Members agreed to hold a book exchange next month.
Action: Anita will request a table by 27 August.
Next meeting: 10 September, 3 p.m.
Recorded by: Leela Das.
An agenda is prepared before a meeting; minutes record decisions afterwards.

### Report
Title: Report on the reading-group meeting
Date: 21 August 2026
Purpose: To record arrangements for a proposed exchange.
Source: The meeting minutes.
Findings: Members agreed to hold an exchange; a table still needs to be booked.
Recommendation: Confirm table availability before announcing the venue.
Prepared by: Leela Das.

### Paragraph
“A reading group gives people an opportunity to share ideas. Members can compare their responses and recommend books to one another. A regular meeting time can help the group continue its discussions.” The opening introduces the focus; the other sentences develop it.

### Short essay
Title: Why shared reading matters
Reading is often a private activity, but discussing a book can also be valuable. A reading group allows different interpretations to meet.
First, readers can explain what they noticed and ask one another questions. Second, the group can introduce members to books they might not otherwise choose. Respectful listening matters because readers may disagree.
Shared reading therefore adds conversation to individual reading. A welcoming group can make both activities more rewarding.

## Twenty common formal-writing errors
Each correction suits the stated context; alternatives and language varieties exist.
1. She go to class. → She goes to class. (agreement)
2. The students was ready. → The students were ready. (agreement)
3. Each student have a card. → Each student has a card. (agreement)
4. He discussed about the issue. → He discussed the issue. (verb pattern)
5. She gave me an advice. → She gave me some advice. (uncountable noun)
6. I have many information. → I have much information. (uncountable noun)
7. He is a honest man. → He is an honest man. (vowel sound)
8. I saw an university. → I saw a university. (consonant sound)
9. I am here since Monday. → I have been here since Monday. (continuing situation)
10. Yesterday she go home. → Yesterday she went home. (past form)
11. I look forward to meet you. → I look forward to meeting you. (preposition + -ing)
12. She is good in drawing. → She is good at drawing. (conventional combination)
13. The news are surprising. → The news is surprising. (agreement)
14. One of the books are missing. → One of the books is missing. (head noun)
15. I did not went. → I did not go. (base verb after did)
16. He can sings. → He can sing. (base verb after modal)
17. Where you are going? → Where are you going? (direct question order)
18. The class ended, we left. → The class ended, so we left. (comma splice)
19. Its raining. → It’s raining. (it is)
20. Please return the book’s. → Please return the books. (plural, not possession).

## 50-minute lesson
0–10 min: Correct three sentences. 10–20: Build a paragraph from a topic sentence and examples. 20–30: Compare a formal letter and an email. 30–40: Groups write a notice using who/what/when/where. 40–47: Turn a short meeting scenario into an agenda and one decision in the minutes. 47–50: Review clarity and audience.

## Practice with answers
1. Correct: “The students was ready.” → “The students were ready.”
2. Which comes before a meeting: agenda or minutes? Agenda; minutes record the meeting afterwards.
3. Improve the subject “Hello”: “Request for projector for English workshop.”
4. Write a report recommendation only after distinguishing evidence from opinion.

## Reading note
The linked Purdue guide compares professional writing genres and their purposes. Use the university’s exam instructions for any required layout.

course-2:3.text:
# Writing skills · models and editing practice

## Formal email model
Subject: Request to use the library room
Dear Librarian,
I am writing on behalf of the reading club to ask whether a room is available on [date] from [time] to [time]. Please let us know the booking procedure and any conditions.
Thank you for your help.
[Name]

The placeholders prevent invention of facts. Add an attachment only if it actually exists.

## Notice and minutes
Notice: “Reading Club Meeting | [Date and time] | [Room] | Members are invited to discuss the next reading selection. Contact: [name].” Minutes record what happened: “Members agreed to request a room. Action: the secretary will email the librarian by [date].” An agenda is a plan before a meeting; minutes are a record after it.

## Edit these
1. “The students is preparing a report.” 2. “Me and my friend has sent the email.” 3. “The meeting was held, we discussed books.”

## Suggested answers
1. “The students are preparing a report.” 2. “My friend and I have sent the email.” 3. “The meeting was held, and we discussed books,” or use two sentences. Follow institutional style and do not mark valid language varieties as inherently wrong.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify email purpose and audience. 10–20: write a subject and request. 20–30: compare agenda and minutes. 30–40: edit the sentences with reasons. 40–50: peer-check completeness and tone.

course-2:4.title: Unit 5 · Personality Development
course-2:4.text:
# Unit 5: Personality Development
Communicative English · Semester 1

## Learning outcomes
Students should be able to explain personal and interpersonal skills, use self-assessment to set a realistic goal, describe emotional intelligence, practise inclusive teamwork and identify a professional ethics issue.

## Personality development and soft skills
In this course, personality development can be understood as reflection on habits and the development of communication, confidence and interpersonal skills. It does not mean that everyone must be outgoing or adopt the same personality. Soft skills are transferable interpersonal and self-management skills such as listening, teamwork, adaptability and problem-solving. They complement subject knowledge and technical skills.

## Self-assessment
Self-assessment involves identifying strengths, areas for development, evidence and a next step. A simple plan: “I can explain ideas in a small group, but rush during presentations. For two weeks I will practise a three-minute talk, record it and ask a peer for one suggestion.” Goals should be specific and manageable; feedback is useful when it describes an observable behaviour rather than labelling a person.

## Emotional intelligence or emotional quotient
Emotional intelligence commonly refers to recognising and managing one’s own emotions and responding thoughtfully to others’ emotions. “Emotional quotient” or EQ is sometimes used as a label or score, but there is no single universally accepted test or one number that fully captures a person’s emotional abilities. In practice: notice frustration, pause, ask for clarification and respond without an attack. Empathy involves trying to understand another’s perspective; it does not mean assuming that you know their feelings.

## Body language
Posture, gesture, facial expression, space and tone can contribute to a message. A relaxed posture may help a speaker appear approachable in some situations. Interpret cues with care: customs, neurodiversity, disability and individual comfort differ. Never treat eye contact, crossed arms or a facial expression as reliable proof of honesty, confidence or intent. Ask respectful questions if a message is unclear.

## Leadership qualities
Leadership can involve setting a shared purpose, listening, allocating tasks fairly, making decisions, supporting others and taking responsibility. A leader who invites ideas, explains deadlines and checks what support is needed may improve group coordination. Leadership is not identical to speaking most or controlling every decision. Rotate roles so different students can practise facilitating, recording and reporting.

## Time management
List tasks, identify deadlines, estimate realistic time and break large tasks into smaller steps. Prioritise important work, add breaks and buffer time, and revise the plan when circumstances change. Example: prepare a presentation by selecting sources on Monday, drafting on Tuesday and rehearsing on Wednesday. Time management is a practical skill, not a guarantee that every student has equal resources or free time.

## Professional ethics
Professional ethics concerns responsible conduct in a role. Relevant principles include honesty, fairness, respect, confidentiality when appropriate, accountability and acknowledging sources. Example: if you use another author’s ideas in a presentation, credit the source; if a classmate shares private information, do not circulate it without a valid reason or consent. Follow institutional rules and seek guidance where obligations conflict.

## 50-minute lesson
0–8 min: Students list a strength and a skill to practise privately. 8–18: Discuss soft skills and observable examples. 18–28: Role-play a misunderstanding; pause, clarify and respond respectfully. 28–38: A group plans a task with rotated roles. 38–45: Build a realistic weekly plan. 45–50: Exit ticket: identify an ethical issue and one responsible response.

## Practice with suggested answers
1. A teammate is late: instead of assuming laziness, ask privately what happened and agree on a plan.
2. You use a quotation in slides: acknowledge the source and check wording.
3. A presentation is due next week: divide preparation into research, draft and rehearsal, allowing time for revision.

## Questions
How can self-assessment lead to an actionable goal? What is the difference between empathy and assuming another person’s feelings? Why should body language be interpreted cautiously? Give two leadership practices and one ethical responsibility.

## Reading note
The linked open textbook discusses communication and perception; use the prescribed course references for additional material on leadership and professional ethics.

course-2:4.title: Personality development · reflection and ethical practice
course-2:4.text:
# Personality development · reflection and ethical practice

## Learning aims
Practise self-assessment, constructive feedback, emotional awareness, teamwork, time planning and professional ethics. Personality is not a fixed checklist of ideal behaviour. A student should not be graded on disclosing personal feelings or conforming to one culturally preferred style.

## Scenarios
1. A group member misses a deadline. Draft a respectful check-in and a plan. 2. You notice a classmate interrupted repeatedly. What can a facilitator do? 3. You are offered an impressive statistic but cannot verify it before a presentation. What do you do? 4. List an urgent task, an important non-urgent task and a realistic rest break.

## Possible responses
1. Ask privately whether support or a revised timeline is needed, then agree on responsibilities. 2. Invite the interrupted person to continue without forcing them to speak. 3. Omit the claim or label it unverified and seek a source. 4. Answers vary; allocate specific time rather than treating busyness as success.

## Emotional awareness
Name a feeling privately if useful, pause and choose an appropriate response. Emotional intelligence is not a diagnosis or a promise of success; avoid inferring emotion from a single gesture. Leadership includes listening, shared responsibility and ethical decisions, not just speaking loudly.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: private self-reflection. 10–20: discuss a neutral teamwork scenario. 20–30: practise a check-in. 30–40: prioritise tasks. 40–50: write a realistic improvement goal.

course-3:0.title: Unit 1 · Reading Comprehension
course-3:0.text:
# Unit 1: Reading Comprehension
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Objectives
Identify main ideas and details; infer meaning using evidence; assess tone, style and rhetorical choices; use skimming, scanning, intensive and extensive reading purposefully.

## Main idea and supporting detail
The topic is what a passage is about; the main idea is what it says about that topic. Supporting details give reasons, examples or evidence. For each paragraph, ask: What is its function? Does it introduce a claim, explain, qualify or conclude? A good title captures the whole passage rather than a single example.

## Inference and critical evaluation
An inference is a conclusion reasonably supported by stated evidence, not a free guess. Notice words such as “some”, “may” and “often”: replacing them with “all”, “must” or “always” may make an answer too strong. Critical reading asks who makes the claim, what evidence is supplied, what assumptions are necessary and whether alternative explanations exist. A claim and proof are different.

## Strategies
Skim for the general direction and structure. Scan for a particular name, figure or term. Read intensively when the exact logic or wording matters. Extensive reading means reading larger quantities, often for broad understanding and vocabulary development. In an exam, preview the questions, read for overall sense and return to the relevant lines; strategy can vary with the test.

## Tone, style and devices
Tone is the writer’s attitude, for example cautious, critical or enthusiastic; support the answer with language from the passage. Style concerns how the writer uses language. Rhetorical devices include contrast, repetition, analogy, rhetorical question and irony. An analogy explains one thing by comparing it with another; it can clarify an argument but does not by itself prove it. Irony depends on context: do not call every humorous sentence ironic.

## Worked exercise
Passage: “The town library extended its weekend hours. Attendance increased, but staff observed that many visitors still had difficulty reaching the building because buses were infrequent. The council is considering a later bus service.”
1. Main idea: the library’s longer hours increased use, while transport remained a problem.
2. Detail: buses were infrequent.
3. Inference: transport may affect some people’s ability to use the library. We cannot infer that all non-users lack transport.
4. Has the council introduced a later bus? No; it is considering one.
5. Tone: informative and measured; the text reports changes and qualifications without exaggerated language.

## 50-minute class
0–10 min: explain topic, main idea and detail. 10–20: skim and title the passage. 20–30: scan for facts and justify an inference. 30–40: evaluate a stronger but unsupported claim. 40–47: identify tone and one rhetorical device in a second passage. 47–50: exit ticket: explain how to test an inference.

## Practice and revision
1. A passage reports one successful trial. Can we conclude a method always works? No; one trial does not establish universal success.
2. Which strategy locates an examination date? Scanning, followed by checking context.
3. Explain how a contrast contributes to an argument using a passage of your choice.

## Reading note
Practise with passages from different genres, including academic prose, reports and opinion writing. Do not assume every exam uses the same pattern or marking scheme.

course-3:1.title: Unit 2 · Functional Grammar
course-3:1.text:
# Unit 2: Functional Grammar
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Parts of speech
A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; a pronoun stands for a noun phrase; a verb expresses an action, state or relation; an adjective modifies a noun; an adverb often modifies a verb, adjective, clause or another adverb; a preposition links a noun phrase to another element; a conjunction connects words or clauses; an interjection expresses an immediate reaction. A word’s function depends on context: “book” is a noun in “a book” and a verb in “book a room.”

## Articles and prepositions
Use “a” before a consonant sound (“a university”) and “an” before a vowel sound (“an hour”); “the” usually identifies a specific or already understood referent. Some nouns in general statements take no article: “Books can help.” Prepositions express relationships, but usage is often conventional: “interested in”, “depend on”, “arrive at the station” and “arrive in Chennai.” Learn phrases in context, not as isolated lists.

## Subject–verb agreement
A singular subject generally takes a singular present-tense verb: “The student reads.” Plural: “The students read.” Find the actual subject, not just the nearest noun: “The list of books is on the table.” With “each”, agreement is normally singular: “Each student has a card.” Some collective nouns vary by dialect and meaning.

## Active and passive
Active: “The committee approved the plan.” Passive: “The plan was approved by the committee.” The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive; a form of “be” and a past participle are used. Retain tense when transforming. Passive is useful when the action or recipient matters more than the actor, but should not hide responsibility when the actor matters.

## Clauses, reported speech and phrasal verbs
A clause has a subject and predicate: “because it rained” is dependent; “the match stopped” can stand independently. “The match stopped because it rained” combines them. In reported speech, pronouns, time expressions and tense may change according to context: She said, “I am tired” → She said that she was tired. Backshift is common after a past reporting verb but is not automatic when a fact still holds. A phrasal verb combines a verb and particle: “look up a word”; “give up” means stop trying. Their meanings depend on context.

## Vocabulary relationships
An idiom is an expression whose meaning may not be predictable from its separate words; “once in a blue moon” means rarely. Synonyms are similar in a given context, not always interchangeable; antonyms express contrast. Use context to select the best answer.

## Practice with answers
1. “She is ___ honest person.” → an (initial vowel sound).
2. “The box of pencils ___ on the table.” → is (subject: box).
3. Change “They built the bridge in 2000” to passive. → “The bridge was built in 2000.”
4. “Because it rained” is a dependent clause; it needs an independent clause to complete that sentence.
5. Report “I am ready,” said Mira. → Mira said that she was ready, in an ordinary past-reporting context.
6. “Look up” in “look up the meaning” means search for information.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify parts of speech in context. 10–20: articles and agreement. 20–30: transform active/passive sentences. 30–40: clauses and reported speech. 40–47: contextual vocabulary. 47–50: one corrected sentence with explanation.

## Exam reminder
Read the complete sentence, identify its meaning and structure, and check agreement and tense after choosing an answer. Explanations above are introductory; context and accepted varieties matter.

course-3:2.title: Unit 3 · Written Communication
course-3:2.text:
# Unit 3: Written Communication
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Paragraphs and essays
A paragraph develops one central point with explanation and support. An essay typically introduces its topic and thesis, develops connected arguments in body paragraphs, and concludes by synthesising the response. For exam writing, interpret the instruction: “discuss” may require several perspectives, while “evaluate” requires reasoned judgement. Plan before writing.

## Description, narration and argument
Description presents features of a person, place or situation through selected details. Narration relates events in a meaningful sequence, using time markers where helpful. Argument makes a claim and supports it with reasons and evidence; acknowledge a relevant counterargument rather than misrepresenting it. Example: Claim: the college should extend library hours. Reason: students need access after class. Evidence should be a verified survey or usage record, not an invented statistic.

## Reports, letters and notes
A report’s headings depend on the question but may include purpose, method, findings and recommendations. A formal letter gives recipient and date as required, a clear purpose, supporting details and a courteous closing; an informal letter uses a tone appropriate to a personal relationship. Note-making selects main points and subpoints, using consistent abbreviations and a clear title or key when required.

## Summary, paraphrase and précis
A summary condenses the central ideas in fresh language. A paraphrase restates a selected passage in different words and structure while preserving its meaning and usually similar scope. A précis is a concise, coherent restatement of a longer passage’s essential argument; follow the exam’s word limit and format. In academic work, credit the original for summaries and paraphrases as well as quotations. Do not insert your own unsupported opinion into a neutral summary.

## Notice and poster
A notice conveys a specific announcement: organisation, heading, date, event or instruction, time, place, relevant audience and contact/signature as required. A poster combines brief text with visual hierarchy for an audience and purpose. Its format depends on the exam; include essential information rather than assuming decoration earns more marks than clarity.

## Worked example
Original: “The college opened a reading room in the evening. Students who worked during the day could use it after their shifts. The library plans to monitor attendance before deciding whether to continue.”
Possible summary: “The college is testing evening reading-room access to help working students and will review attendance before continuing.” This preserves the purpose and conditional future decision without claiming the service is permanent.

## 50-minute class
0–10: identify the purpose and audience of an essay. 10–20: draft a supported paragraph. 20–30: distinguish summary from paraphrase. 30–40: produce a notice with all key facts. 40–47: peer-review for omissions and invented details. 47–50: revise one sentence.

## Review
1. Difference between summary and paraphrase? A summary condenses central ideas; a paraphrase restates a selected passage with its meaning intact.
2. A notice must identify the event, time and place, among other required details.
3. Which claim is stronger: “The change is useful” or a claim with verifiable supporting evidence? The supported claim, assuming the evidence is relevant.

## Examination note
Follow the particular examination’s current word limits and marking instructions; the syllabus itself does not establish one universal format for all competitive exams.

course-3:3.title: Unit 4 · Listening and Speaking Skills
course-3:3.text:
# Unit 4: Listening and Speaking Skills
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Listening and hearing
Hearing is the perception of sound; listening includes attending, interpreting and responding. Listening helps candidates follow instructions, answer relevantly and understand other viewpoints. A useful routine is to focus, note key words, listen to the complete question, ask for clarification where permitted, and check the interpretation before responding.

## Effective speech
A clear speech suits the audience and purpose. Organise a central message, a few logically ordered points and a conclusion. Speak audibly at a comfortable pace, articulate key terms, and use examples accurately. Fluency does not require one accent or uninterrupted speech: effective communication is intelligible, appropriate and responsive. Avoid inventing facts or forcing unfamiliar vocabulary.

## Social exchanges and dialogue
Examples: greeting—“Good morning. How are you?”; request—“Could you please explain the next step?”; clarification—“Do you mean that the form is due on Monday?”; polite disagreement—“I see your point, but I think another factor matters.” Adapt formality to situation. A dialogue requires turn-taking as well as asking and answering questions.

## Persuasive arguments
A persuasive argument makes a specific claim and supplies reasons and appropriate support. Model: “The library should open later on two weekdays because many students have classes during the day. The college could pilot the change and review actual attendance.” Acknowledge limits: longer hours also need staffing and funding. A proposal does not become true merely because it is confidently delivered.

## Elocution
Elocution is the practice of clear and effective spoken delivery. In a short speech, mark pauses at meaningful boundaries, vary emphasis appropriately and rehearse for time. Interpret the speech’s purpose and audience. Volume, speed, stress and intonation can affect clarity; performance should not be judged by an arbitrary claim that only one accent is correct.

## Class practice
Pairs: one student gives three instructions for a campus event; the other paraphrases them before acting. Groups: give a one-minute persuasive proposal, followed by one question and a respectful answer. Elocution: read a short passage twice, first for meaning and then with deliberate pauses.

## Sample questions and responses
1. What is the difference between hearing and listening? Hearing is sound perception; listening actively attends to and interprets it.
2. Give an appropriate clarification. “Could you repeat the last date for submitting the form?”
3. Name two qualities of effective speech. Clear organisation and suitable pacing; other supported answers are possible.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: hearing and listening. 10–20: listening-and-paraphrase exercise. 20–30: social dialogue. 30–40: develop a claim and reason. 40–47: short delivery practice. 47–50: feedback on one specific behaviour.

## Exam reminder
Check the specific test’s interview or speaking instructions. Prepared scripts should not replace listening to the question actually asked.

course-3:4.title: Unit 5 · Study Skills
course-3:4.text:
# Unit 5: Study Skills
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Building vocabulary
Learn words in meaningful sentences. Record definition, part of speech, pronunciation, collocations and an example. Review across several sessions and use the word in your own writing. Check a dictionary when a meaning inferred from context is uncertain. Similar words may differ in register or collocation: accuracy matters more than using difficult words.

## Research and library tools
Begin with a focused question and useful keywords; add synonyms. A catalogue identifies items in a library’s collection. Books can offer sustained treatment; periodicals include journals and magazines, whose purposes vary. A bibliography lists works relevant to or used in a topic. An index helps locate a subject within a book or collection. Evaluate authorship, date, evidence and relevance before trusting a source. Search results are starting points, not automatic proof.

## Note-making and source use
Separate your own ideas from a source’s claims. Record author, title, publication details and page numbers as you read so you can return to the source. Use headings and concise points. Summarising condenses central ideas; paraphrasing restates a passage’s meaning in your own words and structure; quoting reproduces exact wording with quotation marks and an appropriate citation. All three require acknowledgement when using another person’s work. Follow the requested citation style rather than mixing systems.

## References list
A reference list gives readers enough information to locate cited material. Its exact order, punctuation and treatment of authors vary by style, such as MLA or APA. Check the edition of the relevant style guide and your teacher’s instructions. Do not fabricate missing publication information.

## Answering an exam question
1. Read the whole question and underline the task, topic and limits.
2. Allocate time in proportion to marks, while following the exam’s rules.
3. Draft a brief plan: direct answer, relevant points, examples and conclusion where needed.
4. Write legibly and stay within the requested scope; avoid memorised material that does not answer the question.
5. Reserve time to check meaning, omissions, calculations where relevant and grammar.
6. Evaluate your answer against the question and marking guidance, not merely its length.

## Worked example
Question: “Explain two barriers to listening and suggest a response to each.” A relevant plan has two barrier–response pairs: noise → move to a quieter space; unfamiliar terminology → ask for definitions and an example. A generic essay about communication that omits responses does not fully answer the task.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: vocabulary log. 10–20: catalogue, index and bibliography. 20–30: summary versus paraphrase and quote. 30–40: plan an answer to the example. 40–47: peer-check for both required responses. 47–50: self-assessment.

## Questions
Why do paraphrases need citation? What is the difference between a library catalogue and a book index? How can a student use a question’s command words when planning?

## Reading note
The Purdue research guide explains source use. Citation requirements depend on the assignment or exam.

course-4:0.title: Unit I · Working with Grammar
course-4:0.text:
# Unit I: Working with Grammar
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Sentence construction and types
A basic complete sentence has a subject and a finite verb and expresses a complete thought: “The students are discussing the poem.” Sentences can make statements, ask questions, issue requests or commands, and express strong feeling. They may be simple (one independent clause), compound (independent clauses joined) or complex (an independent clause with a dependent clause). In conversation, shorter fragments can also be meaningful in context.

## Parts of speech and auxiliaries
Nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections perform different roles. Auxiliary verbs help form questions, negatives, tense, aspect or modality: “Do you read?”, “She is speaking”, “They have arrived”, “We can try.” Match the auxiliary to the intended meaning; “can” often expresses ability or possibility, while “must” can express strong obligation or inference depending on context.

## Number, agreement and determiners
Singular: “A student is ready.” Plural: “Students are ready.” The subject determines verb agreement: “The quality of the answers is important.” Determiners specify or quantify nouns: a/an, the, this, these, some, many and each. “A university” and “an hour” show that a/an depends on initial sound, not spelling. Context matters when choosing “some” or “any.”

## Active and passive; comparison
Active: “The teacher asked a question.” Passive: “A question was asked by the teacher.” Preserve tense and meaning when changing voice. Comparison: “clear, clearer, clearest”; “important, more important, most important.” Irregular forms include good, better, best. Avoid doubling the comparative: “more better” is not standard edited English.

## Punctuation and common usage
Written speech transcripts still need appropriate capitals, full stops, question marks and commas. Speech itself uses pauses and intonation, not visible punctuation. Compare “She speaks clearly” with “Does she speak clearly?” Common standard-form corrections: “He go” → “He goes”; “She is senior than me” → “She is senior to me.” Do not equate a regional accent with a grammatical error.

## Practice with answers
1. Form a question: “You are ready.” → “Are you ready?”
2. Agree: “Each student ___ a notebook.” → has.
3. Passive: “They completed the task.” → “The task was completed.”
4. Compare: “This road is ___ than that road.” → longer, or another suitable comparative adjective.
5. Identify the auxiliary in “She has finished.” → has.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: construct sentences from word cards. 10–20: auxiliaries and question formation. 20–30: agreement in a dialogue. 30–40: active and passive role-play. 40–47: comparison and corrections. 47–50: exit ticket with one explanation.

## Review
How does an auxiliary help form a question? Why does “list” rather than “books” control agreement in “the list of books is”? When is passive voice useful?

course-4:1.title: Unit II · Vocabulary Building and Pronunciation
course-4:1.text:
# Unit II: Vocabulary Building and Pronunciation
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Word formation
Prefixes attach before a base (un + clear → unclear); suffixes attach after it (teach + er → teacher). Some word classes change through suffixes: decide (verb), decision (noun), decisive (adjective). Form and meaning are not always predictable, so check a dictionary. A compound joins elements, as in “classroom”; spelling conventions differ.

## Word relationships and use
Synonyms are similar in context (begin/start); antonyms contrast (possible/impossible). Homonyms are words with the same spelling or sound but different meanings; terminology varies between dictionaries. For example “bank” can mean a financial institution or the side of a river. One-word substitutes condense a definition: a person who writes poems is a poet. For odd-one-out questions, identify a defensible shared feature: rose, jasmine, lotus, carrot → carrot is a vegetable while the others are commonly classified as flowers.

Idioms may have non-literal meanings: “break the ice” means ease an awkward beginning. Practise joining sentences with appropriate relationships: “It rained. We stayed indoors.” → “Because it rained, we stayed indoors.” Do not join clauses in a way that changes the original meaning.

## Vowels and consonants
Speech sounds are made by the vocal organs; spelling and sound do not correspond one-to-one in English. Vowels generally involve relatively open airflow, while consonants involve some obstruction or narrowing. A phoneme is a sound category that can distinguish meaning in a language or variety. Pronunciation varies legitimately across Englishes, so use a suitable model and seek intelligibility rather than erasing a speaker’s accent.

## Word stress, sentence stress and intonation
Word stress makes one syllable more prominent: in a common pronunciation, REcord is a noun and reCORD is a verb. Check the dictionary for the variety being taught. Sentence stress highlights information relevant to meaning: “I wanted the RED book” contrasts colour. Intonation is the movement of pitch across an utterance; a question may rise or fall depending on its form, meaning and context. Do not present one pitch pattern as universal for every question.

## Practice with answers
1. Change “happy” to a noun: happiness.
2. Antonym of “accept” in many contexts: reject.
3. Join: “She was tired. She completed the work.” → “Although she was tired, she completed the work.”
4. Explain “bank” in “river bank”: land alongside a river.
5. Say “I asked for the RED pen” and then “I asked for the red PEN”; discuss which contrast each emphasis suggests.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: form word families. 10–20: synonyms, antonyms and idioms in context. 20–30: listen and identify prominent syllables. 30–40: practise sentence emphasis and intonation in pairs. 40–47: join sentences with logical connectors. 47–50: record one new word and example.

## Review
Why does spelling not always predict pronunciation? How can sentence stress change the information highlighted? Why should students hear more than one intelligible variety of English?

course-4:2.title: Unit III · Conversational Skills
course-4:2.text:
# Unit III: Conversational Skills
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Beginning and sustaining conversation
A conversation involves listening, responding and taking turns. In a new setting, greet the person, introduce yourself and ask a relevant open or closed question. Example: “Good morning. I’m Meena from the English department. How did you find the workshop?” Follow up using what the person actually says. Respect the other person’s willingness to talk; a conversation is not a list of memorised questions.

## Asking and answering questions
Closed questions often invite a short answer: “Is the library open?” Open questions invite explanation: “What did you find useful about the session?” Use “Could you repeat that?” or “Do you mean…?” to clarify. Answer directly first, then add a relevant detail. Politeness depends on relationship and context, not a fixed formula alone.

## Description
For a person, choose relevant details such as role, interests or observed behaviour; avoid unnecessary assumptions about appearance or identity. For a place, orient the listener and select significant features. For an event, identify what happened, where, when and why it mattered. Example: “The seminar was held in the library on Tuesday. Students discussed how to evaluate online sources.”

## Extempore, persuasive and descriptive speaking
Extempore speaking uses limited preparation; take a moment to organise an opening, two points and a closing. A persuasive talk makes a claim and supports it with reasons and evidence. A descriptive talk helps the listener visualise a subject through purposeful detail. In all cases, adapt your voice, vocabulary and length to the audience; neither loudness nor an unfamiliar accent is a measure of the quality of ideas.

## Narration and character
A narrative usually establishes setting and characters, presents a sequence or problem and describes an outcome. Use time markers such as “first,” “later” and “finally” where useful. To describe a character, distinguish a stated fact from an interpretation: “She returns the lost book” is an action; “she is considerate” is an interpretation supported by that action. Explain situations without presenting an assumption as a fact.

## Model activity
Tell a one-minute account: “On Monday, our class planned a reading event. At first, the room was unavailable. We spoke to the librarian, found another space and held the event on Friday. The experience showed us the value of planning alternatives.” Listeners identify setting, problem, action and outcome; then ask one clarification question.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introductions in pairs. 10–20: open and closed questions. 20–30: describe a place without naming it; partner asks questions. 30–40: one-minute narration. 40–47: brief persuasive speech with one reason. 47–50: constructive peer feedback.

## Questions
What makes a follow-up question effective? How does a descriptive speech differ from a persuasive one? What evidence supports a claim about a fictional character?

course-4:3.title: Unit IV · Group Communication
course-4:3.text:
# Unit IV: Group Communication
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Group discussion
A group discussion is a structured exchange in which participants contribute to a shared purpose. It is not a competition to speak most. Begin by identifying the question and time available. Participants offer relevant points, listen, support claims with examples, respond to others and help the group summarise its position. If disagreement occurs, address the idea rather than attacking the person.

Useful expressions: “Could we define the problem first?” “I would like to add…” “What evidence supports that?” “We seem to agree on two points, but differ on the third.” A facilitator can invite a quieter member without forcing anyone to disclose personal information.

## Assigning tasks and leadership
Divide a task into manageable roles: facilitator, researcher, timekeeper, note-taker and presenter are possible examples. Explain each role, expected output and deadline. Rotate responsibilities so all students practise speaking and coordination. A leader checks progress, clarifies uncertainty and shares decisions; leadership need not mean doing all the work.

## Task completion and cohesion
Example task: plan a college reading event. Agree on audience, venue, budget assumptions, responsibilities and deadline. Each participant reports progress, identifies obstacles and asks for help where needed. Summarise decisions in writing. Group cohesion means a sense of shared purpose and respectful cooperation, not an obligation to agree on everything. Clear goals, fair participation and constructive conflict resolution can support it.

## Group presentations and slides
Organise the presentation with an introduction, coordinated sections and a conclusion. Rehearse transitions between speakers and keep to the allotted time. Slides should support, not replace, speech: use readable text, clear headings and relevant visuals, and credit sources. Do not overload slides or read every word aloud. Check accessibility, including contrast and descriptions of important visuals; provide materials in accessible formats when needed. Slide software is one possible tool, not a prerequisite for every presentation.

## 50-minute lesson
0–8: explain discussion purpose and roles. 8–15: assign roles for the reading-event task. 15–30: groups plan and record decisions. 30–42: each group presents for three minutes. 42–47: peers provide one strength and one improvement. 47–50: members reflect on whether everyone had an opportunity to contribute.

## Assessment checklist
Was the response relevant? Did the student listen and build on a point? Were reasons understandable? Was speaking time shared? Did the group report decisions accurately? Feedback should focus on observable actions, not assumptions about personality or accent.

## Questions
What is the difference between leadership and domination? How can roles improve accountability? What makes a slide useful? How can a group disagree respectfully?

course-4:4.title: Unit V · Listening Skills and Non-verbal Communication
course-4:4.text:
# Unit V: Listening Skills and Non-verbal Communication
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Why listening matters
Listening supports comprehension, cooperation and accurate responses. Hearing sound is not the same as understanding it. Active listening includes paying attention, recognising the speaker’s purpose, paraphrasing a key point and requesting clarification. It does not require agreement with everything said.

## Basics and barriers
Listen first for the situation and general message; then note important details, distinctions and the speaker’s purpose. Noise, a poor audio connection, unfamiliar vocabulary, fatigue, stress, prejudice and rehearsing a reply can interfere.
