What does Michel’s theory of exceptional people do for him? How does the focus on hands shape our understanding? What different meanings might Jeanne’s visit have?

## Before class
Read the prescribed essay or view the assigned film in the department’s edition. These notes are teaching aids, not replacements for the work; interpretations should be tested against specific passages or shots.

course-17:3.title: Jean-Luc Godard · Breathless
course-17:3.text:
# Jean-Luc Godard · Breathless
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Story
In Breathless (1960), small-time criminal Michel Poiccard steals a car and kills a police officer during a pursuit. He reaches Paris and reconnects with Patricia, an American student and aspiring journalist selling newspapers. He tries to obtain money and persuade her to leave with him for Italy, while the police search for him.

Their time together includes extended conversations about love, freedom, identity and their uncertain relationship. Patricia is attracted to Michel but also questions what she feels and what his criminal situation means. The police contact her. Eventually she informs them of Michel’s whereabouts and tells him what she has done. Michel does not initially flee. When the police arrive he is shot and collapses in the street. His final words are difficult for Patricia to understand and vary in translation; she repeats a gesture associated with him and addresses a question about the word used. The film does not make her motives or the meaning of the final exchange completely transparent.

## Technique and context
The film is associated with the French New Wave. Jump cuts can interrupt apparent continuity within a scene, making editing noticeable. Location shooting, references to cinema and a loose crime narrative combine familiarity with disruption. Michel’s imitation of American gangster style is an example of intertextuality: another film tradition becomes part of his self-presentation.

## Teaching questions
How does the film use and unsettle crime-film expectations? What do the jump cuts do to time and movement? How do Michel and Patricia imagine freedom differently? How might different subtitles affect interpretation of the final scene?

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce the French New Wave. 10–22: outline the pursuit and relationship. 22–35: examine editing and cinema references. 35–45: discuss Patricia’s decision without assuming a single motive. 45–50: exit ticket on form and effect.

## Before class
Read the prescribed essay or view the assigned film in the department’s edition. These notes are teaching aids, not replacements for the work; interpretations should be tested against specific passages or shots.

course-17:4.title: Reading film as text · form, discourse and ideology
course-17:4.text:
# Reading film as text · form, discourse and ideology
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## What does “film as text” mean?
A film can be treated as an organised object of interpretation, not because it is literally a written page, but because images, sounds, performances and narrative relations can be analysed. An interpretation begins with precise description: identify a scene, what is visible and audible, the sequence of shots and relevant context.

## Discourse and ideology
A discourse is a way of organising language, images and assumptions around a subject. Ask how a film makes some statements or identities appear obvious and others difficult to express. Ideology refers to patterns of ideas and practices connected with power; a film can negotiate conflicting positions rather than expressing one simple message. Analysis needs evidence from form and context, not just a label.

## Step-by-step method
1. Describe a specific moment: who is present, what happens and what is heard?
2. Identify a formal choice: framing, duration, camera angle, lighting, editing, sound or performance.
3. Explain a possible effect: what does the choice invite a viewer to notice or feel?
4. Connect it to representation or power while recognising alternative readings.
5. Check the film’s historical and production context. A claim about an audience’s actual response needs audience evidence; it cannot be proven from the shot alone.

## Example
A character framed alone in a crowded station might suggest isolation. That is an interpretation supported by composition, not proof of what every viewer feels. Compare the scene’s sound and neighbouring shots before deciding whether the interpretation holds.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish description and interpretation. 10–20: define discourse and ideology. 20–35: analyse a brief film scene in pairs. 35–45: compare two interpretations and their evidence. 45–50: exit ticket on one formal feature and a supported effect.

## Before class
Read the prescribed essay or view the assigned film in the department’s edition. These notes are teaching aids, not replacements for the work; interpretations should be tested against specific passages or shots.

course-17:4.title: Ray, Pandian and Prasad · studying Indian cinema
course-17:4.text:
# Ray, Pandian and Prasad · studying Indian cinema
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Satyajit Ray: What Is Wrong with Indian Films?
In this historically situated critical essay, Ray argues that filmmaking needs imagination, planning and sensitivity to the medium rather than a reliance on imitation or technical gloss. He criticises aspects of contemporary production and calls for films grounded in the contexts they represent. Treat this as Ray’s argument from a particular historical moment, not a timeless verdict on all Indian films. Ask whether his ideas of realism and national style exclude other valuable forms, including popular song-and-dance cinema.

## M. S. S. Pandian: Tamil Cultural Elites and Cinema
Pandian’s essay examines relations between Tamil cultural elites and cinema. A productive starting question is how judgements about taste, respectability, popular entertainment and realism can be connected to caste and class. Do not assume that “elite” describes every person or that one attitude exhausts Tamil film history. Read the article for its historical examples and specific argument before attributing a detailed claim to it.

## M. Madhava Prasad: Ideology of the Hindi Film
Prasad’s study connects cinematic forms to political and economic history. One important concept, “feudal family romance,” helps analyse how certain narratives organise authority through family and social hierarchy, even as they also include modern desires and institutions. It is an analytical category for particular films and historical conditions, not a claim that all Hindi films have one plot. A scholarly review linked below also questions aspects of the historical fit; engage with disagreement rather than treating a framework as a formula.

## Compare and discuss
How does Ray’s judgement of style differ from Pandian’s analysis of cultural authority? How might Prasad connect a family ending to a wider structure of power? Use a scene and the assigned reading to substantiate the comparison.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define historical context. 10–22: identify Ray’s claim. 22–32: discuss who gets to define good taste. 32–42: apply a family-authority question to a film scene. 42–50: exit ticket distinguishing an author’s argument from your own.

## Reading limitation
This is an introductory comparison. Read the specific prescribed extracts for full arguments, historical examples and qualifications.

## Before class
Read the prescribed essay or view the assigned film in the department’s edition. These notes are teaching aids, not replacements for the work; interpretations should be tested against specific passages or shots.

course-17:4.title: Satyajit Ray · Pather Panchali
course-17:4.text:
# Satyajit Ray · Pather Panchali
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Introduction
Pather Panchali (1955) is Satyajit Ray’s Bengali film adapted from Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay’s novel. The film follows a family in rural Bengal through everyday pleasures, poverty and bereavement. This note describes the film, not every event of the novel.

## Story from beginning to end
Harihar Ray, a priest and aspiring writer, struggles to support his family. His wife Sarbajaya manages the household and cares for their daughter Durga; an elderly relative, Indir Thakrun, also lives with them at times. Sarbajaya’s frustration with scarce resources contributes to conflict with Indir, while Durga shares affection and small treats with her.

Apu is born and grows up close to his older sister. The children explore their surroundings, watch travelling entertainers and follow a sweet seller they cannot afford. In a celebrated sequence they move through fields and discover a passing train. Their curiosity and delight coexist with the family’s economic difficulties. Indir leaves after conflict and dies away from the house; the children encounter her body.

Harihar travels in search of work, leaving Sarbajaya to manage an increasingly difficult situation. Durga is accused of stealing a neighbour’s necklace. During the monsoon the children enjoy the rain, but Durga falls ill and dies during a violent storm while her father is away. Do not infer a particular medical diagnosis from a short plot summary.

Harihar returns with gifts, not knowing of the death. When he shows the sari he has bought for Durga, Sarbajaya breaks down and he learns what has happened. As the family prepares to leave, Apu discovers the necklace hidden among Durga’s belongings and throws it into a pond. Harihar, Sarbajaya and Apu depart their village by cart for a new life. The film’s ending does not show the events of the later Apu films.

## Form and interpretation
Attention to landscape, sound, faces, everyday action and changes in pace gives small events weight. The train can be read as an image of discovery and a wider changing world; support an interpretation with the scene rather than treating a single symbolism as compulsory. Sarbajaya’s harshness and tenderness should be considered alongside the pressures she faces.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce family and adaptation. 10–25: map the children’s experiences and the family’s pressures. 25–35: discuss one use of sound or landscape. 35–45: analyse the homecoming and departure. 45–50: exit response on a detail and its effect.

## Questions
How does the film combine play with hardship? What changes when Harihar returns? Why might Apu throw the necklace away?

## Before class
Read the prescribed essay or view the assigned film in the department’s edition. These notes are teaching aids, not replacements for the work; interpretations should be tested against specific passages or shots.

course-17:4.title: Anand Patwardhan · Jai Bhim Comrade
course-17:4.text:
# Anand Patwardhan · Jai Bhim Comrade
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Introduction and content note
Jai Bhim Comrade (2011) is a documentary by Anand Patwardhan made over many years. It addresses caste discrimination, police violence and the politics of Dalit cultural expression. The film includes accounts of deaths and suicide; offer a content note and allow sensitive discussion.

## Structure and major subjects
The documentary takes the 1997 police firing in Mumbai’s Ramabai Ambedkar Nagar as a starting point. Residents had protested the desecration of a statue of B. R. Ambedkar; police opened fire, killing people. The film connects this event with the death of Dalit poet and singer Vilas Ghogre, who died by suicide after the violence.

Rather than following a single fictional plot, the film moves among testimony, songs, archival materials, political gatherings and arguments about caste, labour and collective action. It attends to Ambedkar’s legacy and to tensions and alliances in Dalit and left politics. Interviews and songs allow speakers to articulate experiences and positions, while selection, editing and the filmmaker’s perspective shape how audiences encounter them. The documentary’s construction does not by itself make the events imaginary or the testimony unimportant.

## Key approaches
Ask who is speaking, what knowledge they claim, how the film positions their testimony, and how a song differs from an interview in its emotional and political work. Avoid presenting Dalit communities as passive objects: the film records organised protest and cultural production. Historical claims about the police firing and legal proceedings should be checked against reliable reporting as well as the film.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: establish respectful discussion and historical context. 10–22: outline the event and the documentary’s scope. 22–35: analyse an interview or song in a suitable excerpt. 35–45: discuss editing, evidence and filmmaker position. 45–50: exit ticket distinguishing a documented event from an interpretation.

## Questions
What can song communicate that an interview may not? How can a documentary be constructed and still investigate real events? How does the film relate caste to political organising?

## Before class
Read the prescribed essay or view the assigned film in the department’s edition. These notes are teaching aids, not replacements for the work; interpretations should be tested against specific passages or shots.

course-18:0.title: Content writing · purpose, audience and process
course-18:0.text:
# Content writing · purpose, audience and process
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 1

## What is content writing?
Content writing creates written material for a defined audience and purpose: to explain, inform, help a reader complete a task, build a relationship or support an action. Forms include web pages, articles, newsletters, reports, case studies and product information. Not every piece is an advertisement. A good content writer works with subject specialists, editors, designers and publishers, and checks that claims are supported.

## Role and responsibilities
A writer interprets a brief, researches, identifies the audience’s questions, structures information, drafts, edits and adapts the work to its medium. Responsibilities include accuracy, accessible language, respectful representation, source acknowledgement, deadlines and adherence to the organisation’s style guide. An editor or subject expert may review specialist claims; a writer should not invent credentials or first-hand experience.

## Print and web
A print reader may encounter a continuous page sequence; a web reader may arrive directly at one section from a search or link. Online headings, informative link text and mobile-friendly paragraphs help navigation. Print also needs clear structure. Neither medium requires a fixed sentence length or arbitrary word count. Search engine optimisation (SEO) can make useful content easier to discover, but repeated keywords and empty claims do not substitute for helping the reader.

## The content process
1. Brief: define audience, topic, desired outcome, format, deadline, evidence and approval process.
2. Research: use reliable sources, note publication dates and record links or references.
3. Structure: arrange the answer in a useful order and identify gaps.
4. Draft: use clear headings, examples and a consistent voice.
5. Review: verify claims, links, accessibility, rights and style.
6. Publish and maintain: correct errors and revisit information when circumstances change.

## Worked example
Brief: “Help first-year students find library books.” Audience: new students. Outcome: find a book and know whom to ask. Outline: catalogue search, understanding availability, finding the shelf, requesting help. Do not invent the library’s hours or rules; verify them locally.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare information and persuasion. 10–20: identify audience and purpose in a brief. 20–30: draft a practical outline. 30–42: write the opening and one section. 42–50: peer-check usefulness and identify two facts requiring verification.

## Check yourself
What distinguishes audience from purpose? How does a web heading help a reader? Why is publishing not the end of the process?

course-18:1.title: Content formats · research, drafting and editing
course-18:1.text:
# Content formats · research, drafting and editing
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 2

## From brief to draft
Clarify the reader, objective, length, medium, deadline and constraints. Generate ideas, then research before choosing the strongest supported ones. Organise a logical outline and write a draft. Check the style sheet for spelling, punctuation, capitalisation, terminology, tone and citation conventions. Edit structure and flow before proofreading individual errors.

## Formats and purposes
An essay develops an idea or argument with explanations and evidence. A report presents information or findings for a defined purpose, often with sections and recommendations. Newspaper writing gives readers relevant verified information, distinguishes reporting from opinion and answers important questions clearly. Advertising aims to persuade and should not disguise unsupported claims as facts.

A blog can explain, reflect, report or advise; a useful post has a clear topic, helpful headings and sources where appropriate. A case study describes a particular situation, the action taken and the results, supported by evidence and permission; do not invent customer outcomes. A white paper explores a complex issue or proposed solution in detail and should distinguish evidence from a company’s promotional interest.

## Corporate writing
B2B addresses organisations; a reader may need compatibility, procurement and implementation details. B2C addresses individual consumers; a reader may need price, availability and practical benefits. Neither audience is uniform. A press release gives newsworthy, verifiable information with an attributable contact and date; it is not a guarantee of media coverage. A newsletter selects useful updates for subscribers and makes any promotional purpose clear.

## Tone, jargon and market research
Choose a formal or informal register for the reader and context. Explain necessary specialist terms; avoid jargon used only to sound impressive. Market research can include interviews, surveys and analysis of common questions, but respect consent and privacy. Separate verified findings from assumptions about the audience.

## Example: one fact in two formats
Verified event information: a library workshop is on Friday at 4 p.m. A news brief reports the event and source. An invitation might say, “Join the library workshop on Friday at 4 p.m.” Neither version should invent a venue, registration link or promised outcome.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: unpack a brief. 10–20: compare blog, report and press release. 20–32: outline a case study without fabricating results. 32–42: revise for audience and style sheet. 42–50: exchange proofreading checklists and write one evidence question.

## Questions
How does a case study differ from a white paper? Why can a B2B reader still need plain language? What should be checked before a press release is sent?

course-18:2.title: Visual and interactive content
course-18:2.text:
# Visual and interactive content
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 3

## Visual content
An infographic combines visual organisation with information to make relationships or processes easier to understand. Begin with a clear point and reliable data; label units, dates and sources. Avoid misleading scales, distorted comparisons and visual decoration that obscures the message. An accompanying text summary or data table makes complex information available to readers who cannot use the graphic.

Images and screenshots can illustrate a product, step or situation. Choose images relevant to the message; obtain appropriate permission or a suitable licence. Check screenshots for private information, old interfaces and unreadably small text. Alternative text should convey an informative image’s purpose in context; decorative images can use an empty alternative. A complex chart needs more than a short alt text: supply its information in nearby text or a table.

## Video, memes and demonstrations
A product demonstration shows a real task in a sequence: introduce the goal, show the steps, explain limitations and give the next action. Use accurate captions for meaningful audio and provide a transcript; describe important visual information as needed. Memes and GIFs draw on shared conventions and can create humour, but context, copyright, access and potential offence matter. Avoid essential information conveyed only through a moving image.

The syllabus extract says “30-degree videos.” This may be a formatting or source error; check the original syllabus and teacher’s instruction before assuming it means 360-degree video. If 360-degree video is intended, the viewer can explore a recorded environment; offer an accessible alternative and consider motion sensitivity.

## Interactive content
A quiz asks questions and provides feedback; a poll collects responses; an interactive white paper lets readers navigate or explore information. State purpose, explain how responses will be used, avoid collecting unnecessary personal data and test keyboard and screen-reader access. A poll is not automatically representative research: describe who responded and how they were selected.

## Free and paid tools
Choose tools by task, accessibility, data protection, export format, collaboration, licensing and total cost—not just the “free” label. Free tiers, limits and prices change. Do not upload confidential material to an external service without permission.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare a graphic and its text equivalent. 10–22: sketch an accessible infographic with a source. 22–32: draft a short demonstration script. 32–42: design a poll and identify sampling limitations. 42–50: peer-check rights, accessibility and privacy.

## Questions
What makes a visual misleading? Why do captions and text equivalents matter? What can a voluntary poll legitimately tell us?

course-18:3.title: Social media, public relations and originality
course-18:3.text:
# Social media, public relations and originality
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 4

## Social media writing
A social-media post should fit its audience, platform and purpose while remaining understandable outside its original context. State the main message clearly, use accessible wording and link to a reliable source when a claim needs support. A platform may truncate text or display it differently on a phone, so place essential information where readers can find it. Check images, captions and contrast.

## Public relations
Public relations concerns communication and relationships between an organisation and its publics, including staff, customers, communities and journalists. A PR statement should identify the organisation, explain what is known and what action is being taken, and avoid claiming certainty where facts are still being checked. PR, advertising and independent journalism have different roles even when all use similar channels.

Example: “The library is closed today because of a power issue. We will share an update by 2 p.m.” is useful only if those details have been verified and someone will deliver the update. If the reopening time is unknown, say so rather than inventing one.

## Plagiarism and copyright are not identical
Plagiarism is presenting another’s words, ideas or work as one’s own under the relevant academic or professional rules. Copyright is a legal system governing certain uses of protected works; legal outcomes depend on jurisdiction, rights, licences and exceptions. Attribution alone does not necessarily grant permission to reuse a copyrighted image or text. Conversely, use may be lawful in a situation while still requiring attribution under a professional or institutional policy. Do not treat these notes as legal advice.

## Writing original copy
Record sources while researching. Put copied wording in quotation marks in notes, then draft your own structure and wording. Attribute ideas and quotations, verify permissions and licences, and check any AI-assisted text for accuracy, originality and rights issues. A similarity score is a prompt for review, not proof by itself of plagiarism or innocence.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: analyse an organisation’s audience and purpose. 10–22: write a clear service update. 22–35: distinguish quotation, paraphrase and copied text. 35–45: discuss attribution versus permission using an image example. 45–50: exit ticket naming one check before publication.

## Questions
Why should a crisis message identify uncertainty? Does crediting an image always give permission to use it? What makes a paraphrase genuinely independent?

course-18:4.title: Copywriting for print, email, social media and websites
course-18:4.text:
# Copywriting for print, email, social media and websites
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 5

## Copywriting and audience
Copywriting uses words to support a specific response, such as learning about an event, comparing a product or signing up for a service. It may be persuasive, but should be accurate and clear. Before writing, identify the reader, their problem, the offer, supporting evidence, medium and desired action. A call to action (CTA) tells the reader what to do next; it should match a real destination or process.

## Build and edit a message
A practical sequence is audience need → relevant benefit → evidence → next step. A feature is what something does; a benefit is why that feature may matter to a particular reader. Example: “The reading room has adjustable lamps” is a feature; “Adjust the light for comfortable reading” is a possible benefit. Do not claim every person will find it comfortable, or imply a feature exists without verification.

## Adapt by medium
Print advertising must communicate the offer, necessary conditions and action in the space available. Email marketing needs a meaningful subject line, a relevant message, a clear action and compliance with applicable consent and unsubscribe requirements. Social copy may be brief, but should not omit important qualifications. Website content should help readers understand the offer and complete a task; headings and descriptive links support navigation. Avoid fake urgency, invented testimonials, hidden fees and claims that cannot be substantiated.

## Sample adaptation
For a verified free library orientation: print headline: “Find your way around the library.” Email subject: “Library orientation: Friday at 4 p.m.” Website button: “See orientation details.” Confirm the time, location and link before publication; these examples do not imply a real event.

## Editing checklist
Does the first line address the reader? Is the main claim accurate and supported? Are terms and conditions visible? Is the CTA specific and functional? Can the text be read on mobile? Has a second person checked names, numbers, punctuation and links?

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish features and benefits. 10–20: write an audience brief. 20–32: draft print and email versions of one offer. 32–42: rewrite for a website and social post. 42–50: peer review for clarity, evidence and ethical claims.

## Questions
Why is “everyone needs this” a weak audience definition? What makes a CTA misleading? How can a writer persuade without exaggeration?

course-19:0.title: O. Henry · After Twenty Years
course-19:0.text:
# O. Henry · After Twenty Years
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Story overview
A police officer patrols a quiet New York street at night. A man waits in the doorway of a shop and explains that twenty years earlier, he and his friend Jimmy Wells agreed to meet at this spot at ten o’clock. The restaurant where they parted is gone, but the man has travelled from the West to keep the appointment. When he lights his cigar, the match briefly illuminates his face and a scar. He tells the officer about his friendship and apparent success. The officer leaves.

A little later another man approaches and calls him Bob. Bob believes he is Jimmy. They walk together, but in the brighter light of a shop window Bob notices that his companion’s nose is different and realises that he is not his friend. The stranger is a plainclothes officer, who arrests Bob as a man wanted in Chicago. He hands Bob a note from Jimmy.

The note reveals that the first officer was Jimmy: he had recognised Bob’s wanted face when the match was struck. Jimmy could not bring himself to make the arrest personally, so he obtained another officer to do it. Bob’s hand begins steady as he reads but trembles by the end. The story does not show a long reunion or tell us the outcome of the case.

## Analysis
The surprise ending depends on limited information and the reader’s assumptions about the first officer. The promise reveals loyalty even as the arrest creates a conflict between friendship and duty. The match and shop light enable two different recognitions. Bob’s material success should not be taken at face value as proof of honest achievement.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: predict what an appointment after twenty years might reveal. 10–25: sequence the meeting, recognition and arrest. 25–35: identify clues before the ending. 35–45: discuss Jimmy’s choice. 45–50: exit ticket on the role of light.

## Questions
Who first recognises whom? Why does Jimmy ask another officer to act? How does the note change our understanding of the earlier conversation?

## Full narrative walkthrough for teaching

The story opens with a police officer checking doors on a chilly, nearly deserted New York street. This ordinary patrol establishes an atmosphere of quiet watchfulness. A man stands in the doorway of a closed hardware shop. Before the officer can ask, the man explains that he is waiting for an old friend and that the restaurant once standing there was where they arranged to meet.

The waiting man says that he and Jimmy Wells grew up together. On their last evening, Bob was eighteen and Jimmy twenty. Bob intended to go West to seek his fortune; Jimmy preferred New York. They promised to return to the same place and time twenty years later, whatever their circumstances. The restaurant has since disappeared, but Bob keeps the appointment at its former site. He says that they lost contact after initially corresponding and speaks confidently about his own success.

When Bob lights a cigar, the brief matchlight reveals his face. At a first reading the description seems mainly to help a reader imagine him; after the ending, it becomes a crucial clue. The policeman asks questions and departs. Bob continues waiting. The story does not yet tell the reader what the officer has recognised.

A tall man in an overcoat arrives later and addresses Bob. Believing the newcomer is Jimmy, Bob welcomes him. They walk together and talk. Bob notices that his companion seems taller, but accepts the explanation. Near a brightly lit shop, however, he sees the man's face clearly and realises that the shape of his nose does not match Jimmy's. The light now allows Bob to recognise that his companion is an impostor.

The stranger is a plainclothes officer. He tells Bob he is wanted in Chicago and is under arrest, then gives him a note. The note reveals that the first patrolman was Jimmy. Jimmy recognised Bob when the match illuminated his face, but could not bring himself to arrest his old friend personally, so he arranged for another officer to do it. Bob's hand trembles as he finishes reading. The narrative ends without reporting a trial or the later fate of the friendship.

## Explain how the ending works

The story controls information rather than announcing a false solution. Jimmy's identity and recognition are withheld while his conversation with Bob remains available for a second reading. Two moments of light organise the reversal: matchlight permits Jimmy's recognition, while the shop light permits Bob's recognition of the substitute. The final note changes the meaning of the earlier encounter. Asking students to identify what each character knows at each stage is more precise than simply calling the ending “a twist”.

Jimmy's choice joins loyalty and duty in an uncomfortable way. He keeps the appointment and avoids arresting Bob personally, yet he enables the arrest. Readers can disagree about whether this is compassionate, evasive or professionally appropriate, but they should distinguish an interpretation of his motive from the action stated in his note. Bob honours the appointment, but his confident account of prosperity does not establish that his activities were lawful.

## Answers to teach

Why does the match matter? It briefly reveals Bob's face to the first officer, allowing Jimmy to connect his friend with the man sought in Chicago.

Why does Bob reject the second man's identity? In the electric light he sees a nose unlike Jimmy's; the difference is too great to attribute to age.

What does the note reveal? The first officer was Jimmy, he recognised Bob, and he sent another officer because he could not make the arrest himself.

For an essay, introduce the appointment, explain both recognitions, examine the note and conclude with the conflict between the old friendship and the officer's duty. Use the original story or the assigned anthology for wording; the linked study source should be checked against the prescribed selection.

course-19:0.title: Mina Assadi · A Ring to Me is Bondage
course-19:0.text:
# Mina Assadi · A Ring to Me is Bondage
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Poet and reading note
Mina Assadi (also transliterated Asadi) is an Iranian poet who lives in exile in Sweden (biographical reference: https://prabook.com/web/mina.assadi/2080005). An online English version in Mahmud Kianush’s Modern Persian Poetry has been consulted; the precise translation and selection in Impressions-II have not been checked. This entry remains preliminary until they are compared.

## Poem summary and images
The speaker gives unexpected personal meanings to familiar things. Instead of centring a prayer mat, she imagines roads passing through gardens and associates prayer with happiness and the music of sparrows. Roads, birds and walking suggest movement and freedom. The prayer mat can be read as an image of conventional restriction in contrast to the speaker’s chosen way of praying; the poem does not simply reject prayer or all religion.

She calls solitude happiness, a desert home, and what causes sadness love. These paradoxical definitions unsettle ordinary expectations. The person who plucks a flower is described as unable to see its value; the net separates a fish from its element, suggesting violent confinement. Looking at the sea, the speaker imagines a shifting sense of smallness and vastness when it meets the ocean. A cage makes its possessor a gaoler, while unused thought becomes a wall. The closing returns to roads and gardens.

## Interpretation and form
A standard classroom reading takes the ring as a symbol of marriage experienced as bondage by women, and reads the poem as resistance to restrictive conventions and oppression. This is an interpretation: the poem does not say that every marriage or ring is oppressive. Its repeated personal definitions, contrasts and circular return give the speaker a distinctive voice. Invite different supported readings rather than treating every nature image as having only one fixed meaning.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce poet and context. 10–20: follow the roads and prayer imagery. 20–30: examine fish, net and cage. 30–40: discuss ring, sea and resistance. 40–50: write a supported interpretation and compare the ending with the opening.

## Questions
How do roads and the ring contrast? What does the fish-and-net image suggest? Why is marriage as bondage an interpretation rather than a statement about every marriage?

## Reading note
Compare the online English version with the poem and translation assigned in Impressions-II before citing line numbers or exact wording.

## Detailed sequence of the online version

Important: this walkthrough follows the online English version linked above. The exact translation and any excerpt selected in the prescribed anthology remain unverified. Compare the book before giving line numbers or treating this wording as the assigned text.

The speaker begins with a contrast between a conventional object of prayer and imagined roads through gardens. She identifies the direction of prayer with happiness and imagines praying while travelling, accompanied by birdsong. The passage does not require a simple opposition between spirituality and freedom: the speaker still describes prayer, but reimagines its place and manner.

She next questions ordinary meanings and divisions. Being alone becomes happiness, a desert becomes home and what causes sadness is called love. These statements do not form a conventional dictionary. They make the reader attend to a speaker whose experience may give familiar words unexpected emotional meanings. A small sum is described as wealth; students can ask whether this suggests modest needs, irony, or a contrast with conventional measures of value.

The poem then examines harm through natural images. Someone who plucks a flower is called blind, suggesting a failure to recognise what is being damaged. A net separates a fish from water and is described in terms of killing. The literal actions matter: interpret the images through what happens to the flower and fish before generalising about constraint or possession.

The speaker compares her smallness before the sea with the sea's possible smallness before the ocean. The change of scale unsettles any fixed division between small and great. Later, a walk through remembered gardens becomes freedom; the memory is not necessarily a report of an actual journey taking place at that moment.

Near the close, the possessor of a cage becomes a gaoler, unused thought becomes a wall and a ring becomes bondage. A reading concerned with women's freedom and restrictive marriage conventions is plausible, but the images can also invite a broader discussion of possession and confinement. The poem's return to roads and gardens gives the ending a circular structure and leaves the contrast between confinement and movement active.

## Teaching the interpretation

Ask students to choose one image and complete three stages: describe its literal situation, explain one possible association, and connect it to the speaker's redefinition of a familiar word. For the fish and net, the literal separation from water supports an interpretation of constraint as destructive. Avoid presenting that interpretation as the only possible meaning or treating the speaker's personal definitions as universal rules.

## Guided answers

Why are the repeated definitions important? They let the speaker challenge expected meanings and express a personal relation to freedom, love and possession.

What is the effect of the closing return? The roads and gardens recur after the images of cage, wall and ring, making the contrast between movement and confinement part of the poem's structure.

What remains to check? The anthology's selected text and translator; these notes should not assert an exact edition match until the relevant pages are available.

course-19:0.title: Jamaica Kincaid · Girl
course-19:0.text:
# Jamaica Kincaid · Girl
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Form and overview
“Girl” is a very short work built largely as a sequence of instructions, commonly read as a mother speaking to a daughter. Its domestic and linguistic details evoke a Caribbean setting. The narrative is not organised like a conventional plot with several scenes; the pressure of repeated commands is itself central to its effect.

## What happens
The dominant speaker tells the girl how and when to wash clothes, how to cook, sew, garden, behave in public and manage relationships. Practical knowledge is interwoven with warnings about reputation and sexuality. She tells the girl not to sing benna in Sunday school; the girl briefly protests that she does not do so. The main voice continues, often assuming that the girl is at risk of becoming sexually disreputable.

Near the end the speaker advises the girl to test bread for freshness. The girl asks what to do if the baker refuses to let her touch it. The speaker responds by questioning whether the girl will become the sort of woman the baker would not trust near the bread. The work ends there; it does not tell us what the girl later chooses or becomes.

## Themes and method
The speaker transmits useful knowledge while enforcing restrictive expectations. The rapid, semicolon-linked instructions can feel both protective and overwhelming. The daughter’s two brief responses make unequal speaking power audible. Avoid reducing the mother to a villain or assuming that care cancels the harm of shaming; both can operate together. The story’s particular Caribbean details matter alongside broader questions about gender and social respectability.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: discuss the difference between advice and command. 10–22: classify practical instructions and warnings. 22–35: analyse the two interruptions. 35–45: discuss care and control together. 45–50: exit ticket on the ending’s effect.

## Questions
How does punctuation shape pace? What does the daughter’s limited opportunity to speak reveal? Why does the bread question become a judgement about reputation?

## Full guided reading

The work unfolds mainly as a stream of instructions addressed to a girl. It is commonly read as a mother's voice addressing a daughter, although the text does not supply a conventional scene with named speakers and a narrator explaining their relationship. The voice begins with domestic instructions about washing clothes and moves rapidly among tasks, social behaviour and warnings. There is no ordinary sequence of events that a reader can summarise as a plot with a beginning, crisis and resolution; the accumulating instructions are the action of the piece.

Many instructions transmit practical skills: care of clothes, preparation of food, sewing, growing things and dealing with household situations. Such knowledge can be useful and may express a desire to prepare the girl for adult life. At the same time, the repeated warnings about respectable behaviour make clear that the girl is judged according to gendered expectations. Advice about conduct is mixed with suspicion about her sexuality and reputation.

The girl's first brief response challenges the accusation that she sings benna in Sunday school. This interruption matters because it shows that the listener is not entirely silent and that the dominant voice may be making assumptions about her. It is brief compared with the flow of instructions: the form makes the imbalance in speaking time visible on the page and audible in performance. Benna is a culturally specific reference; explain it in relation to the assigned edition rather than treating it as a generic word for any song.

The instructions continue through public behaviour and personal relationships. The speaker's tone can move from practical instruction to command and shame without a formal transition. The reader therefore needs to hold two possibilities together: the speaker may be passing on survival knowledge within restrictive social conditions, and that same instruction can burden or shame the girl. Neither possibility automatically removes the other.

At the end, advice about checking bread leads to the girl's second question: what if the baker will not let her touch it? The response turns her practical concern into a judgement about the kind of woman she might become. Bread can be read as an ordinary test of freshness and, in an interpretation, as an image tied to trust and reputation. The story ends with the speaker's response; it does not show the girl's future or establish whether she accepts the lesson.

## Form, voice and discussion

The accumulation of imperatives and semicolon-linked clauses creates speed and pressure. Read a short stretch aloud, allowing a pause at each semicolon; then ask where the girl's response interrupts the rhythm. Students can discuss the relationship between form and power without assuming that a long sentence means the speaker has no affection. Avoid assigning the characters' exact biographies or claiming that the story represents every Caribbean family.

## Guided answers and writing task

How do care and control coexist? The voice teaches everyday skills, but also polices reputation and assumes improper behaviour. A good answer gives evidence of both.

Why do the two responses matter? They expose the daughter's limited but significant attempts to answer and make the dominance of the main voice clearer.

How does the ending work? A practical question becomes a judgement about social respectability; the work leaves the future unresolved.

For a longer answer, introduce the instruction-based form, analyse a practical example and a warning, discuss one interruption, and conclude by relating the final exchange to voice and reputation. Check the exact text in Impressions-II before quoting.

course-19:0.title: Grammar 64–74 · articles and nouns (edition check needed)
course-19:0.text:
# Grammar 64–74 · articles and nouns (edition check needed)

## Edition warning
The syllabus gives “Essential English Grammar” (Murphy, 2012) and units 64–74, but the assigned book’s contents page has not been checked. The sequence below follows the publicly available second edition of Essential Grammar in Use, a possible but not confirmed match. Use the headings in Ammu’s book as the authority; different editions have different numbering.

## Possession: useful review
Use apostrophe + s for one owner: “Rina’s book.” With a regular plural ending in s, use an apostrophe after s: “the students’ room.” “Its” shows possession; “it’s” means “it is” or “it has.”

## A/an and plural nouns
Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound: “a university” begins with a /y/ sound; “an hour” begins with a vowel sound. Many plurals add -s or -es; irregular forms include child/children and person/people.

## Countable and uncountable
Countable nouns can have a number: one idea, two ideas. Uncountable uses generally do not take a/an or ordinary plural -s: “some information,” “much advice.” Meaning can change: “a coffee” can mean a cup of coffee.

## A/an and the
Use a/an for a non-specific singular countable item and the when the intended referent is identifiable: “I saw a dog. The dog was sleeping.” Shared context, unique reference and conventional usage affect the choice.

## Institutional expressions, general meanings and names
Compare “go to work,” “go home” and “go to the cinema.” General plurals or mass nouns often omit the: “Books are useful”; “Water is essential.” Geographical names vary: India and Lake Victoria ordinarily have no article; the Indian Ocean and the Himalayas take the. Check examples rather than memorising an absolute rule.

## This, that, these, those and one/ones
This/that are singular; these/those plural. “This chair is near me; those chairs are across the room.” They can also stand without a following noun: “This is mine.” “One” and “ones” can replace a repeated noun: “the blue one”; “the red ones.”

## Practice
1. Correct: “The students book is new” when one student owns it. 2. Choose a/an: ___ hour, ___ uniform. 3. Correct: “She gave me an advice.” 4. Complete: “I saw a film. ___ film was funny.” 5. Choose: “___ books here are mine” (plural, near).

## Answers
1. “The student’s book is new.” 2. an hour; a uniform. 3. “She gave me some advice” or “a piece of advice.” 4. The. 5. These.

## 50-minute plan
0–10: check the actual contents page. 10–20: model articles and ownership. 20–30: sort countable and uncountable uses. 30–40: pair practice. 40–50: review answers and a self-written example.

## Additional teaching examples: useful grammar, not a verified unit map

The following examples teach the subjects described above. They do not establish that each topic falls within units 64–74 of the prescribed Murphy 2012 edition. The contents pages of that edition are still needed.

### Choosing a, an and the

Start with sound and reference. “A university” begins with a consonant sound, while “an hour” begins with a vowel sound. Use a or an with a singular countable noun when introducing one non-specific item: “A student asked a question.” If the listener can identify the item in context, use the: “The student waited for an answer.” This is a useful starting point, not a complete rule for every noun phrase. Compare general plural “Students need feedback” with a specific group “The students in this class need feedback.”

### Countability and possession

Compare “an idea/two ideas” with “some advice/a piece of advice”. Some nouns change use with meaning: “coffee” as a substance and “two coffees” as two cups. For possession, compare “the student's notebook” (one student) and “the students' notebooks” (more than one student). The apostrophe indicates possession; it does not by itself make a noun plural.

### Worked practice

1. Complete: “I saw ___ owl in a tree. ___ owl was quiet.” Answer: an; the. The first phrase introduces one owl; the second refers back to it.
2. Correct: “She gave me an information.” Answer: “She gave me some information” or “a piece of information.” Standard usage treats information as uncountable here.
3. Choose: “___ uniform is clean.” Answer: a, because uniform begins with a consonant sound /y/.
4. Add the possessive for books belonging to several teachers. Answer: “the teachers' books.”
5. Contrast “These books are mine” with “Those books are mine.” Both are plural; the choice commonly distinguishes nearer from more distant things in context.

Invite students to explain each choice and create a new sentence. Where more than one answer is possible because the surrounding situation is unspecified, ask for context rather than marking a single form as universally correct.

course-19:1.title: Raja Rao · The Cow of the Barricades
course-19:1.text:
# Raja Rao · The Cow of the Barricades
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Story overview
A mysterious cow, Gauri, visits the Master on Tuesdays, accepts grain from him and disappears. People seek her, bring offerings and honour her as a sacred figure. The story separately names Mahatma Gandhi and says she has also visited him.

Against colonial rule, the Mahatma’s supporters boycott foreign cloth, government service and taxes. Mill and factory workers build barricades; the Master opposes fighting in the Mahatma’s name, but the workers insist on resistance and prepare for battle. He resigns as their President and meditates to avert bloodshed.

Gauri comes through the tense streets. Workmen lay down their arms and honour her; people help her to the top of a barricade. The soldiers’ chief shoots her in the head, and the narrative says no blood is visible. Seth Jamnalal Dwarkachand (also printed Dwarak Chand) buys two houses by the barricades, makes a loop road and erects a metal statue. Children play around it and toy Gauris circulate. The Master says she waits in the Middle Heavens to be born again when India sorrows before freedom.

## Interpretation
A common classroom interpretation reads the Master as a Gandhi-like or Gandhian figure and Gauri as Mother India, embodying compassion, sacrifice and collective hope. However, the online story distinguishes the Master from the separately named Mahatma: it says Gauri has visited one other person, Gandhi. Treat their identification as an allegorical interpretation, not a literal fact that the story never names Gandhi. Readers can also question how religious imagery represents a diverse nation and how the conflict between workers and the Master complicates a simple message.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the setting and storyteller. 10–20: trace Gauri’s visits. 20–30: map the workers, Master and soldiers. 30–40: discuss the shooting and statue. 40–50: test an allegorical reading against the text.

## Questions
Why do the workers and Master disagree? What happens when Gauri reaches the barricade? How does the statue turn death into public memory? What textual detail complicates identifying the Master literally with Gandhi?

## Reading note
The linked story is an online text; compare spelling and wording with the anthology before quoting.

## Full story explanation

Gauri is a mysterious cow who visits the Master on Tuesdays. She refuses the food offered by his disciples but accepts a handful of grain from him, and then disappears. The community cannot discover where she lives. As word spreads, people approach her with offerings and hopes suited to their own needs: merchants seek prosperity, students success, and others ask for marriage or children. The narrator's account makes her an object of collective religious feeling, while also revealing people's different desires.

The story separately names Mahatma Gandhi as the only other person whose hair Gauri has nibbled. At the same time, Gandhi's supporters resist the colonial government through boycotts and refusal to pay taxes. Repression intensifies, with restrictions on movement and violence. Workers construct barricades. The Master warns that barricades may lead to bloodshed, but workers argue that appeals to love will not change an oppressive government. The story gives weight to both positions rather than resolving the conflict by simply declaring one side foolish.

The danger grows as the authorities bring in troops. Families move to safety, while armed workers prepare to resist. The Master resigns the presidency and meditates in the hope of averting bloodshed. The narrator says that people recognise both the workers' and the Master's positions, yet do not know which way to turn. Gauri, now visiting daily, appears distressed.

When the army advances, Gauri walks towards the barricades. A crowd follows with lights and offerings. Workers at first react angrily, but as she approaches they lay down their weapons and bow. Some soldiers respond to her and join the crowd, shouting in support of the Mahatma. Their chief fires, killing Gauri. The account then shifts to memory: a statue is erected, children play around it, toy Gauris are sold, and the Master imagines her future return when India suffers again before freedom.

The cow can be read as an image of compassion and sacrifice, and her progress interrupts a confrontation between armed sides. The religious, nationalist and communal interpretations arise through what people say and do; they are not all neutral historical facts. Gandhi and the Master are separately named in the text: identifying the Master with Gandhi is an interpretation, not an explicit identification. A useful essay traces the conflict, Gauri's intervention and the changing forms of remembrance after her death.

course-19:1.title: Aldous Huxley · The Beauty Industry
course-19:1.text:
# Aldous Huxley · The Beauty Industry
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Context and argument
In this essay, collected in Music at Night (1931; publication reference: https://www.jonkers.co.uk/rare-book/10870/music-at-night/aldous-huxley), Huxley combines social observation, irony and a serious argument about beauty. He claims that the American beauty industry alone has not been affected by the Depression. He reports approximately £3 million a week, or £156 million a year, spent by American women on appearance, and tentatively compares the annual sum with the revenue of India under British rule. He says he does not know the European figures but assumes they are much smaller. These are Huxley’s historical claims, not independently verified economic statistics or present-day facts; the essay does not give a specific British spending figure in the text consulted.

## Social change and partial success
Huxley associates the industry with changes in women’s social position and a less ascetic Christian attitude towards the body. He credits the campaign with partial success: he observes that more women retain a youthful appearance for longer, helped by improved health as well as cosmetic practices. His prediction that the old-fashioned image of the “old lady” will disappear is an exaggeration about appearance, not a claim that women stop ageing.

## The limitation: the porcelain jar
Huxley also calls the campaign a failure if it aims at complete human beauty. A porcelain jar can be judged by its shape, colour and surface irrespective of its contents, whereas a person is alive and has an experiencing inner life. He argues that expressions, movement and character affect how human beauty is perceived. The analogy supports his claim that outward treatment alone is insufficient; it does not mean that cosmetics are necessarily harmful or that appearance reliably reveals moral character.

## Method and critical response
The essay uses humour, irony, generalisation and comparison, but its argument is not purely satire: Huxley acknowledges benefits and makes a moral and social critique. Question his gender assumptions: he singles out women, risks judging inner lives by appearance and neglects autonomy, pleasure, work and pressures around beauty practices. Discuss the argument without endorsing ageism or judging a person’s worth by their appearance.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the historical context. 10–20: map the spending claim and its limits. 20–30: list benefits he recognises. 30–40: explain the jar analogy. 40–50: evaluate one gender assumption with evidence.

## Questions
Why does Huxley call the campaign both a success and a failure? How do a person and a jar differ in his analogy? What assumptions in his argument can be challenged?

## Reading note
The source links to an online version of the essay. Compare it with the prescribed Impressions-II selection; verify publication details and any quotation in the assigned text.

## Follow Huxley's argument from beginning to end

Huxley begins with a striking claim about American spending on beauty during a trade depression. He cites approximately three million pounds per week and converts this to £156 million per year, comparing that annual figure to the revenue of India as he remembers it. These are historical claims used in his argument, not current statistics; he says he does not know the European figures.

He asks why so much is spent. Greater prosperity is one explanation, but he argues that economic change is not sufficient: spending continues even in difficult conditions. He relates the demand to changing opportunities and expectations for women and to a less ascetic attitude towards the body. His tone is often ironic, and his generalisations reflect his historical point of view rather than an objective account of all women.

He then asks whether the beauty campaign succeeds. In one sense he thinks it does: some people maintain a youthful appearance longer, and habits that improve health may be beneficial. Yet he distinguishes health from the artificial imitation of its outward signs. The distinction prepares his argument that surface appearance does not exhaust beauty.

His comparison with a porcelain vessel makes that claim vivid. A jar's appearance can be judged without regard to its contents; a human being, he argues, is alive and cannot be assessed in the same way. Inner emotional and psychological conditions, in his view, affect outward expression. He describes examples of attractive features undermined by boredom or hardness, and argues that products alone cannot deal with deeper disharmony.

Students should identify this as Huxley's argument, not an established rule for judging people's character from their faces. His claims about women, ageing, attractiveness, health and inner life can be questioned as well as explained. A strong answer sets out his partial acknowledgement of the industry's success, his distinction between imitation and health, and his claim about inward life before offering a reasoned criticism of his assumptions.

course-19:1.title: Grammar 75–83 · pronouns and quantity (edition check needed)
course-19:1.text:
# Grammar 75–83 · pronouns and quantity (edition check needed)

## Edition warning
These topic-to-unit numbers follow a possible second-edition comparison, not a verified contents page for the prescribed 2012 book. Confirm each unit heading before teaching.

## One and ones: useful review
“One” avoids repeating a singular countable noun; “ones” replaces a plural: “I like the blue pen. Which one?” / “The blue ones.”

## Some, any and negative forms
Some commonly appears in affirmative statements and offers: “some tea,” “Would you like some tea?” Any commonly appears in negatives and questions: “I don’t have any”; “Do you have any?” “No” precedes a noun: “no money.” “None” can replace a noun: “How many? None.” Nobody/anybody and nothing/anything express people and things; use one grammatical negative in standard formal examples: “I don’t know anybody” or “I know nobody.”

## Every, all, most, both, either and neither
“Every student has a card” uses a singular verb; “all students have cards” uses plural agreement. “Most students” is general; “most of the students in this class” identifies a group. Both means the two together; either can mean one or the other; neither means not one and not the other. Agreement with neither can vary by construction and register.

## Quantity
Use “many books” with countable plurals and “much time” with uncountable nouns; “a lot of” works with either. In ordinary affirmative speech, “a lot of” is often more natural than “much.” Compare “a few books” (some) with “few books” (not many), and “a little time” (some) with “little time” (not much).

## Practice
1. I have two pens. The blue ___ is mine. 2. Do you have ___ questions? 3. Rewrite “I don’t have any money” using no. 4. Every student ___ (has/have) a card. 5. ___ books / ___ time (many or much).

## Answers
1. one. 2. any. 3. I have no money. 4. has. 5. many books; much time. Context may permit alternatives in other constructions.

## 50-minute plan
0–10: verify assigned headings. 10–20: model substitution and negatives. 20–30: practise quantities. 30–40: pairs explain agreement. 40–50: answer review.

## Extra grammar practice; edition mapping not verified

These are general practice examples, not an assertion that the prescribed 2012 Murphy units 75–83 cover these particular topics. Check the contents pages before assigning unit numbers.

Subject and object pronouns have different positions: “She invited him”; “He invited her.” Possessive determiners precede nouns: “their books”. Possessive pronouns can stand alone: “The books are theirs.” A reflexive pronoun may refer back to the subject: “She taught herself.” Do not use a reflexive simply because it sounds formal: “Please send it to me” is appropriate.

Quantity words depend partly on the noun. “Many books” and “a few books” normally accompany plural count nouns; “much time” and “a little time” accompany an uncountable noun. “Some” and “any” have varied uses: compare an affirmative “We have some paper”, a question “Do we have any paper?” and an offer “Would you like some tea?” Context matters, so these are starting patterns rather than absolute rules.

Practice and answers: 1. “Maya and I finished ___ work”: our. 2. “This folder is not mine; it is ___”: hers is one possible possessive pronoun, depending on the owner. 3. “There are ___ chairs”: many or a few, depending on meaning. 4. “There is ___ water”: some or a little, depending on meaning. 5. “Ravi cut ___ while cooking”: himself. Ask learners to explain noun countability or pronoun reference, not merely supply a word.

course-19:2.title: Seamus Heaney · Digging
course-19:2.text:
# Seamus Heaney · Digging
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Poem summary
At a desk the speaker holds a pen. He hears a spade outside and looks down at his father digging. The sight carries him back to his father’s earlier work digging potatoes, remembered through skilled movements and the cool feel of the crop. He also remembers his grandfather cutting turf in a bog and recalls bringing him milk before the older man returned to work.

The smell of earth and sound of cutting make these memories vivid. The speaker recognises that he does not follow the earlier generations with a spade. Returning to the pen in his hand, he decides to dig with it: writing will be his own form of careful work and exploration.

## Form and interpretation
The poem moves from present observation to memories and back to the pen. The opening compares the pen to a gun; the ending emphasises a different tool and action. Do not insist that the gun image has only one political or personal meaning. Sound patterns, tactile detail and the repeated action of digging honour manual skill while allowing a different vocation. The poem negotiates continuity and difference rather than simply rejecting family work.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: sketch the three generations. 10–22: follow the shifts in time. 22–35: identify sound and sensory details. 35–45: compare pen and spade. 45–50: explain one effect using a precise detail.

## Questions
What triggers memory? How are the father’s and grandfather’s work represented? Why is the final act of digging figurative?

course-19:2.title: Amitav Ghosh · The Town by the Sea
course-19:2.text:
# Amitav Ghosh · The Town by the Sea
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Context and limitation
The account concerns the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 and its consequences in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Anthologies may abridge the longer account; check Impressions-II for exact selection and sequence. The subject involves bereavement and disaster and should be discussed sensitively.

## Outline and central scene
Ghosh accompanies the Director, a scientist, through the ruins of Malacca on Car Nicobar after the tsunami. The Director was away when the earthquake and waves struck; his son survived, while his wife and daughter were lost. The disaster is understood through a particular family as well as a devastated landscape.

Among the wreckage the Director picks up slides from his epidemiological research. He points out his daughter’s yellow paint box but chooses not to take it. Ghosh is struck by that choice and reflects on grief and the life of the mind. Do not turn the decision into proof that the Director values work more than his daughter: grief cannot be reliably judged from a single gesture.

## Papers, identity and planning
In the broader essay Ghosh describes survivors’ lost identity cards, certificates and other documents, showing how the loss of papers can make it harder to prove identity, property or entitlements. He also examines planning that placed settlements near the beachfront, exposing people to coastal hazards. This is a question about human decisions and unequal vulnerability, not a reason to blame victims or claim that one location explains every loss. The linked essay excerpt at https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/incendiary-circumstances-amitav-ghosh/1111826984?ean=2940191875705 provides further context; check whether these passages appear in the assigned extract.

## Reading critically
Distinguish observed actions, reported experience and interpretation. Treat survivors respectfully and do not make assumptions about how grief should be expressed.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: context and sensitivity note. 10–20: identify the Director, place and disaster. 20–30: compare the slides and paint box without judging grief. 30–40: discuss documents and settlement planning. 40–50: write a supported question about the account.

## Questions
What does the Director take and leave? How can lost documents affect survivors? What questions does Ghosh raise about coastal planning?

## Reading note
The linked summary discusses the central scene. The longer essay may differ from the prescribed anthology extract; check Impressions-II before quoting or assessing its scope.

course-19:2.title: Sujata Bhatt · A Different History
course-19:2.text:
# Sujata Bhatt · A Different History
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Poem summary
The opening imagines the Greek god Pan migrating to India. Gods appear in forms associated with the natural world, and trees and books are treated with reverence. The speaker lists ways of handling a book carelessly and asks that pages be turned gently, respecting Sarasvati, associated with knowledge, and the tree from which the paper came.

The poem then turns to questions about language and oppression. Images of violent conquest complicate the earlier reverence for books and learning. The speaker asks how later generations can come to love a language connected with an oppressor’s history. The ending is a question and a paradox, not a declaration that the violence has been forgotten or that the language has only one meaning.

## Form and interpretation
Allusions to Pan and Sarasvati bring different traditions into relation. The shift from respectful instruction to questioning and violent imagery creates tension between language as knowledge and language implicated in power. A language is not literally a person who decides to kill: examine how the rhetorical questions make readers consider its historical uses. Readers can debate the emotional force of the final “love” without claiming that pain is necessarily absent.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the two movements. 10–22: discuss books, trees and deities. 22–35: examine the shift to questions about language. 35–45: discuss inheritance and colonial history. 45–50: exit response explaining one contrast.

## Questions
Why connect a book to a tree? How does the tone change? What makes the later generation’s relationship to language complex?

course-19:2.title: Grammar 84–95 · description and word order (edition check needed)
course-19:2.text:
# Grammar 84–95 · description and word order (edition check needed)

## Edition warning
The following is based on a possible second edition, not the confirmed 2012 prescribed copy. Match headings with the book before teaching.

## 84–85: adjectives and adverbs
Adjectives describe nouns or follow linking verbs: “a careful student”; “The student is careful.” Adverbs often describe actions: “She reads carefully.” Not all adverbs end in -ly; “fast” can be an adjective or adverb.

## 86–89: comparisons and superlatives
Short adjectives often add -er/-est: small, smaller, smallest. Longer ones commonly use more/most: more interesting, most interesting. Compare two things with than: “This path is shorter than that one.” “Not as long as” expresses an unequal comparison. Irregular forms include good, better, best.

## 90–91: enough and too
“Enough” follows an adjective (“warm enough”) but normally precedes a noun (“enough time”). “Too” often means more than desirable: “too hot to touch,” not simply “very hot.”

## 92–95: position and objects
A common pattern is subject + verb + object + place/time: “She reads a book at home every evening.” Frequency adverbs normally precede ordinary verbs but follow be: “He usually walks”; “He is usually early.” “Already,” “yet” and “still” signal timing in context. Give can take two objects (“Give me the book”) or a prepositional phrase (“Give the book to me”); pronouns favour “Give it to me.”

## Practice
1. The child spoke ___ (quiet/quietly). 2. A bus is ___ (large) than a car. 3. There is not ___ time (enough/too). 4. Place usually: “She is early.” 5. Rewrite “Give me it” in a common formal pattern.

## Answers
1. quietly. 2. larger. 3. enough. 4. She is usually early. 5. Give it to me.

## 50-minute plan
0–10: check headings. 10–20: adjectives and adverbs. 20–30: comparisons. 30–40: word-order cards. 40–50: practise and correct.

course-19:3.title: R. K. Narayan · Engine Trouble
course-19:3.text:
# R. K. Narayan · Engine Trouble
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Story from beginning to end
The story, collected in Malgudi Days (1943), is set in the fictional town of Malgudi. Its first-person narrator, the Talkative Man, wins a road engine in a lottery at the travelling fair Gaiety Land, held on the Gymkhana ground. What initially looks like a valuable prize immediately becomes a problem: it is large, heavy and difficult to move or sell. The fair’s management allows it to remain temporarily, but after the fair leaves the municipality demands that the narrator remove it or pay rent for the space.

Unable to find a buyer, he pays rent and spends increasing amounts trying to deal with the machine. When the ground is needed for another event, he arranges to move it to a friend’s property. He hires a temple elephant, fifty labourers and Joseph, a dismissed bus driver, to help move and steer the engine. Their efforts are not coordinated. The machine damages a compound wall, the elephant becomes agitated, and the owner and authorities hold the narrator responsible. What was supposed to be a windfall has become a source of debt, public embarrassment and domestic tension.

A visiting swami announces a performance involving a road engine driven over his body. The narrator hopes that allowing his engine to be used will finally solve his transport problem. The dangerous demonstration is stopped by the authorities, so this plan fails too. He considers leaving town.

An earthquake then shifts the engine into a disused well. The narrator fears another liability, but the well’s owner had been ordered to close it and welcomes the machine because it effectively fills the opening. The owner agrees to settle the problem and cover expenses in return for leaving the engine there. An accident finally resolves what careful efforts could not. The narrator is relieved.

## Technique and themes
First-person narration, escalating complications and reversals make the story comic. The prize’s supposed value depends on the owner’s ability to store, move or use it. Coincidence and absurdity shape the resolution; the story does not require readers to believe that disasters are generally fortunate. Consider the narrator’s perspective and the other people affected by his schemes.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: discuss whether every prize is useful. 10–25: make a cause-and-effect chain from lottery to failed moves. 25–35: analyse the swami episode and earthquake. 35–45: discuss irony and practical value. 45–50: exit ticket explaining the final reversal.

## Questions
Why is the engine a burden? How does each attempted solution create another problem? Why does the well owner welcome it?

## Reading note
The linked summary supports the main plot; compare the story and collection details with the assigned anthology.

course-19:3.title: Erich Fromm · Is Love an Art?
course-19:3.text:
# Erich Fromm · Is Love an Art?
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Context and central question
“Is Love an Art?” is associated with the opening of Fromm’s The Art of Loving (1956). The exact course extract should be checked. Fromm asks whether love is a skill requiring knowledge and effort or a pleasant feeling that happens by chance. He argues for the former.

## Main line of argument
Fromm suggests that many people focus on being loved—becoming attractive, successful or desirable—rather than developing their own capacity to love. A second assumption treats love mainly as a problem of finding the right object, rather than practising an ability. A third confuses the initial experience of falling in love with the continuing work of loving. These are Fromm’s diagnoses of cultural attitudes, not universal facts about every relationship.

If love is an art, he argues, a person must give it serious attention, learn both theory and practice, and recognise that improvement takes effort. In the broader book he links mature love with care, responsibility, respect and knowledge; check whether those later discussions occur within the assigned extract before attributing them to the opening alone.

## Evaluate the argument
Fromm’s framework invites reflection on attention, reciprocity and whether consumer habits shape relationships. Ask whether the analogy with an art has limits: relationships also depend on other people’s agency, social conditions, consent and circumstances beyond one person’s control. Effort does not obligate anyone to remain in an unsafe or unwanted relationship.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish falling in love from sustaining care. 10–22: map the three assumptions Fromm questions. 22–35: assess his art analogy. 35–45: offer an example and a counterexample. 45–50: write one reasoned agreement or disagreement.

## Questions
What does it mean to treat love as a capacity? Why does Fromm distinguish being loved from loving? What are the limits of the skill analogy?

course-19:3.title: Grammar 96–106 · time, place and prepositions (edition check needed)
course-19:3.text:
# Grammar 96–106 · time, place and prepositions (edition check needed)

## Edition warning
Topic numbers below come from a possible second-edition comparison; confirm the assigned book before claiming an exact unit mapping.

## 96–98: time expressions
“At” commonly marks clock times (“at 5”), “on” days and dates (“on Monday”), and “in” months, years and longer periods (“in June”). “From … to” specifies a range; “until” an endpoint. “Since” marks a starting point and “for” a duration: “since 2020,” “for three years.” “During” precedes a noun phrase (“during the film”); “while” commonly introduces a clause (“while we watched”).

## 99–104: place and movement
In often places something within an area, at identifies a point or venue, and on indicates a surface, route or conventional usage: “in the room,” “at the station,” “on the table.” Context changes the best choice: “at the school” and “in the school” can focus on different things. Under, behind, opposite, over and through express spatial relations. “Go to college” but “go home.” “By bus,” “with a pen” and “about a book” are conventional combinations.

## 105–106: combinations
Many adjectives select a preposition: “good at,” “interested in,” “afraid of.” After a preposition, an -ing form can follow: “good at drawing.” Verbs also combine conventionally: “listen to music,” “look at a picture,” “wait for a friend.” Learn combinations with a meaningful sentence, not by translating one word at a time.

## Practice
1. Meet ___ Monday ___ 3 p.m. 2. She has lived here ___ 2020. 3. He is good ___ drawing. 4. We walked ___ the tunnel. 5. Listen ___ the instructions.

## Answers
1. on; at. 2. since. 3. at. 4. through. 5. to. Other prepositions can work in different contexts.

## 50-minute plan
0–10: check actual headings. 10–20: create a time line. 20–30: describe a room and movement. 30–40: practise adjective/verb combinations. 40–50: corrections and exit ticket.

course-19:4.title: Communication, greetings, requests and telephone skills
course-19:4.text:
# Communication, greetings, requests and telephone skills
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Understanding communication
Communication involves producing, receiving and interpreting messages in a context. A sender’s intention is not automatically the same as the listener’s understanding. Feedback—questions, paraphrases and responses—helps identify misunderstandings. Noise can include poor audio, ambiguous wording, interruptions or different assumptions.

## Greetings and introductions
Choose an appropriate greeting for the relationship and situation. In a formal introduction, give your name and relevant role: “Good morning. I’m Meena, a student in the English department.” In an informal setting, a shorter greeting may be appropriate.
