This section of The Discovery of India reflects Nehru’s search for a way to think about truth, values and public life. He wrote the book during imprisonment in the 1940s. Treat the essay as a situated argument, not a definitive account of all religion or all science.

## Argument
Nehru criticises dogma and superstition as he has encountered them in organised religion, while recognising the human search for meaning and ethical values. He values science for its disciplined inquiry, willingness to test ideas and ability to expand knowledge and material possibilities. Yet he is troubled by a purely factual science detached from questions of purpose and human values.

He seeks an approach in which scientific temper is allied with philosophical reflection and openness to what remains unknown. This does not mean that religious claims are automatically scientific, or that science alone answers every moral question. Ask how his argument distinguishes scientific methods from their social uses.

## Reading critically
Identify where he is describing his own responses and where he makes general claims. Compare his vision with Aurobindo’s account of cultural renewal and ask how the two writers balance inherited traditions and modernity.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define dogma and inquiry. 10–22: trace his critique of religion. 22–32: list science’s achievements and limits. 32–42: discuss philosophy and values. 42–50: write a balanced account of his position.

## Questions
Why does Nehru value scientific temper? Why does he think factual knowledge alone is insufficient?

course-29:4.title: Amartya Sen · An Approach to Justice
course-29:4.text:
# Amartya Sen · An Approach to Justice
Indian Writing in English II · Semester 5

## Context and central distinction
“An Approach to Justice” is the introduction to The Idea of Justice. Sen distinguishes seeking a perfectly just set of arrangements from comparing feasible alternatives to reduce injustice. He argues that assessment must consider actual lives and outcomes, not only institutions and rules as ideally designed. Institutions matter; his criticism is not that they can be ignored.

## Three children and a flute
Anne can play the flute; Bob is poor and has no toys; Carla made the flute. Each offers a different reason for receiving it: effective use or pleasure, need and equality, or entitlement through labour. Sen uses the case to show that serious and potentially impartial reasons can conflict; he does not present a single obvious winner that resolves every theory of justice. Public reasoning must engage with competing grounds.

## Niti and nyaya
Sen uses a distinction from Sanskrit thought: niti concerns organisational propriety and correct conduct, while nyaya points to justice as realised in the lives and world people actually experience. For him, evaluating an apparently proper rule also requires asking what happens under it, including behaviour and social conditions.

## Apply
Compare two practical policies for access to education: who can actually attend, participate and benefit? Explain evidence and competing values rather than assuming that a formally equal rule produces equal opportunity.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: pose the flute case. 10–22: identify three reasons. 22–32: distinguish ideal arrangements from realised outcomes. 32–42: compare two education policies. 42–50: defend a judgment while recognising a competing reason.

## Questions
Why do Anne, Bob and Carla each have a claim? How do arrangements and realised justice differ?

course-30:0.title: A · Finding a suitable internship
course-30:0.text:
# A · Finding a suitable internship
Internship · Semester 5

## What the syllabus asks
Define career goals and identify prospective employers or hosts. The course description specifically envisions outreach in which undergraduate students support working adults in neighbouring coastal and rural communities with basic communication and writing. The description also mentions professional settings, so check which placements and host organisations your college approves.

## A practical sequence
1. Write two or three goals: for example, practise listening to adult learners, design an accessible English activity, and learn to document work responsibly.
2. With the faculty coordinator, identify a potential local organisation, community group or approved workplace. Do not promise training or contact participants on behalf of the college without authorisation.
3. Ask about location, safety, supervision, working hours, language preferences and accessible timings. Discuss whether the placement genuinely matches both the course and the community’s needs.
4. Choose tentative goals with the host rather than assuming learners are deficient. Adults bring existing languages, work skills and expertise; English learning should build on those strengths.
5. Record the name and role of the person contacted, response and next step without collecting unnecessary personal data.

## Planning a respectful outreach session
With consent, ask what participants want to use English for—perhaps introductions, a simple workplace message or reading a notice. Use Tamil or another shared language for explanation where helpful, and adapt to different literacy levels. Participation should be voluntary. Arrange a supervised and accessible venue.

## Suggested 50-minute preparation session
0–10: list goals. 10–20: discuss community strengths and needs. 20–30: brainstorm suitable hosts. 30–40: assess safety and access. 40–50: draft three questions for the coordinator.

## Reflection
Which placements match your goals and the course description? How will you find out what participants actually want to learn?

This is practical guidance, not an official form, approval or placement. The syllabus labels A–D as course-content sections, not formal units. Confirm all requirements with the college.

course-30:1.title: B · Application, follow-up and interview
course-30:1.text:
# B · Application, follow-up and interview
Internship · Semester 5

## Preparation
Confirm the approved application procedure and whether the placement requires an introduction letter. Read the host’s description and write a short, truthful résumé: education, communication skills, relevant teaching or volunteering and contact details. Do not invent experience or include sensitive documents unless the authorised process requires them.

## Sample professional email
Subject: Inquiry about an approved undergraduate internship

Dear [name or role],
I am an undergraduate English student at [college]. I am exploring an internship that supports adult communication and writing skills. I would be grateful to know whether your organisation hosts students and what the application process involves. My faculty coordinator can provide details of the course requirements.
Thank you for your time.
[Name and contact]

Personalise and confirm the recipient before sending. After a reasonable interval, one polite follow-up can ask whether the message was received; do not repeatedly pressure the host.

## Interview practice
Prepare a brief introduction, one example of teamwork, and how you would ask adult learners about their goals. Ask about supervision, hours, safety, accessibility and what information you may share. Dress appropriately for the setting as directed; a dress code should be safe, accessible and respectful.

## Suggested 50-minute preparation session
0–10: examine a host description. 10–20: draft a short introduction. 20–30: practise interview questions in pairs. 30–40: edit the email for clarity. 40–50: prepare two questions for the host.

## Reflection
How does your experience match the placement? What do you need to know before accepting?

This is practical guidance, not an official form, approval or placement. The syllabus labels A–D as course-content sections, not formal units. Confirm all requirements with the college.

course-30:2.title: C · Enrollment and approvals
course-30:2.text:
# C · Enrollment and approvals
Internship · Semester 5

## Syllabus sequence
The published course content says to complete an Internship Registration Form, obtain approval signatures from the major faculty advisor and internship coordinator, and enroll through the internship office; it says the student cannot self-enroll. Names of offices and procedures may have changed, so verify current forms and instructions with your college. This app does not submit a form or enroll you.

## Practical checklist
1. Confirm eligibility, approved host, supervisor and whether the role fits the course.
2. Obtain the current form through the college’s official channel. Complete dates, placement details and contact information accurately.
3. Obtain the required faculty-advisor and coordinator approvals in the order your college specifies; ask where the signed form must go.
4. Confirm that the responsible office has completed enrollment. Save an acknowledgement securely.
5. Agree on the schedule, supervision, reporting process and safeguarding or accessibility arrangements before beginning.

Never upload identification, signatures or participants’ personal details into an unsecured form or public repository. These notes cannot verify a placement’s approval.

## Suggested 50-minute preparation session
0–10: arrange the published steps. 10–20: identify who can answer procedural questions. 20–30: review a blank sample form, if supplied by the college. 30–40: discuss privacy. 40–50: write a personal checklist.

## Reflection
Who confirms your enrollment? Which details must be checked before your first day?

This is practical guidance, not an official form, approval or placement. The syllabus labels A–D as course-content sections, not formal units. Confirm all requirements with the college.

course-30:3.title: D · Hours, reports and reflection
course-30:3.text:
# D · Hours, reports and reflection
Internship · Semester 5

## Check the actual rules first
The syllabus specifies a minimum of 80 work hours per credit hour. For this listed four-credit course, that arithmetic is 320 hours. The document also mentions reports, a self-assessment, an employer evaluation and Blackboard deadlines. **Confirm the currently applicable hour requirement, forms, deadlines, placement conditions and submission system with your college before making commitments**; this app cannot establish whether those details have changed.

## Keeping a log
Record date, start and end times, approved activity, learning and supervisor confirmation in the format the college requires. Separate planning, direct work and reflection if instructed. Record actual hours only; do not backdate, fabricate attendance or assume travel counts. Protect participant privacy: use anonymous descriptions unless informed consent and college policy permit identification.

## Suggested report structure
Title and placement details; approved objectives; description of the host’s work; responsibilities and activities; one anonymised communication or teaching activity; what worked and what changed based on participant feedback; challenges and ethical decisions; skills learned; and a short evaluation of how the placement relates to educational and career goals. Attach only documents requested through an approved channel.

## Sample adult-English activity: 50 minutes
0–5: agree on a practical goal with learners. 5–15: model a short spoken greeting and workplace request. 15–25: practise in pairs, allowing translation. 25–35: jointly draft a short message. 35–45: participants adapt it to their own situation. 45–50: invite optional feedback and one question. This is a suggested activity, not a mandated internship session.

Ask the supervisor about the employer evaluation and submit the self-assessment by the confirmed deadline. Never claim credit until the college confirms completion.

## Suggested 50-minute preparation session
0–10: locate the current official requirement. 10–20: practise an honest log entry. 20–30: outline an anonymised report. 30–40: adapt the sample activity. 40–50: write one strength and one learning goal.

## Reflection
What does the printed syllabus say about hours, and who confirms the current rule? How can you report learning while protecting privacy?

This is practical guidance, not an official form, approval or placement. The syllabus labels A–D as course-content sections, not formal units. Confirm all requirements with the college.

course-31:0.title: Introduction · New literatures and translation
course-31:0.text:
# Introduction · New literatures and translation
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## What the course means
The course surveys writing associated with regions beyond Britain, including Sri Lanka, the Caribbean, Australia, Latin America, Canada, Japan, China, New Zealand and Africa. “New literatures” is an institutional label, not a claim that these societies lacked literature before English or European colonialism. Many have long, diverse oral and written traditions.

## Language and power
English spread through trade, migration and colonial rule, but writers use it in different ways, drawing on local speech, Indigenous languages and literary traditions. Some works on this syllabus, including those of Borges, Saramago, Mishima and Gao, were originally written in languages other than English and are studied in English translation. Translation choices matter; compare a passage’s translator and edition, not just the author’s nationality.

## Reading comparatively
Ask how each work represents place, class, gender, migration, colonial rule and ecology. Avoid treating a whole continent or nation as a uniform culture. Settler-colonial and Indigenous experiences, for example, are not interchangeable. A comparison should link specific passages and allow important differences to remain.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: question the label “new.” 10–20: map listed regions. 20–30: identify original language and translator. 30–40: compare two accounts of place. 40–50: write a comparison without generalising a region.

## Questions
Why can “new” be misleading? What changes when a work is read in translation?

course-31:1.title: Kenneth Slessor · Country Towns
course-31:1.text:
# Kenneth Slessor · Country Towns
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Summary · non-detailed in syllabus
The speaker addresses Australian country towns, recalling their trees and squares, farmers, old public houses and general stores. An out-of-date entertainment notice lies under flies, suggesting a place where time moves slowly. On verandas people sleep; dogs seem to lick the sunshine and settle again after a distant sound. In the final stanza the speaker asks the towns for shade, sweetness, a bench and sleep, imagining an afternoon so leisurely that late day feels like noon.

## Technique
Playful sound, vivid similes and accumulated local details create a comic, sleepy atmosphere. The poem’s affectionate caricature is one perspective on country life, not a complete account of those communities or of Indigenous histories.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify setting. 10–20: paraphrase town details. 20–30: discuss old notice and sleeping dogs. 30–40: examine the speaker’s invitation to rest. 40–50: write about tone.

## Questions
How does the poem make time seem slow? What is the effect of addressing towns directly?

course-31:1.title: David Malouf · The Year of the Foxes
course-31:1.text:
# David Malouf · The Year of the Foxes
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Summary · non-detailed
A speaker remembers being ten when his mother, seeing a chance to make money, brings fox-fur garments into the family sitting room for sale. Brisbane women arrive to buy them during wartime. At night the child imagines the foxes crying, their eyes and tails alive with danger. Yet among elegant cups and glasses the fur pieces remain dead animals. Later the fashionable buyers fasten the limp paws and wear the furs out into the street.

## Reading
The contrast between living imagination and dead commodities links childhood memory, wartime consumption and animal life. Domestic luxury is both ordinary and unsettling. The speaker’s dream should not be confused with a claim that the furs are literally alive.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map household and buyers. 10–20: sequence the sale. 20–30: compare dream and display. 30–40: discuss fashion and the animal body. 40–50: describe the poem’s mixed tone.

## Questions
Why do dead foxes appear alive to the child? How do luxury objects alter the scene?

course-31:1.title: Margaret Atwood · Journey to the Interior
course-31:1.text:
# Margaret Atwood · Journey to the Interior
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Summary · detailed
The speaker compares a journey into the mind with travel through a physical landscape. Hills and routes may look simple from a distance but become complicated when approached. The interior resembles an overgrown territory with shifting light and obstructing branches, yet differs from ordinary exploration: reliable maps and fixed routes are unavailable. Familiar small objects and fragments of thought interrupt the journey; the speaker wonders whether she is moving in circles. The ending warns that inward exploration can be dangerous and requires keeping one’s bearings.

## Close reading
The opening comparison between similarity and difference builds an extended metaphor, but mind and landscape never match perfectly. Changes of scale—from broad terrain to domestic objects—show how attention shifts. Irregular lines and movement across line breaks can make the reader experience uncertainty. “Getting lost” is an image of the difficulty of self-understanding, not a medical diagnosis.

## Discuss
Does the poem promise a final discovery, or emphasise the journey and its risks? Support either view with a detail from your assigned edition.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: sketch the landscape. 10–20: paraphrase similarities. 20–30: list differences and distractions. 30–40: discuss the danger of losing direction. 40–50: explain one image in a short paragraph.

## Questions
Why are maps unreliable in the interior? How do domestic details interrupt the journey?

course-31:1.title: Claire Harris · Framed
course-31:1.text:
# Claire Harris · Framed
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Summary · non-detailed
The speaker addresses a viewer who has bought a painting of island houses. Within the apparently picturesque image stands a woman carrying laundry, wearing worn shoes and bearing the marks of labour. The speaker recalls a close relationship with her: the woman gives the speaker the better plate and cup while keeping less for herself, works constantly and hopes for a different future for her. The speaker studies, distances herself and later leaves. The painting is put away, but the speaker imagines herself still inside it, pushing against its frame.

## Reading
A decorative picture becomes a way to examine unequal labour, aspiration, shame, memory and representation. The speaker’s relation to the woman can be discussed through textual evidence without inventing a relationship the poem does not explicitly settle. The frame both captures and restricts what an outsider sees.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: describe the painting. 10–20: trace the working woman’s actions. 20–30: discuss the speaker’s response. 30–40: interpret the frame. 40–50: explain the difference between picturesque view and lived labour.

## Questions
What does the buyer’s picture conceal? Why does the speaker push against the frame?

course-31:1.title: A. D. Hope · Moschus Moschiferus
course-31:1.text:
# A. D. Hope · Moschus Moschiferus
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Summary · non-detailed
Subtitled “A Song for St Cecilia’s Day,” the poem describes hunters seeking musk deer for the scent-bearing glands valued in perfume. As the animals grow scarce, hunters conceal themselves and one plays a flute. The beautiful music draws a deer from cover, where poisoned arrows kill it. The hunters remove the musk and leave the bodies. The closing address to Cecilia, patron of music, sets praise of music against its use as a trap.

## Reading
The poem connects beauty, commercial demand and violence. Its figures for numbers and predicted extinction are claims within the poem, not current conservation statistics. Discuss the irony of a song that celebrates music while showing music used to destroy.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: explain the title and setting. 10–20: sequence the hunt. 20–30: compare the music with its result. 30–40: discuss consumer demand. 40–50: write about the final address.

## Questions
How does the flute change the hunt? Why is the dedication to Cecilia ironic?

course-31:1.title: Derek Walcott · Ruined House — title to verify
course-31:1.text:
# Derek Walcott · Ruined House — title to verify
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Title check · preliminary
The syllabus says “Ruined House.” A widely documented Walcott poem is “Ruins of a Great House”; it is likely but not verified that this is the intended text. Confirm the prescribed title and edition before relying on this guide.

## If the assigned poem is Ruins of a Great House
The speaker moves through the decayed remains of a grand house and its grounds. Rot, bones, limes and broken architecture evoke the passing of wealth and empire while calling attention to violence that made such grandeur possible. References to British literary and historical figures bring the culture of empire into the poem itself. The speaker’s anger at colonial crimes meets an impulse toward compassion, complicated by an allusion to John Donne’s reflections on human interconnectedness.

## Reading
The house’s ruin does not automatically erase historical harm: the poem suggests that its legacy persists. Avoid turning the ending into either simple forgiveness or the denial of anger. Check all allusions in the assigned edition.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: verify the title. 10–20: map images of decay. 20–30: trace the historical references. 30–40: discuss rage and compassion. 40–50: write a qualified interpretation.

## Questions
Why must the title be checked? How do ruin and continuing injustice coexist?

course-31:1.title: Dom Moraes · Sinbad
course-31:1.text:
# Dom Moraes · Sinbad
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Summary · detailed
The speaker addresses the legendary sailor Sinbad through compressed images of wind, waves, graves, diamonds, birds and travel. Journeys cross countries and require new maps. Old friends disappear into strange places while new acquaintances offer gestures whose warmth is uncertain. The speaker offers advice about choosing a rock and travelling companions, then returns to the wind and its unpredictable course. The final observation suggests that some people never know a stable home.

## Reading
The poem invokes the voyages of Sinbad without simply retelling all seven tales. Its fragmented lines and abrupt images make travel feel disorienting as well as adventurous. A travelling identity is one possible reading; avoid asserting that every line records an event in Moraes’s own life or assigning a single fixed meaning to every image.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce the legendary traveller. 10–20: trace sea and wind. 20–30: compare old and new friends. 30–40: discuss home and movement. 40–50: explain an image using two possible readings.

## Questions
What does the allusion to Sinbad contribute? Why is travel both exciting and unsettling?

course-31:1.title: Jorge Luis Borges · A Compass
course-31:1.text:
# Jorge Luis Borges · A Compass
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Summary · detailed
In this poem, originally “Una brújula” in Spanish, the speaker imagines everything as words in a language through which someone or something continually writes the world’s history. Ancient cities, the speaker and other people all pass through that immense, confused text. The speaker’s own life is difficult to understand, like a riddle or code; Babel suggests a multitude of voices and disorder. Behind names lies something that cannot be named. The speaker senses its shadow in the delicate moving needle of a compass, which reaches imaginatively towards a distant sea and resembles a clock in a dream or a stirring sleeping bird.

## Reading
An everyday instrument of orientation becomes an image of mystery rather than a final answer. Compare the huge scale of world history with the tiny needle. Translation can change rhythm, rhyme and individual word choices; identify your translator. This is a poem, not Borges’s detective story “Death and the Compass.”

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the language metaphor. 10–20: paraphrase history and Babel. 20–30: study the shift to the compass. 30–40: compare clock and bird images. 40–50: explain how direction coexists with mystery.

## Questions
Why compare the world to language? What can a compass suggest without solving the mystery?

course-31:2.title: José Saramago · Blindness — major story sequence
course-31:2.text:
# José Saramago · Blindness — major story sequence
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Content and access note
The novel contains confinement, sexual assault and violence. Blindness is used as a literary metaphor, a choice that blind readers and disability scholars may contest. Do not equate real blindness with moral failure, helplessness or social collapse. The novel was originally written in Portuguese; check your translator.

## The epidemic and quarantine
An unnamed driver suddenly sees only white while stopped at a traffic light. A man who helps him home steals his car and also loses his sight. An ophthalmologist examines the first man but cannot explain the condition; he and other patients soon become blind. Authorities confine affected people in a disused asylum guarded by soldiers. The doctor’s wife falsely claims to be blind so she can accompany him; she remains able to see.

## Life inside
More people arrive, food and sanitation deteriorate, and soldiers’ fear produces violence. A group of armed internees seizes the food and demands valuables. When valuables run out, the group demands that women be sent to them; the women are sexually assaulted and one dies. The doctor’s wife later kills the leader with scissors. Another woman sets fire to the occupiers’ ward. Survivors escape as the asylum burns and discover the epidemic has spread beyond the walls.

## City and fragile community
The doctor’s wife guides a small group through a city of hunger and disorder, including her husband, the first blind man and his wife, the girl with dark glasses, the boy and an old man with an eye patch. They find food and shelter in the doctor’s home and try to care for one another. A dog comforts the doctor’s wife. Her sight gives her practical power and a heavy burden; the others also form relationships and contribute to the group.

## Ending and interpretation
Members of the group unexpectedly regain their sight. Neither the cause nor the cure is explained. The wife fears for a moment that her own sight might fail. The novel asks about institutions, fear and responsibility, but its allegorical use of disability should be debated critically. This is a story guide, not a chapter-by-chapter commentary.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: set content and disability-aware boundaries. 10–20: trace epidemic and confinement. 20–30: discuss control of food. 30–40: compare harm and mutual care. 40–50: question the blindness metaphor.

## Questions
How do institutions shape the crisis? What are the risks of using blindness as a metaphor for ethical failure?

course-31:2.title: Romesh Gunesekera · Reef — story sequence
course-31:2.text:
# Romesh Gunesekera · Reef — story sequence
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Narrative frame
The adult narrator Triton, now living in England, meets a young Sri Lankan at a petrol station. The encounter leads him back through memories of his childhood and work in Sri Lanka. The story’s retrospective voice matters: what we learn of others comes through Triton’s attention and limitations.

## The household
As a boy Triton enters the home of Mister Salgado, an educated man interested in marine life and the erosion of coral reefs. The older servant Joseph intimidates him; after Joseph is dismissed and the cook Lucy leaves, Triton takes increasing responsibility for the household. He becomes a skilled cook, finds purpose in feeding guests and watches conversations about science and politics.

## Nili and change
Salgado’s relationship with Nili transforms the house. Triton helps create their shared occasions through elaborate meals and is emotionally invested in their happiness. Their relationship later breaks down amid jealousy and tension. Outside the house political conflict grows, although the sheltered domestic viewpoint does not show every event directly.

## Departure
Salgado and Triton leave for England. Triton gradually builds a more independent life and eventually runs a restaurant. Salgado later returns to Sri Lanka after news concerning Nili; Triton remains in London. Their different trajectories complicate the earlier bond between employer and servant.

## Interpretation
The reef suggests an ecosystem and a vulnerable boundary, but it need not stand for only one thing. Compare ecological change with political instability and ask how class and service shape Triton’s admiration. Verify chapter divisions in the assigned edition.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: explain the memory frame. 10–20: map the household. 20–30: trace Nili’s arrival and departure. 30–40: compare reef and political change. 40–50: write about Triton’s viewpoint.

## Questions
How does food mediate relationships? What can Triton observe, and what might his loyalty obscure?

course-31:2.title: Chinua Achebe · Things Fall Apart — major story sequence
course-31:2.text:
# Chinua Achebe · Things Fall Apart — major story sequence
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Content note
The novel includes domestic violence, the death of children, colonial violence and suicide. It depicts Igbo communities with internal debate and variation, not a single timeless “African culture.”

## Umuofia and Okonkwo
Okonkwo becomes respected through wrestling, farming and hard work, determined not to resemble his indebted father Unoka. His fear of appearing weak influences his treatment of his family. After a conflict between communities, the boy Ikemefuna comes to live in Okonkwo’s household. He grows close to Nwoye and calls Okonkwo father. When the community decides Ikemefuna must die, an elder advises Okonkwo not to take part; afraid of seeming weak, Okonkwo strikes him. Nwoye is deeply affected.

## Family and exile
Okonkwo values his daughter Ezinma, whose mother Ekwefi has endured the deaths of other children. Community ceremonies, stories and institutions show a complex social world, not just Okonkwo’s viewpoint. At the funeral of the elder Ezeudu, Okonkwo’s gun accidentally kills Ezeudu’s son. Because the killing is accidental, he and his family must leave for seven years. His maternal relatives receive him in Mbanta; his friend Obierika helps protect his interests.

## Mission and colonial rule
During exile missionaries gain converts, including Nwoye, who finds something meaningful in their message. His choice reflects both colonial intervention and tensions already present in his family and community. Political power and courts grow alongside the mission. On returning to Umuofia, Okonkwo finds the situation changed. Mr Brown’s approach to local leaders differs from that of his successor Mr Smith; neither stands for every colonial actor.

## Crisis and ending
After a convert unmasks an ancestral spirit during a ceremony, clan members destroy the church. The District Commissioner summons and imprisons leaders, including Okonkwo, and they are humiliated and fined. At a later meeting Okonkwo kills a court messenger; the others do not follow him into war. He dies by suicide. The commissioner imagines reducing the complex life to a small part of his own colonial book, exposing the violence of an outside narrative that refuses local voices.

## Interpretation
Analyse Okonkwo’s choices and gendered expectations alongside colonial institutions; neither alone explains the whole novel. This outline covers major events rather than all chapters.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: locate community and protagonist. 10–20: trace Ikemefuna and family. 20–30: explain exile and Nwoye’s conversion. 30–40: follow church and court conflict. 40–50: discuss the commissioner’s final framing.

## Questions
Why does Okonkwo join Ikemefuna’s killing? How does Achebe challenge the commissioner’s account of the community?

course-31:3.title: Yukio Mishima · The Damask Drum
course-31:3.text:
# Yukio Mishima · The Damask Drum
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Context and warning
Mishima adapts a traditional Japanese Noh story into a modern setting. Read the assigned translation and distinguish this version from the older play. The plot includes humiliation and suicide.

## Story
An elderly janitor working in a Tokyo office building becomes infatuated with a woman associated with a dress shop across the way. Others learn of his feelings and cruelly tell him that he can win her attention if she hears him beat a drum. The drum is covered in damask cloth and cannot sound in the way promised. His effort becomes an impossible test and a spectacle for others. Humiliated and despairing, he kills himself.

His ghost returns and continues the effort to make himself heard. Unlike the revenge of the traditional version as commonly described, the modern version leaves the woman unable to hear the ghostly drum, and his suffering continues. The silence raises questions about desire, cruelty, communication and the limits of revenge.

## Performance
Discuss sound and silence, the modern office and the presence of a ghost. A person’s refusal to return affection does not itself justify harassment; distinguish the janitor’s longing from the deliberate humiliation by others.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce adaptation and content warning. 10–20: sequence the impossible task. 20–30: compare living man and ghost. 30–40: discuss sound and cruelty. 40–50: compare modern and traditional versions cautiously.

## Questions
Why is the drum an impossible promise? What does silence do in performance?

course-31:3.title: Jack Davis · No Sugar
course-31:3.text:
# Jack Davis · No Sugar
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Context and content
Set in Western Australia during the Great Depression, the play depicts the Millimurra–Munday Aboriginal family under racist so-called protection policies. It includes forced removal, imprisonment and sexual violence. Its characters speak in English and Nyoongah; language is part of the play’s resistance and community life.

## Northam and forced removal
Gran, Jimmy, Milly, Sam and their family live at Government Well near Northam, managing inadequate rations and limited opportunities. Jimmy and Gran challenge officials. Authorities plan to move the Aboriginal community to Moore River, using alleged disease as a justification while disregarding the families’ wishes. The family is removed despite its protests.

## Life at Moore River
The settlement is controlled by officials, including superintendent Neal. The family maintains relationships, humour and resistance under restriction. Joe and Mary fall in love; Mary becomes pregnant. They escape together and return toward Northam, but are caught. Joe is imprisoned and Mary is returned to the settlement.

## Violence and ending
Neal punishes Mary, whipping her after she resists work that she fears will expose her to his sexual advances. Gran and Milly support her, and her baby is born at the settlement. During an official Australia Day ceremony Jimmy challenges the rhetoric of protection; he collapses and dies. Joe returns, names the baby Jimmy after his uncle and obtains permission to leave with Mary and their child. Their departure suggests continuing family and resistance, not an end to the system’s violence.

## Performance
Contrast official speeches with family dialogue and song. The play dramatises colonial control from an Aboriginal perspective and should be read in relation to the particular people and policies it represents.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce setting and content. 10–20: trace forced removal. 20–30: discuss Joe and Mary. 30–40: compare official language with family experience. 40–50: consider the ending and song.

## Questions
What does “protection” mean to the officials and the family? How does family support function as resistance?

course-31:4.title: Gao Xingjian · The Temple
course-31:4.text:
# Gao Xingjian · The Temple
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Translation and story
The assigned story is available in Mabel Lee’s English translation from Chinese. A narrator and his new wife Fangfang, happy on their honeymoon after difficult years, leave a delayed train on impulse to explore a town. The apparently peaceful place turns out to be busy and commercial. Directed to an old temple, they cross a river, climb a hill and find a neglected building with broken walls, weeds and traces of ordinary agricultural use.

A stern-looking man arrives carrying melons. He shares one with the couple, who offer cake in return. A boy with him wants to catch grasshoppers. The narrator asks if the child is his son; the man explains that he is a cousin’s child whom he hopes to adopt. When Fangfang asks about his wife, he says nothing and walks away. The couple recognise that their question may have touched a painful subject, but the story does not explain his circumstances.

They notice a precarious roof tile that may fall. From a distance they watch the man and boy leave together; the child runs ahead and back, holding his cage. Fangfang playfully imagines that the man caught the five grasshoppers the boy wanted. The story closes with the narrator returning to the memory of the temple.

## Reading
The fleeting encounter qualifies the couple’s happiness with an awareness of other lives and unspoken pain. The tile suggests vulnerability, but the text does not say it falls or injures anyone. Hospitality crosses the travellers’ initial assumptions about the man.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map the journey. 10–20: describe the temple. 20–30: trace food and conversation. 30–40: discuss silence and the loose tile. 40–50: write what the ending does and does not establish.

## Questions
How do the couple’s assumptions change? What remains unspoken about the man?

course-31:4.title: Katherine Mansfield · A Suburban Fairy Tale
course-31:4.text:
# Katherine Mansfield · A Suburban Fairy Tale
New Literatures in English · Semester 5

## Story sequence
Mr and Mrs B sit in their warm suburban dining room after wartime rationing, enjoying breakfast and discussing desirable food. Their small, delicate son Little B notices hungry sparrows outside in the cold and asks his parents to feed them. Absorbed in their newspaper and meal, they dismiss his request and refuse to open the window.

Behind the curtain Little B sees the sparrows become little boys in brown coats, crying for food. He tries to make his parents see and hear, while his father dismisses talk of famine. The parents discover their child apparently outside among the hungry boys, himself asking for food. They finally open the window and invite them in, but the boys turn back into sparrows and fly away. The story ends before any simple rescue is achieved.

## Reading
The fairy-tale transformation interrupts the comfort of the breakfast room. The parents’ abundance and denial contrast with the child’s imaginative attention to hunger. The boundary of the window separates security from need; its opening comes too late. Discuss whether the transformation is literal, imagined or deliberately unresolved.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare inside and outside. 10–20: track the parents’ food talk. 20–30: retell the transformation. 30–40: discuss famine and the late opening. 40–50: write about the ending’s ambiguity.

## Questions
Why do the parents finally act? What does the story leave uncertain about the transformation?

course-32:0.title: What is linguistics? Dimensions and fields
course-32:0.text:
# What is linguistics? Dimensions and fields
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Definition and method
Linguistics is the systematic study of human language: its structure, use, acquisition and change. A linguist can collect utterances, record patterns, propose a generalisation and test it against further evidence. Description asks how a language variety works; prescription recommends forms for a particular social purpose. Studying a non-standard variety descriptively does not mean denying the practical value of a formal written convention.

## Core dimensions
Phonetics studies how speech sounds are produced, transmitted and perceived. Phonology studies their organisation and contrast in a language. Morphology examines word structure; syntax examines how words form larger structures. Semantics studies conventional meaning, while pragmatics studies meaning in context, including what a speaker implies.

## Interdisciplinary work
Sociolinguistics investigates language variation, identity and social power; psycholinguistics examines processing and acquisition; neurolinguistics relates language to the nervous system; computational linguistics develops and studies computational models; applied linguistics addresses practical questions such as language teaching. Historical linguistics investigates change and relationships across time. These fields overlap.

## Language and linguistics
English, Tamil and Indian Sign Language are languages; linguistics is a discipline that studies languages. Signed languages are full human languages with their own structure, not merely gestures or copies of spoken languages. Fluency in several languages is valuable but is not a substitute for studying evidence and analysis.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish language and the discipline. 10–20: map core branches. 20–30: sort examples by field. 30–40: compare description and prescription. 40–50: propose a question and evidence.

## Questions and practice
Which branch studies word structure? Which might study accents and social identity? Answer: morphology; sociolinguistics.

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:0.title: Language as a symbolic system
course-32:0.text:
# Language as a symbolic system
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Signifier and signified
In Saussure’s model a linguistic sign joins a signifier—the associated sound pattern—and a signified, a concept. For example, the English sound pattern for “tree” is associated by speakers with a concept of a tree. The signified is a concept, not simply the physical tree itself. A written word can represent the sign, but Saussure’s original discussion distinguishes the linguistic sound-image from marks on a page.

## Convention and arbitrariness
There is generally no natural necessity connecting the sequence /triː/ to the concept: other languages use different words. This is arbitrariness of the sign. Speakers cannot individually replace words at will and expect to be understood; conventions are shared socially. Sound symbolism and onomatopoeia complicate a claim that every connection is completely arbitrary.

## Beyond vocal symbols
The syllabus emphasises vocal symbols; spoken languages do use them, but human language is not restricted to speech. Signed languages use visual-manual signs with their own linguistic systems. Some signed forms resemble what they refer to, yet conventional signs also need to be learned and can vary across languages.

## Value and relations
A sign’s value is shaped by its relationships to other signs in a system. Analyse a word in a phrase and contrast it with alternatives rather than treating words as isolated labels.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare a word across known languages. 10–20: identify form and concept. 20–30: test arbitrariness and exceptions. 30–40: discuss spoken and signed modalities. 40–50: write a signifier/signified example.

## Questions and practice
In the word “tree,” what is the signified? Why does arbitrariness not mean that individuals can change conventions at will?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:1.title: Airstream and organs of speech
course-32:1.text:
# Airstream and organs of speech
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Airstream mechanisms
Most English speech uses pulmonic egressive airflow: air from the lungs moves outward through the vocal tract. Airstream direction and source matter: some languages also use ejectives with glottalic egressive airflow, implosives typically with glottalic ingressive airflow, and clicks using a lingual/velaric airstream mechanism. These are not ordinary English phonemes; avoid presenting English as the measure of possible speech.

## From lungs to lips
Air passes through the trachea and larynx. Vocal folds in the larynx may vibrate, producing voicing. Above them, the pharynx, mouth and nasal cavity shape the sound. When the velum is lowered, air can pass through the nose, as in [m] and [n]; when raised, nasal airflow is blocked for typical oral sounds.

## Active and passive articulators
An active articulator moves towards another surface: the lower lip and parts of the tongue are common examples. A passive articulator is the surface approached, such as the upper teeth, alveolar ridge or hard palate. For [f], the lower lip approaches the upper teeth; for [t], the tongue approaches the alveolar region in a common English articulation. Different speakers and languages can use different contact patterns.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: draw the airway. 10–20: identify lungs, larynx and cavities. 20–30: test voicing gently with fingers at the throat. 30–40: identify active/passive articulators. 40–50: compare oral and nasal airflow.

## Questions and practice
What makes [f] labiodental? What changes when the velum is lowered?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:1.title: Classifying consonants: voicing, place and manner
course-32:1.text:
# Classifying consonants: voicing, place and manner
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Three labels
A consonant can be described by voicing, place of articulation and manner of articulation. For instance [p] is a voiceless bilabial plosive: the lips close, airflow is blocked then released, and the vocal folds do not vibrate during the closure. [b] is its voiced counterpart in a basic description. Actual voicing timing varies by accent and context.

## Places
Bilabial: both lips, [p b m]. Labiodental: lower lip and upper teeth, [f v]. Dental: tongue near teeth, [θ ð] in many English descriptions. Alveolar: tongue near the ridge behind upper teeth, [t d n s z l]. Postalveolar: tongue behind that ridge, [ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ]. Palatal: tongue body near hard palate, [j] as in “yes.” Velar: tongue body near soft palate, [k ɡ ŋ]. Glottal: at the glottis, [h] in many descriptions.

## Manners
Plosive: complete closure followed by release, [p t k]. Nasal: oral closure with nasal airflow, [m n ŋ]. Fricative: narrow constriction creates turbulent noise, [f s ʃ]. Affricate: stop closure followed by a fricative release, [tʃ dʒ]. Approximant: articulators approach without the friction of a fricative, [j w ɹ]. Lateral approximant: airflow passes around the tongue’s side, [l].

## Exercise with answers
Describe [m]: voiced bilabial nasal. Describe [s]: voiceless alveolar fricative. Describe [k]: voiceless velar plosive. IPA [j] is the initial sound in “yes,” not the usual English letter j sound.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: hear a voiced/voiceless contrast. 10–20: locate places on a mouth diagram. 20–30: practise manners. 30–40: describe [m], [s] and [k]. 40–50: compare articulatory descriptions.

## Questions and practice
How do [s] and [z] differ? Answer: primarily in voicing in this basic classification.

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:1.title: Vowels and cardinal-vowel reference points
course-32:1.text:
# Vowels and cardinal-vowel reference points
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## How vowels differ
Vowels are described using approximate tongue height (close to open), tongue position (front to back), lip rounding and other properties such as duration or nasalisation. The labels describe relative tongue positions, not an exact photograph of a mouth. A diphthong involves a movement in vowel quality within a syllable; a monophthong has relatively stable quality.

## Cardinal vowels
Daniel Jones’s cardinal vowel system supplies learned reference qualities for describing vowels across languages; they are not a list of the vowels of English or of any one speaker. The eight primary reference vowels are commonly listed in order as [i e ɛ a ɑ ɔ o u], moving down the front and then up the back of the vowel space. The front set is unrounded; the back set has [ɑ] unrounded and [ɔ o u] rounded. The scheme is partly articulatory and partly auditory; trained listening is important.

## Example and caution
In many English accents, the vowel of “see” is represented broadly /iː/ and that of “sit” /ɪ/. These symbols and precise qualities depend on the transcription convention and accent. Cardinal [i] is a reference point, not an assertion that all “see” vowels are exactly identical to it. IPA vowel charts show rounded members to the right when two symbols share a cell.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: contrast vowel and consonant. 10–20: explain height, backness and rounding. 20–30: sketch the vowel quadrilateral. 30–40: locate primary reference vowels. 40–50: distinguish a reference quality from a language’s phoneme.

## Questions and practice
What are the three main articulatory dimensions? Why are cardinal vowels not simply an English vowel list?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:1.title: Phonemes, allophones and minimal pairs
course-32:1.text:
# Phonemes, allophones and minimal pairs
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Phonetics versus phonology
A phone is a speech sound in phonetic description, usually shown in square brackets [ ]. A phoneme is a contrastive category in a particular language or variety, conventionally shown between slashes / /. Phonemic and phonetic representations serve different analytical purposes; symbols are not letters of ordinary spelling.

## Minimal pair
Two words make a minimal pair when their forms differ in one sound in the same position and their meanings differ. In many English varieties “fan” /fæn/ and “van” /væn/ show /f/ versus /v/. The spelling change happens to match the sound change here, but sound—not the number of letters—is the test.

## Allophones and distribution
Allophones are contextually or otherwise varying realisations of one phoneme in an analysis. In many English accents, initial /p/ before a stressed vowel is aspirated [pʰ] in “pin,” while after /s/ it is typically unaspirated [p] in “spin.” This pattern is associated with complementary distribution: each variant appears in different environments. It is illustrative, not a claim that every English speaker has identical phonetics or that [pʰ] and [p] are allophones in every language. In some languages aspiration distinguishes words.

Free variation means alternatives can occur in the same environment without changing lexical meaning, though style, region or social context may influence their choice. Complementary distribution alone is not sufficient to prove that two very dissimilar sounds are allophones; phonetic similarity and the wider system also matter.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: contrast sounds and spelling. 10–20: define phone and phoneme. 20–30: test fan/van. 30–40: compare pin/spin aspiration. 40–50: distinguish complementary distribution and free variation.

## Questions and practice
What evidence does fan/van provide? Does a difference between [pʰ] and [p] necessarily signal different phonemes in every language?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:1.title: Suprasegmentals: stress, rhythm, pitch and tone
course-32:1.text:
# Suprasegmentals: stress, rhythm, pitch and tone
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Beyond individual segments
Suprasegmental features extend over or organise syllables and larger stretches of speech. Stress is prominence; pitch concerns perceived frequency; intonation is the pattern of pitch across an utterance. Length, timing and rhythm also contribute to prosody.

A stressed English syllable is often longer and clearer, and may carry a pitch movement, but prominence is not simply shouting. In some varieties “REcord” as a noun and “reCORD” as a verb differ in stress and vowel quality. Sentence prominence can shift to highlight a contrast: “I wanted TEA” may contrast tea with coffee.

Tone languages use pitch patterns to distinguish lexical or grammatical meanings; intonation can also structure utterances. Tone is not equivalent to an English question tune, and signed languages have their own non-manual and timing features. Patterns vary with language, dialect and communicative context.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify individual sounds. 10–20: contrast word stress. 20–30: say a sentence with different focus. 30–40: distinguish pitch, tone and intonation. 40–50: write an example.

## Questions and practice
How is word stress different from sentence prominence? Why is pitch not the same thing as tone in every language?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:2.title: Phonemic transcription: a guided method
course-32:2.text:
# Phonemic transcription: a guided method
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Choose a variety first
A phonemic transcription represents contrastive categories, not spelling or every detail of an individual performance. Write / / for phonemic transcription and [ ] for a phonetic transcription. The International Phonetic Alphabet provides symbols, but conventions and phoneme inventories vary by accent.

The examples below use a broad, traditional non-rhotic British teaching transcription; they are practice in that convention, not a judgment that Indian English or another accent is inferior. Dictionary notation can differ. Non-rhotic here means /r/ is normally not pronounced after a vowel unless a following vowel permits linking.

## Worked examples
• “cat” /kæt/: three phonemes, despite the three letters coincidentally matching the number of symbols.
• “ship” /ʃɪp/: three phonemes; the letters sh represent one consonant.
• “chair” /tʃeə/: two phonemes in this broad teaching analysis, /tʃ/ and /eə/. Some modern British descriptions use a different vowel symbol; phoneme counts depend on analysis.
• “teacher” /ˈtiːtʃə/: primary stress before the first syllable, and no final /r/ in this non-rhotic model.
• “about” /əˈbaʊt/: primary stress before the second syllable; the first vowel is schwa.

## Practice with answers
Transcribe “dog,” “fish” and “pen”: /dɒɡ/, /fɪʃ/, /pen/ in this model. In other accents the vowel in “dog” can differ. Compare your own pronunciation and a dictionary’s accent label, and do not mix two transcription systems in one answer without explaining it.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify accent and notation. 10–20: transcribe ship and cat. 20–30: practise stress marks. 30–40: transcribe the three exercise words. 40–50: compare with a dictionary and discuss variation.

## Questions and practice
Why is “ship” three phonemes rather than four letters? What does /ˈ/ mark?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:2.title: Word stress: syllables and prominence
course-32:2.text:
# Word stress: syllables and prominence
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Identify the syllable
A syllable normally has a nucleus, often a vowel; consonants can occur before or after it. Word stress is relative prominence assigned to a syllable. In IPA, primary stress /ˈ/ is written immediately before the stressed syllable, and secondary stress /ˌ/ before a less prominent stressed syllable where relevant.

## Examples
In the teaching convention used here, “TAble” /ˈteɪbəl/ is initially stressed, while “aBOUT” /əˈbaʊt/ has stress on the second syllable. In many English accents the noun “REcord” /ˈrekɔːd/ and verb “reCORD” /rɪˈkɔːd/ contrast in stress and vowel quality; pronunciation differs across varieties. Unstressed syllables often have reduced vowels such as schwa /ə/, but not every unstressed vowel is schwa.

## Analysis practice
1. Mark the stressed syllable in TAble, aBOUT, and TEAcher.
2. Explain why a stress mark is written before, not after, the syllable.
3. Listen to a dictionary recording in a named accent. The best evidence is the spoken form, not an invented universal rule based solely on spelling.

Do not equate stress solely with loudness: duration, vowel quality and pitch can all contribute.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: clap or mark syllables without requiring vocal participation. 10–20: listen for prominence. 20–30: mark the three examples. 30–40: compare noun and verb record. 40–50: explain schwa and variation.

## Questions and practice
Where is primary stress in /əˈbaʊt/? Answer: the second syllable. Can unstressed syllables contain vowels other than schwa? Yes.

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:2.title: Sentence stress, pitch and intonation
course-32:2.text:
# Sentence stress, pitch and intonation
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Prominence and focus
Sentence stress is the prominence given to a word or syllable in a phrase. English speakers often highlight new or contrastive information. In “AMMU brought the book,” a possible contrast is who brought it; in “Ammu brought the BOOK,” it may be what she brought. The surrounding conversation determines the interpretation; capitals here merely show prominence.

## Pitch and intonation
Pitch is perceived highness or lowness, related to vibration frequency for voiced sounds. Intonation is the changing pitch pattern across a phrase. A rise, fall or fall–rise may signal meanings such as continuation, completion, surprise or a question, but no single contour has one fixed meaning in all contexts or varieties. Yes/no questions can rise, while a question can also fall.

## Teaching practice
Give learners three short contexts before saying the same sentence with different prominence. Ask which word answers the question. Avoid stereotypes about an accent sounding “wrong” or “uneducated.” Participation may include pointing to a transcript, hearing a recording or observing a pitch display; speech production is not mandatory for every learner.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: ask a context question. 10–20: mark prominence in two answers. 20–30: compare pitch contours. 30–40: interpret the same contour in different contexts. 40–50: write a short explanation.

## Questions and practice
In answer to “Who brought the book?”, which word might receive focus in “Ammu brought the book”? Answer: Ammu.

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:3.title: Morpheme, morph and allomorph
course-32:3.text:
# Morpheme, morph and allomorph
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Definitions
A morpheme is a minimal meaningful or grammatical unit in an analysis. A morph is a form that realises a morpheme in a particular word. Allomorphs are alternative realisations of the same morpheme, often conditioned by sound or grammar. A word may contain one morpheme, as “book,” or several, as “books” = BOOK + plural.

## Free and bound
A free morpheme can occur independently as a word: “book.” A bound morpheme cannot usually stand alone in that function: plural -s or the prefix un-. Roots provide a lexical core; affixes attach to a base. Prefixes occur before, suffixes after; infixes are inserted within a base in languages that use them. A word and a morpheme are not synonymous: “unhappy” is one written word with more than one morpheme.

## Allomorphs of English plural
In a common pronunciation, “cats” ends [s] after voiceless /t/, “dogs” ends [z] after voiced /ɡ/, and “buses” ends [ɪz] after a sibilant. These are forms of the plural morpheme, not three different plural meanings. “Children” uses an irregular plural form; not every plural is formed by adding the regular suffix. Actual realisations vary by accent.

## Practice
“Unhelpful” can be analysed un- + help + -ful. “Walked” has WALK + past tense, whose suffix is typically [t] in that context. Analyses of some words are disputed; specify the evidence rather than assuming every string of letters is a morpheme.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare word and morpheme. 10–20: segment books and unhappy. 20–30: compare cats, dogs and buses. 30–40: classify free and bound forms. 40–50: check two answers.

## Questions and practice
What is the difference between a morpheme and an allomorph? Identify the plural allomorph in cats: [s] in the example accent.

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:3.title: Inflection, derivation and word formation
course-32:3.text:
# Inflection, derivation and word formation
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Inflection versus derivation
Inflection marks grammatical information without usually creating a new lexeme or changing word class: “walk” → “walked” marks past tense; “book” → “books” marks plural. Derivation forms a new lexeme and may change class or meaning: “happy” → “happiness” adds a noun-forming suffix; “happy” → “unhappy” changes meaning without changing class. The distinction varies across languages and individual analyses.

## Other processes
Compounding joins bases, as “toothbrush” or “blackboard”; its meaning is not always fully predictable. Reduplication repeats all or part of a form and can mark different meanings in different languages. Conversion changes a word’s grammatical use without an overt affix, as noun “email” to verb “to email.” Blending joins parts of words, as “brunch”; clipping shortens a word, as “lab” from “laboratory.” Borrowing adopts a form from another language.

## Worked analysis
“Teachers” = teach + derivational -er + inflectional plural -s. “-er” forms a noun referring to a person associated with teaching; plural -s marks more than one. Not every English word ending in the letters er contains this suffix, so analyse meaning and structure, not letters alone.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define inflection and derivation. 10–20: analyse walk/walked and happy/happiness. 20–30: sort compounds, blends and clippings. 30–40: segment teachers. 40–50: discuss a locally known example.

## Questions and practice
Is -s in books inflectional? Yes. Does derivation always change word class? No, as in happy/unhappy.

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:3.title: Sandhi and grammatical categories
course-32:3.text:
# Sandhi and grammatical categories
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Sound at a boundary
Sandhi refers to sound changes conditioned at or near the meeting of forms. Internal sandhi occurs within a word; external sandhi occurs between words. Sanskrit grammatical traditions describe many such rules systematically, and analogous boundary effects can be studied in other languages. Do not assume a single rule applies to all languages or speakers.

In some English speakers’ connected speech “ten books” may have [m] before [b], as the final nasal takes on the following bilabial place. This is a possible assimilation, not a compulsory spelling change or a universal pronunciation. Sanskrit examples should be analysed using the assigned system and diacritics.

## Grammatical categories and parts of speech
Categories such as number, tense, person, aspect and case encode grammatical distinctions in different ways. English nouns commonly distinguish singular/plural; verbs can distinguish present/past. Languages do not all mark the same distinctions, and a grammatical category need not be expressed by a separate suffix.

Parts of speech classify words by grammatical behaviour: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, determiners, prepositions and others. A word’s class is determined by distribution and use, not just by a simple meaning label. “Run” can be a verb (“they run”) or a noun (“a run”).

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: locate a word boundary. 10–20: explain assimilation. 20–30: distinguish internal and external sandhi. 30–40: identify tense and number. 40–50: compare noun and verb uses of run.

## Questions and practice
What changes in a possible “ten books” pronunciation? Why is a part of speech not determined by spelling alone?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:4.title: Linguistic knowledge, competence and performance
course-32:4.text:
# Linguistic knowledge, competence and performance
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Knowledge of language
Speakers and signers know patterns they can use to understand or produce new utterances. Linguistic knowledge includes categories, combinations, sound or sign patterns and meanings. Much of it is implicit: a speaker need not be able to state a grammatical rule to use it.

## Chomsky’s distinction
In a classic formulation, competence is a speaker–hearer’s underlying linguistic knowledge, while performance is actual use in particular situations. Hesitation, memory limitations, distraction and social context may affect performance. The distinction is a theoretical tool, not a claim that a slip makes a speaker incompetent. Actual examples and judgments help researchers infer knowledge, but they are evidence to interpret, not a transparent window into it.

Communicative competence is a broader idea associated with Dell Hymes: effective language use also involves knowing what is appropriate in a social situation. Different frameworks define and investigate these concepts differently; a community’s variety must not be judged by the rules of another variety.

## Practice
A learner knows a pattern but hesitates when tired. The rule knowledge can be discussed as competence; the hesitating utterance is performance. List other possible explanations before claiming to know what a person has mentally represented.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce a familiar slip. 10–20: distinguish knowledge from an utterance. 20–30: examine judgment as evidence. 30–40: compare communicative competence. 40–50: write a cautious example.

## Questions and practice
Does a hesitation prove absence of competence? No. Why should judgments be interpreted within a variety?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:4.title: Syntax, categories and tree diagrams
course-32:4.text:
# Syntax, categories and tree diagrams
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Words in structure
Syntax studies how words combine into phrases and sentences. Lexical categories include noun (N), verb (V), adjective (Adj) and adverb (Adv); functional categories include determiners (Det), among others. A phrase is a group of words organised around a head. “The child” is a noun phrase (NP); “reads a book” is a verb phrase (VP).

## A simple phrase marker
For “The child reads a book,” a simplified labelled bracket notation represents the same hierarchy as a tree:
[S [NP [Det The] [N child]] [VP [V reads] [NP [Det a] [N book]]]]
S stands for sentence; the first NP is the subject, and the second NP is the object of reads. Draw S at the top, branch to NP and VP, then add the labelled words and second NP as the brackets show. Other frameworks use different labels and more layers.

## Rules and tests
For this illustration, S → NP VP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP. These are simplified rules for the example, not an exhaustive account of English. A constituent is a unit within the structure. Substitution provides one clue: “The child” can be replaced by “she” in a suitable context. A single test does not always settle a disputed analysis.

## Practice
Make a matching bracket structure for “A student reads the poem.” Answer: [S [NP [Det A] [N student]] [VP [V reads] [NP [Det the] [N poem]]]].

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: sort categories. 10–20: find subject and predicate. 20–30: work through the bracketed tree. 30–40: draw the practice example. 40–50: check each branch against the rules.

## Questions and practice
In the example, which NP is the object? Answer: “a book.” What does a phrase marker show? Hierarchical grouping.

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:4.title: Generative grammar and structural ambiguity
course-32:4.text:
# Generative grammar and structural ambiguity
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## What “generative” means
A generative grammar is a formal system intended to characterise possible structures in a language using a finite set of principles or rules. It aims to explain linguistic knowledge, not to prescribe “proper” usage or imply that people consciously recite rules. Generative approaches have changed over time; do not treat one tree or terminology as the only version.

## Hierarchy and ambiguity
“I saw the person with binoculars” can mean I used binoculars to see the person, or I saw a person who had binoculars. A structural analysis represents the phrase “with binoculars” as attaching in different places: roughly, to the verb phrase in the first reading or the noun phrase in the second. Context can favour one reading; not every listener finds both equally natural.

## Related sentence patterns
“The teacher praised the student” and “The student was praised by the teacher” share participants but differ in grammatical arrangement. Transformational analyses relate structures using formal operations; modern accounts differ about the details. Do not describe a passive as simply reversing word order: it introduces auxiliary be and a participle, and a by-phrase may be omitted.

## Practice
For “The student was praised,” identify the understood person praised: the student. Is the person who praised explicitly named? No.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: explain a grammar as a system. 10–20: use an ambiguity. 20–30: show alternative attachments. 30–40: compare active and passive. 40–50: explain why approaches differ.

## Questions and practice
Explain two readings of “I saw the person with binoculars.” Why is a passive not merely a reversal of words?

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-32:4.title: Semantics and synchronic / diachronic variation
course-32:4.text:
# Semantics and synchronic / diachronic variation
Introduction to Linguistics · Semester 6

## Semantics
Semantics studies conventional linguistic meaning in words, phrases and sentences. Lexical semantics considers relations such as synonymy (similar meaning), antonymy (opposition) and polysemy (related senses of one word). Perfect interchangeability is rare: context can distinguish near-synonyms. Compositionality is the principle that the meaning of a complex expression depends on its parts and how they combine; idioms show that interpretation is not always transparently predictable.

Semantics is often distinguished from pragmatics, which considers context-dependent inference. If someone says “It is cold here,” the sentence describes temperature; in context it might also function as a request to close a window. The request is an inference, not the only meaning of the sentence.

## Two perspectives on language
A synchronic study examines a language or varieties at a particular time: for example, comparing how groups use a present-day pronunciation. A diachronic study investigates change over time: for example, comparing earlier and later English plural patterns. Both are analytical perspectives; a synchronic snapshot does not imply a language is uniform or unchanging.

Words, pronunciation and grammar change, and variation may reflect geography, social networks, context and generations. Avoid claiming that older forms are inherently better or that all speakers of a region behave alike.

## Practice
Classify “comparing present-day varieties of Tamil” as synchronic and “tracing English vowels over centuries” as diachronic. Explain why the first study can still find variation.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define semantics. 10–20: distinguish sentence meaning from an inferred request. 20–30: compare synchronic and diachronic examples. 30–40: create one example of each. 40–50: check against definitions.

## Questions and practice
Is comparing a language across centuries synchronic or diachronic? Diachronic. Does synchronic study exclude variation? No.

Teaching note: examples depend on the language, speaker and descriptive framework. Compare the assigned textbook and use the indicated variety when transcribing.

course-33:0.title: From the 1890s to modern poetry
course-33:0.text:
# From the 1890s to modern poetry
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## A change, not a clean break
At the end of the nineteenth century, British and Irish poetry included Victorian inheritance, aestheticism, symbolism, empire and debates about religious belief, industrial society and artistic form. Thomas Hardy bridges periods rather than fitting neatly into an automatic division between Victorian and modern. The early twentieth century brought experiments in diction, image, perspective and form, alongside continuing use of sonnets, ballads and other inherited structures.

## Georgians and war
“Georgian poetry” often refers to writers associated with anthologies published in the reign of George V. Landscape and accessible lyric are common, but the poets are diverse; do not equate every pastoral poem with a single political viewpoint. The First World War (1914–18) produced very different responses: Brooke’s patriotic idealisation and Owen’s account of a wounded veteran cannot simply be merged into one “war poetry” position.

## Imagism and modernism
Imagism favoured direct treatment, precision and economical language; its practitioners and publications changed over time. Pound’s and Eliot’s wider modernist work uses resources such as allusion, abrupt juxtaposition, multiple voices and formal experiment. Eliot’s The Waste Land should not simply be labelled an Imagist poem: the syllabus groups works under that heading, but the poem exceeds the movement.

## Irish poetry
The Irish literary revival developed through cultural and political debates, folklore, theatre and poetry. Yeats’s work connects Irish traditions with mythology, modern politics and his own symbolic system. Avoid treating Irish writing as merely a branch of English nationalism.

## Comparative method
Compare how landscape works in Belloc and how a city works in Eliot, or how Brooke and Owen present a soldier. Identify voice, form, historical context and a difference; movements are useful descriptions, not rigid boxes.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: timeline and prior ideas. 10–20: compare landscape and city. 20–30: define Imagism without reducing modernism to it. 30–40: compare two wartime perspectives. 40–50: write one continuity and one change.

## Discussion and revision
How do Imagism and modernism overlap without being identical? Why should Georgian poets not all be treated alike?

course-33:1.title: Hilaire Belloc · The South Country
course-33:1.text:
# Hilaire Belloc · The South Country
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary in sequence
Living in the Midlands, the speaker remembers the hills of the south and imagines walking there with childhood companions. He acknowledges the distinctive landscapes of northern and western England, yet describes the South Country, especially Sussex, with particular affection. Pines, sand and the bare Downs revive his sense of home.

The poem’s mood darkens when the speaker admits he cannot recover all that is lost and fears solitude in old age. He imagines friendship among people of the Sussex Weald and, if fortune permits, a thatched house near woods and sea, filled with local songs and old friends.

## How it works
Repetition, simple rhythms and recurring references to landscape give the poem a song-like quality. Place is emotional and social, not merely scenery: the desired country promises continuity and companionship. Its praise of southerners is the speaker’s affectionate preference, not an objective ranking of regions. Notice that the wished-for home remains a future hope rather than an event already achieved.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map the speaker’s locations. 10–20: paraphrase the landscape. 20–30: trace the turn to loneliness. 30–40: discuss the imagined house. 40–50: write about place and memory.

## Discussion and revision
Why does the speaker remember childhood friends? How does anxiety complicate the celebration of Sussex?

course-33:1.title: G. K. Chesterton · A Prayer in Darkness
course-33:1.text:
# G. K. Chesterton · A Prayer in Darkness
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The speaker asks heaven not to make personal anguish the centre of the universe: even if the speaker descends into despair or dies by suicide, the world should continue to be nourished and grass should grow. The next stanzas acknowledge sun, rain and fruit, then express gratitude that stars, moth and flower remain beyond the speaker’s power to damage through grief or anger.

The final image imagines Christ at the Crucifixion hearing crickets despite accounts of the darkened sun. It juxtaposes extreme suffering with the continuance of ordinary life. The speaker’s imagined response is a theological and poetic claim, not a factual account that students must accept.

## Interpretation and care
Prayer, apostrophe, seasonal images and sharp contrasts move between darkness and gratitude. The poem can be read as seeking humility and comfort in a world not controlled by personal pain, while its difficult suggestion of divine “scorn” complicates easy consolation.
