It refers to suicide; discuss the imagery sensitively without suggesting that distress should be dismissed or that a person should endure it alone.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the prayer’s addressee. 10–20: paraphrase the four stanzas. 20–30: compare grief and nature. 30–40: interpret the Crucifixion image with care. 40–50: explain one tension.

## Discussion and revision
How do images of ordinary life continue beside suffering? Why is the ending open to more than one response?

course-33:1.title: D. H. Lawrence · A Sane Revolution
course-33:1.text:
# D. H. Lawrence · A Sane Revolution
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The speaker proposes revolution for enjoyment rather than solemnity, hatred, money or a conventional political programme. He mischievously dismisses equality and a revolution supposedly made for the working classes, imagining instead people able to live as independent “little aristocracies.” The final movement opposes exhausting labour to work that might be enjoyed.

## Tone and questions
The poem’s repeated imperatives and colloquial, deliberately provocative statements make it sound like a spoken challenge. Its irony unsettles expectations: “sane” does not mean careful policy, and the speaker’s rejection of equality deserves critical scrutiny, not automatic endorsement. Ask whose freedom a revolution defined this way might secure and whose structural inequality it might overlook.

## Reading strategy
Trace each “don’t” to the alternative proposed. Then distinguish the speaker’s playful provocation from a complete or coherent blueprint for social reform.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define revolution and tone. 10–20: list rejected motives. 20–30: analyse humour and imperatives. 30–40: debate the equality claim. 40–50: write a balanced response.

## Discussion and revision
What distinction does the speaker draw between work and labour? What makes the poem’s politics provocative?

course-33:1.title: Rupert Brooke · The Soldier
course-33:1.text:
# Rupert Brooke · The Soldier
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
A soldier imagines dying abroad. He asks to be remembered through the idea that his buried body would make a corner of foreign soil permanently English. He presents England as the source of his body, landscape, experiences, friendship and values. In the concluding movement he imagines his purified heart returning those gifts in a peaceful, idealised afterlife.

## Form and interpretation
The 14-line sonnet gives a formal, concentrated shape to patriotic feeling. Personification makes England a nurturing presence; images of flowers, rivers and home turn national identity into intimate memory. The poem was written early in the First World War and expresses a particular ideal of sacrifice, not the only contemporary experience of it.

The phrase about a foreign field can be read both as devotion and as a claim that English identity transforms another land; invite discussion of whose land and perspective are absent. Compare with Owen’s “Disabled”: the contrast is useful but neither poet stands for every soldier.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: note speaker and imagined situation. 10–20: paraphrase the octave and sestet. 20–30: examine England as a nurturing figure. 30–40: question national perspective. 40–50: compare with Owen.

## Discussion and revision
How does the sonnet connect the soldier’s body and homeland? What does the poem leave outside its idealised vision?

course-33:1.title: Robert Graves · The God Called Poetry
course-33:1.text:
# Robert Graves · The God Called Poetry
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The speaker imagines poetry as an ancient god who trains the poet through increasingly difficult feats, like a creature jumping through hoops. The playful image of a singing cricket or grasshopper suggests both performance and dependence on a demanding master. Poetry is older than the landscape and appears in different voices and forces.

The god’s conflicting commands push the poet toward both harsh denunciation and gentler, compassionate song. Poetry is a powerful, contradictory presence rather than one fixed mood; the speaker must learn to respond to its opposing impulses.

## Techniques
Personification turns an art into an unpredictable deity. Comic comparisons sit beside images of immense age and authority, making artistic vocation at once exhilarating and demanding. Contrast the poet’s apparent freedom to sing with the master’s power to command. Read the assigned text carefully before reducing the poem to a single moral about art.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify speaker and god. 10–20: track the performance images. 20–30: compare contrary instructions. 30–40: discuss power and creativity. 40–50: write an interpretation.

## Discussion and revision
Why is the hoop-jumping image both comic and serious? What do the god’s contrasting voices suggest about poetry?

course-33:2.title: Siegfried Sassoon · The Poet as Hero
course-33:2.text:
# Siegfried Sassoon · The Poet as Hero
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The speaker addresses listeners who know his angry attacks on war and ask why his earlier sweetness has changed. He recalls an idealised youthful image of himself as a shining knight seeking the Grail. He now says goodbye to Galahad, the chivalric figure, and replaces heroic fantasy with anger, hatred and the memory of killed friends. His songs become an attempted response to the wrongs done to them and a source of absolution.

## Analysis
The sonnet form joins an inherited heroic tradition to a voice that questions heroic display. Arthurian allusion makes the change of self-image vivid. Yet the closing desire to avenge wounds is not entirely peaceful: the poem exposes the speaker’s own violent feelings even as it rejects a romantic picture of war. “Absolution” invites debate about whether poetry can heal guilt, avenge friends or only express grief.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: explain the Grail and Galahad. 10–20: paraphrase the speaker’s change. 20–30: analyse the address to listeners. 30–40: discuss anger and absolution. 40–50: contrast Brooke.

## Discussion and revision
Why does the speaker reject Galahad? How does the poem complicate a simple opposition between violence and protest?

course-33:2.title: Wilfred Owen · Disabled
course-33:2.text:
# Wilfred Owen · Disabled
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary in sequence
A young veteran sits in a wheeled chair, waiting for dark; he has lost limbs in war and depends on others. Sounds of boys playing bring memories of an earlier life when he was admired, active and physically confident. The poem moves back to the night he decided to enlist: drink, uniform, social approval and a desire to impress contributed to his decision; he was underage, but an officer accepted him.

After injury, his return draws little public celebration. He remembers compliments from before the war and observes that people now treat him differently. At the end he anticipates institutional routines and wonders why the people who should put him to bed do not come.

## Form and interpretation
Shifts between past and present make social abandonment visible; sound and colour contrast earlier pleasure with the present setting. Owen criticises recruitment culture and public neglect, not merely an individual decision. Discuss the period’s assumptions about masculinity and attractiveness critically: disability does not make a person’s life inherently worthless. The veteran’s isolation is intensified by social attitudes and lack of support, not simply by his impairment.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify present and flashback. 10–20: reconstruct recruitment and return. 20–30: examine sound, colour and contrast. 30–40: discuss social responses to disability. 40–50: compare a claim with evidence.

## Discussion and revision
What influences the veteran’s enlistment? How do public attitudes contribute to his isolation?

course-33:2.title: Thomas Hardy · The Children and Sir Nameless
course-33:2.text:
# Thomas Hardy · The Children and Sir Nameless
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
Sir Nameless complains about children playing in his park and congratulates himself on having no offspring. Hoping to preserve his greatness, he commissions a large armed alabaster effigy for after his death. Three hundred years later, church restorers cannot trace his descendants and put the statue in the floor beneath schoolchildren’s seats. Their shoes wear away its name and nose; bored during the sermon, they wonder who the old stone man was.

## Analysis
The irony is carefully constructed: the children he rejected become the agents of his physical and historical erasure. His chosen memorial does not deliver the control over remembrance he imagined. Three eight-line stanzas compress centuries into a brief narrative. The poem questions pride and monuments, but need not be reduced to an instruction that everyone must have children; time, chance and institutions also shape what survives.

## Placement in the syllabus
The poem appears in the unit headed “War Poets,” but its story concerns memory, vanity and time rather than a battlefield. Do not invent a war setting to force a match with the heading.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: narrate the three stages. 10–20: explain the commissioned effigy. 20–30: identify the final reversal. 30–40: consider memory and institutions. 40–50: write on irony.

## Discussion and revision
What happens to the effigy after 300 years? Why is the ending ironic?

course-33:2.title: W. H. Auden · Refugee Blues
course-33:2.text:
# W. H. Auden · Refugee Blues
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
A speaker addresses a beloved companion as German Jewish refugees face exclusion. The city contains wealth and poverty, yet no home for them. Their former country remains on the map but is inaccessible; old passports cannot renew themselves like a tree. A consul’s declaration that a person without a passport is officially dead clashes with the speakers’ undeniable survival. A committee postpones help, while public prejudice and Hitler’s threat make danger explicit.

Animals appear to move or receive shelter more freely than the refugees. In a dream a huge building offers them no room; the ending imagines soldiers searching for the pair in snow.

## Form and historical context
Recurring three-line stanzas, repeated address and refrain draw on blues lyric techniques. Blues has African American musical roots; the poem adapts a tradition rather than inventing it. The 1939 setting concerns Nazi persecution and restrictive asylum policies. Its intimate “you and me” makes bureaucratic decisions personal, while the repeated contrasts between life and official recognition expose the cruelty of treating documents as more real than people.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: outline 1930s context. 10–20: trace passport and committee scenes. 20–30: listen to repeated phrases and form. 30–40: compare animals and refugees. 40–50: discuss the ending.

## Discussion and revision
Why is “officially dead” ironic? What does the recurring address to a loved one achieve?

course-33:2.title: Stephen Spender · Ultima Ratio Regum
course-33:2.text:
# Stephen Spender · Ultima Ratio Regum
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The title means “the last argument of kings,” a phrase associated with guns as instruments of power. The speaker sees a young person dead under olive trees and contrasts that particular life with the economic and military forces behind the shooting. The boy had no prominent place in employment records, fashionable institutions or newspapers; a wall separates the powerless from wealth.

In the remembered scene, spring petals and the casually dropped cap give way to machine-gun fire. The final section asks readers to consider a life counted as valueless by bureaucratic and economic measures, and asks whether the expenditure of bullets can justify the death.

## Analysis
The contrast between spring imagery and industrial weapons makes violence interrupt ordinary possibility. Monetary and statistical language is used ironically, not as the speaker’s own measure of human worth. The poem is commonly associated with the era of the Spanish Civil War; the text does not establish every detail of the boy’s biography, so avoid inventing his identity or motives.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: translate the title. 10–20: trace images of the young person. 20–30: contrast money and life. 30–40: analyse the final questions. 40–50: write one evidence-based paragraph.

## Discussion and revision
Why does the speaker invoke economic records and bullets? How does spring imagery affect the scene?

course-33:3.title: T. S. Eliot · The Waste Land: map and method
course-33:3.text:
# T. S. Eliot · The Waste Land: map and method
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## What kind of poem?
Published in 1922, The Waste Land is a five-part modernist poem made from shifting voices, scenes, registers, languages and literary or religious allusions. It has no single straightforward plot or reliably continuous speaker. Its discontinuities invite readers to make connections without assuming that every voice is Eliot’s personal opinion. Ezra Pound’s editorial role in shaping the published poem is important.

## Five-part map
1. The Burial of the Dead: spring, memory, a distressed landscape, prophecy and the crowd in an unreal city.
2. A Game of Chess: a luxurious interior and anxious conversation juxtaposed with a pub conversation about Lil and Albert.
3. The Fire Sermon: the Thames, fishing, voices and a typist’s encounter, followed by allusions to Augustine and the Buddha.
4. Death by Water: the drowned Phlebas and a warning to remember mortality.
5. What the Thunder Said: a difficult journey through drought and ruins, thunder’s commands and fragments of possible peace.

## Recurring questions
Water can suggest both renewal and drowning; fragments can be ruins and resources for rebuilding. The poem’s treatments of gender, sexuality, class, empire and antisemitic stereotypes deserve critical discussion rather than unqualified celebration. Its ending does not establish that the whole world has been healed. Use the next five notes to teach each section in sequence.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: place 1922 and the war. 10–20: map five sections. 20–30: track water across the poem. 30–40: identify changing voices. 40–50: distinguish interpretation from a single plot.

## Discussion and revision
Why is it risky to assign every voice to one speaker? How can water carry opposing meanings?

course-33:3.title: The Waste Land · I. The Burial of the Dead
course-33:3.text:
# The Waste Land · I. The Burial of the Dead
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Sequence
Spring, conventionally a season of renewal, is described as cruel because it stirs memory and desire from apparently protective winter. A voice recalls childhood in the mountains and a sledging episode; the poem then moves into a dry landscape of broken images. An encounter associated with hyacinths ends in a moment of speechless uncertainty. A fortune-teller, Madame Sosostris, displays cards including a drowned figure. The scene shifts to a London crowd crossing the bridge under the pressure of modern routine and literary echoes of the dead.

## Teach the connections
Rather than treating these episodes as one continuous autobiography, ask what happens when remembering or awakening is painful. The fortune-teller’s warning about water is not a simple plot prediction that resolves all later imagery. The confrontation with Stetson and the buried corpse disturbs the boundary between planting and death. The city crowd can evoke alienation and the aftermath of war; Dantean echoes make historical and literary layers interact.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map the changes in voice. 10–20: discuss spring and winter. 20–30: examine prophecy. 30–40: connect crowd and burial images. 40–50: write one supported interpretation.

## Discussion and revision
Why is spring’s usual symbolism reversed? What is unsettling about the buried corpse?

course-33:3.title: The Waste Land · II. A Game of Chess
course-33:3.text:
# The Waste Land · II. A Game of Chess
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Sequence
A richly decorated interior is described through objects, perfume and literary allusions, including the violent myth of Philomela. A tense exchange follows: one speaker presses for conversation and reassurance, while the other’s responses are fragmentary or internal. A second scene shifts to a pub voice telling another woman about Lil, her husband Albert’s return, her health, appearance and the pressures placed on her. Repeated closing-time calls interrupt the account; the section ends with echoes of Ophelia’s farewells.

## Interpretation
The juxtaposition links different social settings without making the experiences identical. Communication is strained, and intimacy is shaped by violence, economics, gender expectations and reproductive pressure. Chess suggests strategic relations, but not every figure needs to be assigned a chess piece. Philomela’s story of rape and silencing should be handled sensitively. Lil is talked about by another voice; ask how that affects our access to her experience.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the two settings. 10–20: annotate voice changes. 20–30: discuss silence and speech. 30–40: analyse Lil’s situation with care. 40–50: compare the scenes without flattening class differences.

## Discussion and revision
How do the two scenes contrast? Why does the Philomela allusion complicate the beautiful interior?

course-33:3.title: The Waste Land · III. The Fire Sermon
course-33:3.text:
# The Waste Land · III. The Fire Sermon
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Sequence
The Thames appears with traces of litter and absent festivities, while voices and fragments move between river, city and memory. A fisher figure and the prophet Tiresias become points of connection. The typist comes home; a young man visits and initiates a mechanical sexual encounter that the poem presents as indifferent and lacking mutual intimacy. The typist resumes her routine afterwards.

The section moves through further river voices and allusions to Augustine and the Buddha’s Fire Sermon. “Fire” can suggest desire, spiritual suffering and the possibility of release, though the different traditions cannot simply be equated.

## Close reading
Ask who sees, who speaks and what information is missing. Tiresias’s presence does not make every other character reducible to him. Discuss the encounter’s imbalance and lack of meaningful consent carefully; avoid blaming the typist. Note how quotations from song, ritual and canonical literature mingle with ordinary modern settings.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map river and city. 10–20: identify Tiresias. 20–30: discuss the typist episode sensitively. 30–40: compare fire and water. 40–50: analyse a shift in register.

## Discussion and revision
How does the Thames connect different fragments? Why should the typist’s viewpoint not be assumed to be fully known?

course-33:3.title: The Waste Land · IV–V. Death by Water and What the Thunder Said
course-33:3.text:
# The Waste Land · IV–V. Death by Water and What the Thunder Said
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## IV. Death by Water
Phlebas the Phoenician, once concerned with profit and loss, has drowned; currents have carried away the details of his worldly life. The brief section addresses the reader, urging remembrance of a shared mortality. Water here destroys rather than automatically purifies.

## V. What the Thunder Said
Images of rock, thirst, difficult travel and ruined cities dominate. A mysterious additional figure accompanies travellers in one passage; the chapel and the approach of rain raise possibilities that remain unstable. Thunder’s syllable “Da” prompts references to giving, sympathy and self-control from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. The speaker then gathers fragments, including several languages and literary references, ending with the repeated Sanskrit word “Shantih,” traditionally associated with peace.

## Interpreting the ending
Some readers hear a movement toward renewal; others stress discontinuity and unresolved crisis. Both should be tested against the words rather than presented as certain recovery or total despair. Eliot adapts religious materials through his own cultural position: discuss the source tradition respectfully and avoid treating it merely as exotic decoration.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: paraphrase Phlebas. 10–20: follow the journey through drought. 20–30: explain the thunder references. 30–40: compare alternative endings. 40–50: write a claim and evidence.

## Discussion and revision
Why does Phlebas complicate water as a symbol? Does the final word prove complete renewal? Explain.

course-33:3.title: Ezra Pound · The Return
course-33:3.text:
# Ezra Pound · The Return
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The speaker calls attention to a group returning hesitantly, their slow and wavering movement compared with snow in the wind. They are identified as gods once associated with awe and winged shoes. Silver hounds accompany them; remembered as swift and dangerous, the hunters and leash-men now seem slow and pale.

## Form and interpretation
Uneven line lengths, pauses and shifts in rhythm enact hesitation before recalling earlier speed. Classical imagery evokes a possible return of ancient powers, but the poem does not give a simple narrative explaining where they have been or exactly what their return means. Readers may see a revival of neglected artistic or spiritual energies, or the diminished survival of old gods; these are interpretations rather than stated facts.

The condensed image and musical movement relate to Pound’s modernist experiments. The poem was written around the time of early Imagism, but it should be read as a particular work, not as a checklist of movement rules.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify repeated movement words. 10–20: contrast returning gods and remembered speed. 20–30: read line breaks aloud or silently. 30–40: offer alternative interpretations. 40–50: support one with detail.

## Discussion and revision
How do rhythm and line breaks suggest hesitation? What changes between the past and the returning figures?

course-33:3.title: “An Expostulation” · attribution needs confirmation
course-33:3.text:
# “An Expostulation” · attribution needs confirmation
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Important syllabus uncertainty
The syllabus attributes “An Expostulation” to “C. D. Lewis,” normally understood as Cecil Day-Lewis. A poem with that exact title beginning with a complaint against science-fiction writers is widely attributed to C. S. Lewis, a different author. The title match alone does not establish that the syllabus intended this poem or that it intended to name C. S. Lewis. Confirm the assigned anthology or ask the department before teaching an attribution.

## Conditional orientation only
If the assigned text is C. S. Lewis’s poem subtitled “Against too many writers of science fiction,” its speaker questions journeys across immense fictional space that reproduce familiar earthly plots, and asks for strangeness, beauty and wonder instead. Its argument contrasts scale with imaginative discovery. This is not a verified summary of a Cecil Day-Lewis text.

## Classroom step
Compare author initials, opening line, subtitle and publication details in the prescribed edition. Once identified, replace this outline with an edition-specific reading. Do not silently substitute one author for the other.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare names and initials. 10–20: locate the assigned text. 20–30: compare title and opening line with a reliable edition. 30–40: discuss the conditional text only if confirmed. 40–50: record the bibliographic evidence.

## Discussion and revision
Why are C. S. Lewis and C. Day-Lewis not interchangeable? Which evidence would establish the intended poem?

course-33:3.title: Ted Hughes · The Hawk in the Rain
course-33:3.text:
# Ted Hughes · The Hawk in the Rain
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The first-person speaker struggles through rain and mud, feeling the earth pull at each step and the wind beat the body. Above, a hawk appears to hang still and controlled in the violent air. Its unshaken eye becomes a fixed point for the speaker, who contrasts the bird’s apparent mastery with human vulnerability.

In the final movement the speaker imagines a possible future in which the storm eventually throws the hawk down and its blood meets the land. This is a projection of mortality, not a report that the hawk has already crashed.

## Technique
Violent verbs and alliteration make weather and earth feel physically forceful. The vertical contrast between human below and bird above is complicated by their shared exposure to death. The hawk can be read as an image of will, instinct or a disturbing ideal of mastery, but the poem does not tell us exactly what the bird thinks.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map speaker and hawk. 10–20: collect weather verbs. 20–30: compare movement and stillness. 30–40: distinguish imagined future from observed action. 40–50: explain one reading of the hawk.

## Discussion and revision
Why is the hawk’s final fall conditional? What links the bird and the speaker despite their different responses?

course-33:4.title: W. B. Yeats · The Second Coming
course-33:4.text:
# W. B. Yeats · The Second Coming
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The opening describes a falcon moving beyond the falconer’s hearing as order seems to break apart: violence spreads, innocence is overwhelmed, and the most certain voices may be the worst. Expecting revelation and a Christian Second Coming, the speaker instead receives a disturbing vision from “Spiritus Mundi,” a concept of a shared symbolic store.

A sphinx-like shape with a lion’s body and a human head moves through desert sand. Darkness returns, but the speaker imagines a new historical era awakening after twenty centuries. The poem ends with a question about a rough beast moving towards Bethlehem to be born.

## Interpretation
The widening gyre relates to Yeats’s cyclical theory of history, while the inverted nativity makes birth ominous rather than reassuring. Written after the First World War amid wider upheaval, the poem does not identify the beast with one specific politician or event. Its rhetorical question and unresolved image make the future frighteningly uncertain.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: explain falcon/falconer. 10–20: map order and disorder. 20–30: examine the unexpected vision. 30–40: discuss cyclical history and Bethlehem. 40–50: write a supported interpretation.

## Discussion and revision
What expectation does the title create and how is it unsettled? Why should the beast not be assigned one certain identity?

course-33:4.title: Rudyard Kipling · Epitaphs of the War
course-33:4.text:
# Rudyard Kipling · Epitaphs of the War
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## What the sequence does
An epitaph is an inscription associated with the dead. Kipling’s sequence uses short imagined inscriptions in different voices and situations rather than telling one continuous story. The syllabus does not specify which individual epitaphs are assigned; confirm the course anthology before claiming that a particular selection is prescribed.

## Representative readings
“Common Form” gives the dead a bitter explanation that blames an older generation’s lies. “A Dead Statesman” imagines a politician confronting the young people killed through his falsehoods. “The Coward” gives a compressed account of a man led to death, inviting thought about fear and judgment. “Hindu Sepoy in France” acknowledges the bravery of an Indian soldier through a British speaker who does not know his religious powers; it invites discussion of both recognition and the limits of an imperial perspective.

Other epitaphs range from affirming military transformation to bitter irony, grief or accusation. Do not flatten the sequence into one anti-war slogan, or assume every speaker is Kipling. His own son John died in the First World War; biography can illuminate grief but should not be used as automatic proof for every voice.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define epitaph. 10–20: compare two contrasting voices. 20–30: consider irony and brevity. 30–40: discuss imperial perspective. 40–50: check which epitaphs the class is assigned.

## Discussion and revision
How does an epitaph give the dead a voice? What differs between the dead statesman and the Hindu sepoy?

course-33:4.title: Philip Larkin · The Whitsun Weddings
course-33:4.text:
# Philip Larkin · The Whitsun Weddings
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary in sequence
On a hot Whitsun Saturday, a speaker travels south by train. The journey begins with an almost empty carriage and observations of houses, farmland, canals, towns and industry. At successive stops the speaker gradually notices wedding parties on platforms and newly married couples boarding the train.

He observes relatives’ clothing and reactions: pride, embarrassment, boredom and excitement appear together. The couples sit in the same carriage without necessarily knowing one another. Their separate lives share this brief hour as the train approaches London. As it slows, the ending imagines a shower of arrows travelling out of sight and becoming rain.

## Interpretation
The poem moves from detached observation to an imaginative sense of shared transition. Its portraits can sound affectionate, comic or class-conscious and judgmental; students can test these tones against details. The final arrows and rain suggest several possibilities, including release, change, fertility or disappointment. They do not settle the future of each marriage. Whitsun is a Christian festival period; the poem presents wedding journeys, not a single ceremony.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: plot the train route. 10–20: identify changes in the speaker’s attention. 20–30: compare wedding guests’ reactions. 30–40: debate the final image. 40–50: explain tone using evidence.

## Discussion and revision
What links couples who do not know one another? Why can the final image support more than one reading?

course-33:4.title: Robert Bridges · Melancholia
course-33:4.text:
# Robert Bridges · Melancholia
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary
The poem describes desire turning toward despair: the sufferer forgets other people and praise, finding temporary relief in sleep. Uncertainty, once a space for hopeful ambition, now looks like a dark, starless wall. The second movement addresses the sufferer sharply as a “fool” for impossible desires and impatient despair, arguing that joy, love, beauty and youth still exist even when they cannot be felt.

## Form and interpretation
The 14-line poem moves from a description of suffering to an admonition. Darkness and constriction contrast with the imagined continuing splendour of the world. Its final claim that the sufferer is figuratively dead expresses the poem’s severe judgment; it is not a medical diagnosis or sound advice to blame people experiencing depression. Readers can question the speaker’s limited compassion while also exploring the contrast between outer life and inner perception.

## Edition check
Search results sometimes misattribute another poem called “Melancholia” to Bridges. The intended Bridges poem begins by describing the “sickness of desire”; check the assigned edition.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: paraphrase the first eight lines. 10–20: identify the shift in address. 20–30: compare dark imagery and continuing beauty. 30–40: discuss the judgment sensitively. 40–50: write on tone.

## Discussion and revision
What changes about uncertainty in the poem? Why should its severe rebuke not be treated as mental-health advice?

course-33:4.title: Louis MacNeice · Prayer Before Birth
course-33:4.text:
# Louis MacNeice · Prayer Before Birth
Modern Poetry · Semester 6

## Summary in sequence
An imagined unborn speaker repeatedly asks to be heard, comforted, provided for, forgiven and protected. Early threats include frightening creatures; the poem quickly turns toward dangers created by human beings: confinement, deception, drugs and violence. The speaker also asks for water, grass, trees, sky and an inner light.

The prayer anticipates being made to participate in wrong and asks for forgiveness and preparation for future encounters. It begs not to be turned into an obedient mechanism or an interchangeable object. The final extreme plea asks for death rather than such complete destruction of self.

## Analysis and context
The repeated opening and escalating requests imitate a litany. Alliteration and accumulation make danger feel relentless. The poem’s Second World War context informs its fear of coercion, but the unborn voice is an imaginative dramatic device, not a literal report of a baby’s thoughts. Its ending is disturbing: discuss it as a poetic expression of fear, not a recommendation for real-life action.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the imagined speaker. 10–20: group the requests. 20–30: examine repetition and sound. 30–40: discuss coercion and the ending sensitively. 40–50: write about one contrast between fear and hope.

## Discussion and revision
Why is the unborn voice effective? How does the poem connect individual identity with coercion?

course-34:0.title: Modern and postwar theatre: a working map
course-34:0.text:
# Modern and postwar theatre: a working map
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## The syllabus spans several periods
Modern British, Irish, European and American drama includes works before as well as after the Second World War. Wilde’s The Importance of Being Earnest and Shaw’s Arms and the Man belong to the 1890s; Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral is from the 1930s. Do not call all the prescribed plays postwar simply because the unit asks about postwar theatre.

Realist and naturalist drama developed domestic settings, social pressures and psychologically motivated conflict; symbolism and verse drama explored other ways of presenting inner or spiritual experience. After 1945, theatre responded in diverse ways to war, reconstruction, class, empire and social change. British “kitchen-sink” drama is often linked with Osborne’s Look Back in Anger; American theatre includes Miller’s critique of success and family life. These labels identify tendencies, not total national styles.

## Epic theatre
Brecht developed epic theatre before and after the war. Narration, songs, visible theatrical devices, episodic scenes and direct address can encourage critical distance, often called the alienation or defamiliarisation effect. The aim is not to prevent all feeling, but to invite audiences to question social arrangements and imagine alternatives. The Caucasian Chalk Circle links a custody story with a land dispute through this theatrical method.

## Theatre of the Absurd
Critic Martin Esslin used the term for diverse plays that challenge conventional plot, stable meaning and communication. It was not a formally unified group speaking with one voice. In Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, repetition, pauses and contradictory memories coexist with physical comedy and companionship; uncertainty need not mean that “nothing matters.”

## Performance lens
For any play ask: what can an audience see and hear, who controls space, how do pauses or props matter, and what effect might a different staging produce?

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: place the plays on a timeline. 10–20: distinguish realism, verse drama and epic theatre. 20–30: compare a narrator and direct address. 30–40: explore repetition in absurd drama. 40–50: state one limit of a label.

## Discussion and revision
Why are not all these plays postwar? How does Brechtian distance differ from simply removing emotion?

course-34:1.title: T. S. Eliot · Murder in the Cathedral
course-34:1.text:
# T. S. Eliot · Murder in the Cathedral
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## Setting and structure
Eliot’s verse drama reimagines the 1170 murder of Archbishop Thomas Becket in Canterbury. It has two parts separated by an interlude. The women of Canterbury form a chorus, giving collective voice to fear and, later, witness. The play is an interpretation of history, not a substitute for independent historical evidence.

## Part I: return and temptation
After exile, Thomas returns amid tension with King Henry II. Priests and the chorus debate what his return will bring. Four tempters offer pleasure, political office, an alliance with barons and finally the glory of martyrdom. The fourth is hardest: Thomas must reject the desire to die for personal pride or fame while remaining faithful to what he understands as his duty.

## Interlude and Part II
In a Christmas sermon Thomas reflects on celebration, sacrifice and the nature of martyrdom. On 29 December four knights confront him. Priests urge him to escape and eventually bring him into the cathedral. He refuses to turn it into a fortress; the doors are opened, and the knights kill him. The knights then directly address the audience with arguments justifying their act. Their defence is a dramatic perspective to examine, not an objective verdict. Priests and chorus respond to the death.

## Performance and themes
Verse, chant, chorus and sudden prose addresses connect spiritual conflict to public theatre. Discuss church and state, motive versus outward action, and the ordinary people who bear the consequences of political violence.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map the historical conflict. 10–20: compare the four temptations. 20–30: discuss the sermon. 30–40: stage the knights’ audience address. 40–50: assess its effect.

## Discussion and revision
Why is the fourth temptation distinct? What does the chorus contribute that Thomas’s speeches do not?

course-34:1.title: Samuel Beckett · Waiting for Godot
course-34:1.text:
# Samuel Beckett · Waiting for Godot
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## Act I
Vladimir and Estragon meet by a tree and wait for Godot. They talk, quarrel, consider leaving or hanging themselves, and pass time with routines involving boots and hats. Pozzo arrives leading Lucky by a rope, demonstrates his authority and orders Lucky to dance and then think; Lucky’s long fragmented speech ends when the others stop him. After Pozzo and Lucky depart, a boy reports that Godot will not come today but will come tomorrow. The pair say they will leave, but the stage direction has them remain.

## Act II
The pattern recurs with differences: the tree has leaves; the men’s memories are uncertain. Pozzo returns blind, accompanied by Lucky, now mute. After they fall, helping becomes a confused collective struggle. Pozzo denies or cannot recall meeting the pair earlier. A boy again brings a postponement; whether he is the same boy is not firmly established by the play. The pair contemplate departure and again do not move.

## How to read and stage it
Repetition is not identical: changing bodies, a tree and uncertain memory matter. The rope makes unequal power visible, while dependence complicates the relationship. Humour, affection, suffering and philosophical uncertainty coexist. Godot’s identity is never definitively explained; it is not correct to say the play proves he is God. Consider how silence, timing and physical action create meaning beyond the words.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: reconstruct Act I. 10–20: list differences in Act II. 20–30: stage a short silent waiting exercise. 30–40: discuss power and dependence. 40–50: defend an interpretation without fixing Godot’s identity.

## Discussion and revision
What changes between the acts? Why is “Godot is definitely God” not a settled answer?

course-34:2.title: George Bernard Shaw · Arms and the Man
course-34:2.text:
# George Bernard Shaw · Arms and the Man
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## Act I
During the Serbo-Bulgarian War, Raina admires her fiancé Sergius’s apparently heroic cavalry charge. A fleeing Swiss professional soldier fighting for Serbia, Captain Bluntschli, climbs into her room. He carries chocolate rather than extra cartridges and offers a practical view of war. Raina hides him from pursuers; with Catherine’s help he eventually escapes wearing Major Petkoff’s old coat.

## Act II
The war has ended. Petkoff and Sergius return; Sergius is frustrated with military advancement. His and Raina’s highly romantic exchange contrasts with his flirtation with Louka, the servant. Bluntschli returns to give back the coat, risking exposure of the earlier secret. The men welcome his help with military logistics, while Raina’s feelings grow more complicated.

## Act III
Bluntschli handles practical orders; Raina reveals that she had placed an inscribed photograph in the coat. Louka tells Sergius about the hidden soldier, and a proposed duel dissolves as the romantic misunderstandings unravel. Petkoff finds the photograph, although Raina briefly removes it from the coat. Nicola relinquishes his claim to Louka; Sergius and Louka become engaged. Bluntschli and Raina also agree to marry after his age and inherited wealth are clarified.

## Interpretation
Shaw contrasts glamorous heroic poses with survival, logistics and social reality. Yet practical Bluntschli’s wealth also helps make the marriage acceptable, which complicates a simple victory over class. Examine Louka’s agency and the limits imposed by service.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: contrast heroic and practical descriptions. 10–20: reconstruct the coat’s journey. 20–30: examine Louka and class. 30–40: stage a confrontation. 40–50: discuss comedy and war.

## Discussion and revision
Why is chocolate important? Does the ending fully escape class and money?

course-34:2.title: Bertolt Brecht · The Caucasian Chalk Circle
course-34:2.text:
# Bertolt Brecht · The Caucasian Chalk Circle
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## Prologue and frame
Two groups dispute use of a valley after wartime displacement. Their debate about who should work the land introduces a sung story that tests possession against socially useful care. Editions and productions may vary in their treatment of the prologue and names.

## Governor’s child and Grusha’s flight
After a coup, Governor Georgi Abashwili is killed and his wife Natella flees, leaving the child Michael behind amid the chaos. The servant Grusha, initially hesitant and aware of the danger, takes the child and carries him through a dangerous journey, including a precarious bridge. She seeks shelter with her brother and later enters a marriage of convenience to provide the child with a household. Her fiancé Simon’s return complicates their relationship when he sees her with a child and husband.

## Azdak and the test
A parallel strand follows village scribe Azdak, unexpectedly made judge during political turmoil. His decisions are irregular and often favour poor people, though his methods are also open to criticism. When Natella seeks Michael, partly to secure his inheritance, a custody case brings the stories together. Azdak orders the child placed in a chalk circle and tells both women to pull. Natella pulls; Grusha lets go rather than hurt Michael. Azdak awards the child to Grusha, disposes of the estate for public use, and in the same proceeding signs a divorce that frees her from her marriage. Azdak later disappears.

## Epic method
The singer, songs and episodic structure make the action openly theatrical. The closing principle favours those who care for or productively use things, but ask whether the play’s stylised test is a sufficient model for real custody decisions. Its relation to earlier Chinese and biblical stories can be explored without treating the plots as identical.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map the land dispute. 10–20: follow Grusha’s choices. 20–30: introduce Azdak. 30–40: stage and question the chalk test. 40–50: connect form and social argument.

## Discussion and revision
How do the valley and child disputes correspond? What makes Azdak’s justice both attractive and problematic?

course-34:3.title: John Osborne · Look Back in Anger
course-34:3.text:
# John Osborne · Look Back in Anger
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## Act I
Jimmy Porter, his wife Alison and their friend Cliff share a cramped room. Jimmy’s verbal attacks on class, politics and Alison punctuate an ordinary Sunday. Rough play between Jimmy and Cliff upsets the ironing board and Alison burns her arm. Alison privately tells Cliff she is pregnant but has not told Jimmy. Jimmy and Alison’s affectionate bear-and-squirrel game offers a temporary refuge from conflict. News that Alison’s friend Helena will visit provokes Jimmy’s hostility; he cruelly imagines Alison suffering the loss of a child.

## Act II
Helena learns more about the marriage and contacts Alison’s father, Colonel Redfern. Jimmy recalls watching his father die from wounds connected with the Spanish Civil War. When Hugh’s mother, who helped him financially, is dying, Jimmy asks Alison to accompany him; she goes to church with Helena instead. Alison leaves with her father. Helena remains, tells Jimmy about the pregnancy, and after an angry exchange they begin a relationship.

## Act III
Helena has taken Alison’s place in the household. Cliff plans to leave. Alison returns, having suffered a miscarriage. Helena decides that her relationship with Jimmy is wrong and leaves. Jimmy and Alison confront her loss and their pain, then return to their bear-and-squirrel game.

## Interpretation
The play’s postwar class anger and domestic realism are central, but Jimmy’s intelligence and frustration do not excuse his emotional cruelty. The final tenderness can be staged as reconciliation, retreat or an uncertain combination; the play does not prove the relationship’s problems are solved. Discuss miscarriage without presenting it as a deserved punishment.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map the household. 10–20: follow shifts in relationships. 20–30: discuss class and verbal power. 30–40: stage the animal game in two ways. 40–50: assess the ending.

## Discussion and revision
What does the bear-and-squirrel game provide? Why might the ending be both tender and troubling?

course-34:3.title: Arthur Miller · Death of a Salesman
course-34:3.text:
# Arthur Miller · Death of a Salesman
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## Act I: home and memory
Willy Loman returns early from a sales trip, too exhausted and distracted to drive safely. Linda urges him to ask for local work. Their adult sons Biff and Happy are visiting. Willy slips between present conversations and memories of Biff’s school football promise, the neighbour Bernard, and his successful brother Ben. Charley offers Willy work, which he refuses, though he accepts financial help. Linda tells the sons that Willy’s difficulties include attempts to take his own life. Biff proposes seeking business support from his former employer Bill Oliver.

## Act II: the failed hopes
Willy asks Howard for a local position and is fired. Bernard, now successful, and Charley offer contrasts to Willy’s values. Biff waits for Oliver, who does not remember him as he hoped; he steals Oliver’s pen and recognises the gap between his former position and his fantasies. At a restaurant the sons struggle to tell Willy the truth and leave him behind. Willy’s memories reveal that young Biff discovered him with another woman in a Boston hotel, shattering Biff’s faith in his father.

Willy buys seeds and attempts to plant them at night. In conversation with an imagined Ben he considers the life-insurance payment as a legacy. Biff confronts him and weeps; Willy understands his son’s love but still clings to the idea that his death can help him. Willy drives away and dies by suicide.

## Requiem
At the sparsely attended funeral Linda, Biff, Happy, Charley and Bernard respond differently. Biff questions Willy’s dreams; Happy intends to pursue them; Charley defends the vulnerability of a salesman’s life. Linda’s final words about paying off the house are painfully double-edged.

## Form and care
The play’s fluid transitions stage memory, not a simple chronological sequence. Discuss the pressure of economic insecurity and ideals of success without treating suicide as a solution or romantic sacrifice.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish present from memory. 10–20: track Biff and Willy’s hopes. 20–30: discuss the Boston revelation. 30–40: analyse seeds and the funeral. 40–50: compare characters’ readings of success.

## Discussion and revision
Why does Biff’s meeting with Oliver matter? What does the small funeral challenge?

course-34:4.title: Oscar Wilde · The Importance of Being Earnest
course-34:4.text:
# Oscar Wilde · The Importance of Being Earnest
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## Act I: London identities
In London, Jack Worthing uses the name Ernest and invents a troublesome brother as an excuse to leave his country responsibilities. His friend Algernon invents an invalid named Bunbury for similar escapes. Jack proposes to Gwendolen, who is attracted to the name Ernest. Her mother Lady Bracknell refuses consent after learning that Jack was found as a baby in a handbag at Victoria Station.

## Act II: the country house
Algernon arrives at Jack’s country home pretending to be the fictional brother Ernest and courts Jack’s ward Cecily. She has already imagined a romance with that name. Jack arrives intending to announce his brother’s death, only to find Algernon impersonating him. Gwendolen visits; she and Cecily first clash when each believes herself engaged to Ernest, then discover both men have deceived them. The men arrange to be christened Ernest.

## Act III: the handbag
The women seek explanations. Lady Bracknell initially approves Cecily’s fortune but Jack withholds consent to her engagement while his own is blocked. The mention of Miss Prism prompts a revelation: years earlier she accidentally put a manuscript in a pram and a baby in her handbag, leaving the bag at the station. The bag identifies Jack as Lady Bracknell’s sister’s son and Algernon’s older brother. Military records reveal his father’s name was Ernest, the name Jack was given. The couples reunite and the title’s pun returns.

## Analysis
Epigram, reversals and implausible coincidence satirise respectability, class, marriage and the gap between appearance and conduct. The ending rewards aristocratic ancestry as well as mocking its importance: this tension is part of the comedy.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: draw the invented identities. 10–20: follow who loves which “Ernest.” 20–30: stage the tea scene. 30–40: analyse the handbag revelation. 40–50: discuss satire and its limits.

## Discussion and revision
What is Bunburying? Why is Jack’s final identity both a resolution and a joke?

course-34:4.title: J. M. Synge · Riders to the Sea
course-34:4.text:
# J. M. Synge · Riders to the Sea
Modern Drama · Semester 6

## Opening: a family waiting
In a cottage on the Aran Islands, Cathleen and Nora receive clothing taken from a drowned man found far north. Their brother Michael is missing. They hide the bundle from their mother Maurya until they can check whether it belongs to him. Maurya has already lost her husband and other sons to the sea and fears for Bartley, her remaining son.

## The journey and recognition
Bartley plans to take horses to a fair despite dangerous conditions. Maurya tries to stop him and does not give him a blessing as he leaves. The sisters send her after him with bread. While she is away they identify Michael’s clothing through its stitching, confirming his death.

## Vision and ending
Maurya returns saying she saw Bartley on the red mare and Michael, in fine clothes, riding behind on the grey pony; her distress prevented her giving Bartley the bread and blessing. The vision is a dramatic experience of the supernatural, not something the audience can independently verify. Neighbours bring Bartley’s body: the grey pony knocked him into the sea. Maurya blesses the dead and, in grief, acknowledges that no one lives forever.

## Reading and staging
This one-act tragedy combines domestic work, economic necessity, religious practice and mourning. The sea sustains the island community while threatening life; it is more than a simple villain. Maurya’s final composure need not mean that grief has disappeared. Notice how offstage events, clothing, the loaf and sound bring the wider world into a small room.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify each family member. 10–20: follow the clothing and bread. 20–30: discuss vision and offstage action. 30–40: examine the sea as livelihood and threat. 40–50: interpret Maurya’s final response.

## Discussion and revision
How do the sisters identify Michael’s clothes? Why does Bartley’s decision involve both danger and livelihood?

course-35:0.title: Lord Jim · From youthful dreams to the Patna inquiry
course-35:0.text:
# Lord Jim · From youthful dreams to the Patna inquiry
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Opening and narrative method
Jim, the son of an English clergyman, grows up imagining adventurous acts of courage at sea. The opening moves across time: we first learn of his later work as a water-clerk, then his training and career. A storm on a training ship reveals a gap between his imagined heroism and hesitation in action. Later an injury leaves him in port; he signs on as chief mate of the ageing Patna.

## The voyage
The steamer carries hundreds of Muslim pilgrims. After an underwater collision, the officers fear that a damaged bulkhead will give way; there are too few usable boats for everyone. Jim becomes caught between a sense of duty and the panic of the other officers. He jumps into their boat, leaving the pilgrims aboard. The ship does not sink: a French gunboat finds and tows it, and the pilgrims survive. Their survival does not erase the abandonment.

## The inquiry and Marlow
Jim attends the official inquiry; the officers’ certificates are cancelled. Marlow, initially a spectator at the hearing, becomes involved in Jim’s story. Over conversation, Jim attempts to explain the jump and Marlow listens, judges and revises his understanding. Captain Brierly, a respected officer connected to the inquiry, dies by suicide, complicating any easy division between confident professional and failed man.

## How to read
The event emerges through delayed, overlapping accounts rather than a single immediately complete scene. Ask whose words we hear and whose experience is left marginal. The pilgrims are essential to the ethical issue, yet the narrative gives them much less individual attention than Jim.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish chronology from order of telling. 10–20: reconstruct the voyage. 20–30: discuss the inquiry. 30–40: examine the pilgrims’ limited perspective. 40–50: explain a narrative delay.

## Discussion and revision
Did the Patna sink? Why does its survival not settle the ethical question?

course-35:0.title: Lord Jim · Patusan, friendship and Jewel
course-35:0.text:
# Lord Jim · Patusan, friendship and Jewel
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## After the inquiry
Marlow helps Jim find work in ports, but reminders of the Patna repeatedly drive Jim away. Marlow consults the trader Stein, who reflects on romantic ideals and recommends a post in Patusan, a remote river district. Stein sends a silver ring as a token of friendship for his old associate Doramin.

## Arrival and alliances
Rajah Allang detains Jim, who escapes and reaches Doramin’s community. Doramin’s son Dain Waris becomes a close friend. Jim helps organise an attack on Sherif Ali’s stronghold, including the difficult movement of artillery. His success and subsequent conduct earn considerable trust; he becomes known as Tuan Jim.

## Jewel and the cost of a new life
Jim falls in love with Jewel, the daughter of the deceased woman associated with the trading post and stepdaughter of the resentful Cornelius. Jewel fears abandonment, drawing on what she has seen of her mother’s life. Jim promises not to leave her. Marlow visits and sees Jim’s apparent security, while also questioning whether the new role fully resolves the earlier crisis.

## Critical perspective
Patusan is not an empty stage created for a European hero: Doramin, Dain Waris, Jewel and Tamb’ Itam have interests and relationships of their own. The novel’s colonial language and unequal attention to non-European characters deserve scrutiny. Avoid treating Marlow’s judgments as neutral truth.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: locate Jim’s repeated departures. 10–20: trace the ring and alliance. 20–30: discuss Jewel’s fears. 30–40: question the colonial viewpoint. 40–50: write about trust.

## Discussion and revision
What does Stein’s ring enable? Why does Jewel fear Jim will leave?

course-35:0.title: Lord Jim · Brown’s arrival and the ending
course-35:0.text:
# Lord Jim · Brown’s arrival and the ending
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## The narrative frame changes
Marlow’s spoken account ends before the full story is known. Later a selected listener receives a packet of documents, including Marlow’s written reconstruction. Marlow draws on different reports, including accounts from Tamb’ Itam, Jewel and the dying Gentleman Brown. The layered sources leave room for uncertainty and bias.

## The crisis
Brown and his armed followers arrive seeking supplies and are contained after fighting with local forces led by Dain Waris. Jim negotiates safe passage for them and accepts responsibility for the decision. Cornelius secretly guides Brown along a back channel. Tamb’ Itam delivers Jim’s message and silver ring to Dain Waris, but Brown’s men then attack the camp and kill Dain Waris. Tamb’ Itam kills Cornelius during the aftermath.

## Jim’s choice
Jewel and Tamb’ Itam urge Jim to defend himself or escape. Jim instead goes to the grieving Doramin, who shoots him. For Jim, accepting the consequences may appear to recover a sense of honour; for Jewel it breaks his promise not to abandon her. Marlow cannot close the story with a single uncontested judgment.

## Teaching focus
Compare Jim’s two decisions under pressure: abandoning the Patna and trusting Brown. Neither event is identical. Ask whether the ending places Jim’s ideal of honour above the living people who depend on him.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the sources in the packet. 10–20: map the river and ambush. 20–30: compare Jim’s and Jewel’s viewpoints. 30–40: debate honour and responsibility. 40–50: write an evidence-based judgment.

## Discussion and revision
How does Brown evade Dain Waris’s guard? Why might Jewel see Jim’s final action as betrayal?

course-35:1.title: Sons and Lovers · Chapters 1–6: the Morel family
course-35:1.text:
# Sons and Lovers · Chapters 1–6: the Morel family
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Publication and setting
The syllabus prints 1915, but the novel was first published in 1913; 1915 is the publication year of Lawrence’s The Rainbow. Compare the assigned edition. The novel begins in a Nottinghamshire mining community, focusing on Gertrude Morel, her miner husband Walter and their children.

## Chapters 1–3
Gertrude’s early attraction to Walter gives way to disappointment over money, drinking, deception and anger. During a violent quarrel he locks her outside while she is pregnant. Paul is born into an increasingly strained home. Walter’s illness and financial insecurity expose the family’s dependence on work and neighbours. Gertrude increasingly invests hope and affection in her eldest son William.

## Chapters 4–6
Paul grows sensitive to his mother’s moods and to conflict at home. He begins work at a Nottingham surgical-appliance firm; art and imagination remain important to him. William advances in London and becomes engaged to a fashionable woman, but dies after illness. Gertrude’s grief is overwhelming. When Paul later becomes dangerously ill with pneumonia, she nurses him and her emotional life turns increasingly toward him.

## Interpretation
A psychoanalytic reading may examine desire, rivalry and family attachment, but it is one interpretive lens, not a clinical diagnosis of fictional people. Class, industrial labour, gender and constrained choices also shape the household.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: locate the mining setting. 10–20: map Morel family relations. 20–30: trace William’s career and death. 30–40: discuss Paul’s illness and maternal attachment. 40–50: compare psychological and social explanations.

## Discussion and revision
How does the family’s economic position affect Gertrude’s choices? Why should Freudian analysis not be the only lens?

course-35:1.title: Sons and Lovers · Chapters 7–11: Miriam, art and conflict
course-35:1.text:
# Sons and Lovers · Chapters 7–11: Miriam, art and conflict
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Chapters 7–8
During recovery and afterwards Paul spends time at the Leivers family’s Willey Farm. He and Miriam develop an intense friendship involving books, conversation, learning and the natural world. Attraction is complicated by embarrassment, religious expectations and Paul’s uncertainty. His mother feels threatened by Miriam’s influence. Family tensions continue, including conflict with Walter and concern about Arthur’s choices.

## Chapters 9–10
Paul breaks with Miriam but cannot make a clean emotional separation. She introduces him to Clara Dawes, a woman interested in women’s rights and separated from her husband Baxter. Paul gains recognition for painting and develops his work as an artist. These developments broaden the novel beyond a simple triangle of mother, son and lover.

## Chapter 11
Paul and Miriam attempt a sexual relationship, but expectations of sacrifice, guilt and mutual misunderstanding make it painful. Paul eventually breaks away again. Read Miriam as a person with ambitions, religious beliefs and decisions, not merely as an obstacle to Paul’s development; his account of what she wants is not necessarily the whole truth.

## Key question
The mother–son bond can illuminate Paul’s divided loyalties, but it does not excuse his cruelty or establish that Miriam alone is responsible for their difficulty.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare farm and mining town. 10–20: trace Paul and Miriam’s friendship. 20–30: identify Clara and artistic work. 30–40: examine narrative sympathy and gender. 40–50: state a non-reductive interpretation.

## Discussion and revision
What draws Paul and Miriam together? What pressures make intimacy difficult?

course-35:1.title: Sons and Lovers · Chapters 12–15: illness and aftermath
course-35:1.text:
# Sons and Lovers · Chapters 12–15: illness and aftermath
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Chapters 12–13
Paul and Clara begin an affair after the break with Miriam. Clara’s independence and marriage to Baxter Dawes complicate any easy account of freedom. Paul and Baxter come into conflict, including a physical fight. Meanwhile Gertrude’s health deteriorates and a tumour is discovered. Paul’s pleasure and anxiety increasingly coexist.

## Chapter 14
Paul visits Baxter during illness and the former rivals begin to understand one another. Gertrude’s cancer advances. Paul and Annie care for her during a difficult decline. Distressed by her suffering, Paul puts a large quantity of morphia in her milk; she dies later. This ethically troubling fictional act should not be presented as a guide to real medical decisions. Clara and Baxter ultimately move toward reconciliation.

## Chapter 15
Paul and his father leave the family house for separate lodgings. Grieving, Paul struggles to work or paint and is drawn toward thoughts of death. Miriam meets him and raises marriage, but he refuses. In the final movement he turns away from darkness toward the town. This suggests a possibility of continuing, not a guarantee that he is healed or that every relationship is resolved.

## Analysis
The ending combines bereavement, dependence and uncertain survival. Treat the novel’s depictions of grief and suicidal thoughts sensitively, and allow students to question the costs of Paul’s relationships for Miriam and Clara.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: follow Paul and Clara. 10–20: trace illness and caregiving. 20–30: discuss ethical uncertainty. 30–40: examine the final image. 40–50: write a cautious interpretation.

## Discussion and revision
How does Paul’s relationship with Baxter change? What does the final movement suggest without proving?

course-35:2.title: A Portrait of the Artist · Chapters 1–2
course-35:2.text:
# A Portrait of the Artist · Chapters 1–2
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Chapter 1: childhood, school and politics
The novel begins with a child’s sensory impressions and a story told by his father; language and perception develop with Stephen Dedalus. At Clongowes Wood College he experiences homesickness and school hierarchies. At Christmas dinner adults argue bitterly about Charles Stewart Parnell, nationalism and the Catholic Church, introducing political conflict through a child’s incomplete understanding.

Back at school Father Dolan strikes Stephen’s hands with a pandybat after wrongly assuming he has broken his glasses to avoid work. Encouraged by classmates, Stephen appeals to the rector, who promises to speak to Dolan. The boys celebrate Stephen, though later developments complicate the apparent triumph.

## Chapter 2: family decline and first desire
The Dedalus family’s finances worsen and they move. Stephen’s schooling continues at Belvedere, where a teacher offers him a place. He encounters Emma and later acts in a school play, experiences his father’s nostalgia during a visit to Cork, and wins prize money that he spends generously but cannot make last. Desire, isolation and guilt intensify; near the chapter’s end he seeks out a sex worker.

## Technique
The third-person narration stays close to Stephen’s changing awareness, so childhood impressions and later intellectual language feel different. Avoid reducing the novel to a straightforward account of Joyce’s own life: it is shaped fiction.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: chart childhood impressions. 10–20: map the dinner argument. 20–30: explain the pandybat episode. 30–40: track family decline. 40–50: discuss changing narrative language.

## Discussion and revision
Why does Stephen appeal to the rector? How does the family’s loss of money shape his development?

course-35:2.title: A Portrait of the Artist · Chapters 3–5
course-35:2.text:
# A Portrait of the Artist · Chapters 3–5
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Chapter 3: fear and confession
After the sexual experiences closing Chapter 2, Stephen is absorbed in what he understands as sin. A religious retreat includes sermons describing death, judgment and hell in vivid detail. Frightened by the possibility of damnation, he seeks confession away from school and receives communion. The chapter shows a powerful subjective religious experience; readers need not accept its theology as medical or moral fact.

## Chapter 4: priesthood and the shore
Stephen follows strict devotional routines. A priest suggests he might have a vocation, but Stephen recognises that a clerical life would confine him. As the family’s finances continue to deteriorate, he looks toward university. Near the sea he sees a girl wading, whom he perceives through bird imagery. The experience becomes for him an awakening to beauty and artistic possibility. The girl’s own perspective is not developed.

## Chapter 5: university and departure
Stephen debates language, nationality, religion and aesthetics with fellow students including Davin, Lynch and Cranly. He explains ideas of beauty and artistic form, writes a villanelle associated with Emma, and refuses his mother’s request that he perform Easter religious duties. In conversation with Cranly, he describes a wish to pursue art through independence and exile, even at the cost of isolation. Diary entries close the novel with plans to leave Ireland and an invocation of his mythic namesake Daedalus. The departure is anticipated; the ending does not narrate a completed career abroad.

## Interpretation
Stephen’s self-definition resists family, church and nationalism, yet his claims can be self-dramatising. Examine gender, class and colonial language alongside his quest for artistic freedom.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map fear and confession. 10–20: compare priesthood and the shore. 20–30: outline the university debates. 30–40: discuss diary form and exile. 40–50: evaluate Stephen’s claims.

## Discussion and revision
Why does Stephen refuse the priestly path? What changes when the narrative ends in diary form?

course-35:3.title: Mrs Dalloway · Morning, the city and memory
course-35:3.text:
# Mrs Dalloway · Morning, the city and memory
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Form and context
Woolf’s 1925 novel follows one June day in post-First World War London while moving continually into memory and between minds. It is not organised into universally agreed numbered chapters: editions divide the text differently. These guides use broad narrative sequences, not invented chapter numbers.

## Flowers and public space
Clarissa Dalloway goes out to buy flowers for the evening party. London sounds, the striking clocks and chance encounters stimulate memories of her youth at Bourton, including Peter Walsh and Sally Seton. A motorcar attracts public speculation; an aeroplane writing in the sky becomes another event through which attention passes among different observers.

## Septimus and Rezia
Among those in the city are Septimus Warren Smith, a veteran distressed by his wartime experiences and visions of his dead friend Evans, and his Italian wife Lucrezia (Rezia), who is anxious and isolated. The novel moves between their experiences rather than making Rezia merely an observer of his suffering.

## Peter’s visit
Clarissa returns home and mends her dress. Peter, recently returned from India, visits unexpectedly. Their conversation activates memories of her refusal of his proposal and her marriage to Richard. The feelings between them are unresolved and contradictory; neither character supplies an unquestionable account of the past.

## Technique
Track a clock, sound or passing object as the narration shifts viewpoint. “Stream of consciousness” is a useful term, but Woolf also uses free indirect discourse and carefully structured transitions.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map the day. 10–20: follow the flowers and car. 20–30: compare Clarissa’s and Rezia’s viewpoints. 30–40: examine the Peter visit. 40–50: explain one transition.

## Discussion and revision
How does the city connect people who do not meet? Why should edition-dependent section numbering be used cautiously?

course-35:3.title: Mrs Dalloway · Doctors, afternoon and the party
course-35:3.text:
# Mrs Dalloway · Doctors, afternoon and the party
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## The doctors and private worlds
Septimus and Rezia consult Sir William Bradshaw, who proposes rest and separation from her. The novel questions a medical authority that values conformity and control; distinguish this historical fictional critique from a general rejection of modern mental-health care. Septimus’s memories and perceptions convey both distress and a rich subjective life.

Richard lunches with Lady Bruton and Hugh Whitbread, then brings Clarissa flowers, unable easily to express his love in words. Their daughter Elizabeth spends time with her tutor Miss Kilman and later travels through London. These episodes show different relations to class, religion, work and the city.

## Septimus and the party
At home Septimus and Rezia share a brief moment over a hat she is making. When Dr Holmes comes and Septimus fears loss of control and separation, he dies by suicide. Peter later hears the ambulance without knowing whose death it marks. At Clarissa’s party, Sally returns and Sir William’s wife mentions the death of a young man. Clarissa, who never met Septimus, withdraws briefly and reflects on his death and her own life, then returns to her guests; Peter’s perception of her closes the novel.

## Interpretation and care
Clarissa’s response is complex and personal, not a model for how to interpret or respond to suicide. Compare their experiences without claiming their class, suffering or choices are identical. The party can be read as a fragile act of connection as well as a display of social privilege.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: track the doctors’ power. 10–20: compare Richard, Elizabeth and Rezia. 20–30: trace the ambulance and party news. 30–40: discuss Clarissa’s response sensitively. 40–50: write about connection and difference.

## Discussion and revision
How does Clarissa learn about Septimus? What do shared public sounds achieve in the novel?

course-35:4.title: The Heart of the Matter · Colonial setting and the loan
course-35:4.text:
# The Heart of the Matter · Colonial setting and the loan
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## The syllabus label
The unit calls Greene and Golding an “antimodernist trend.” Treat this as a topic for inquiry rather than proof that neither writer uses modern techniques. Greene’s psychological interiority and Golding’s symbolic patterning complicate a simple opposition between modernism and antimodernism.

## The colonial community
In a British West African colony during the Second World War, police officer Major Henry Scobie has a reputation for honesty. He is passed over for promotion. His wife Louise, lonely and unhappy in the expatriate community, wants to leave for South Africa. Wilson, newly arrived and drawn to Louise, is later revealed to be investigating corruption. Colonial hierarchies shape whose experiences receive attention.

## Pressure and obligation
Scobie investigates the suicide of a young official, Pemberton, whose debts trouble him. Unable to obtain a bank loan for Louise’s passage, Scobie borrows from Yusef, a Syrian trader with interests in smuggling. This creates an obligation to a person Scobie should keep at professional distance. A Portuguese ship’s captain and a letter also test Scobie’s official duties.

## Interpretation
Pity and responsibility motivate Scobie, but they can become possessive or self-deceptive. Ask whether his decisions allow other people a real choice, and how colonial power affects Ali, his longtime servant. The novel contains suicide and religious distress; handle both with care.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map the setting and characters. 10–20: examine promotion and Louise’s departure. 20–30: trace the loan. 30–40: question pity and power. 40–50: evaluate the unit label.

## Discussion and revision
Why does Scobie borrow from Yusef? Why is “antimodernist” not a complete description of technique?

course-35:4.title: The Heart of the Matter · Helen, Ali and the ending
course-35:4.text:
# The Heart of the Matter · Helen, Ali and the ending
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## The affair and blackmail
After Louise leaves, survivors of a shipwreck arrive. Scobie encounters Helen Rolt, a young widow; his sympathy develops into an affair. He feels responsible for both Helen and Louise and lies to avoid hurting them. A compromising letter falls into Yusef’s hands, enabling Yusef to pressure Scobie into assisting a transaction connected with the Portuguese ship.

## Faith and suspicion
Louise returns, aware of the affair although she does not immediately confront him. Scobie’s Catholic beliefs make him feel unable to reconcile his continuing relationship with confession and communion, yet he cannot bring himself to abandon Helen. Suspecting Ali of knowledge or disloyalty, he speaks to Yusef; Yusef arranges Ali’s death. Scobie did not knowingly order the killing, but recognises his part in exposing Ali to danger.

## Death and aftermath
Feeling trapped and believing his death will release others, Scobie plans suicide so that it will appear natural. He dies after taking accumulated medication. His belief that death solves the problem is a character’s desperate judgment, not a conclusion readers must accept. Wilson notices evidence suggesting that the death was intentional; Louise later speaks to Father Rank, who cautions against assuming human beings can judge the full extent of God’s mercy.

## Critical reading
Compare pity with responsibility and control. The book’s moral questions matter, but so do the unequal voices in its colonial setting: Ali’s life must not be treated solely as a step in Scobie’s spiritual journey.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: trace the letter. 10–20: map competing obligations. 20–30: discuss Ali and colonial power. 30–40: examine the final conversation sensitively. 40–50: write about pity.

## Discussion and revision
How does Yusef gain leverage? Why is Scobie’s responsibility for Ali morally complicated?

course-35:4.title: Lord of the Flies · Chapters 1–4
course-35:4.text:
# Lord of the Flies · Chapters 1–4
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Chapter 1: The Sound of the Shell
After an aircraft crash during wartime, British schoolboys find themselves on an island without adult supervision. Ralph and Piggy discover a conch and use it to summon others. Ralph is elected chief; Jack retains leadership of the choir, who become hunters. Ralph, Jack and Simon explore and confirm they are on an island. Jack hesitates to kill a trapped pig.

## Chapter 2: Fire on the Mountain
An assembly adopts the conch as a speaking rule. A younger boy speaks fearfully of a beast. The boys light a signal fire using Piggy’s glasses, but it spreads into the forest. Afterwards the boy with the birthmark cannot be found; the text suggests, but does not explicitly show, his death.

## Chapter 3: Huts on the Beach
Ralph and Simon work on shelters while most boys abandon the task. Jack is absorbed in hunting, producing tension between meat and protection. Simon retreats to a secluded clearing, where his sensitivity to the natural world becomes apparent.

## Chapter 4: Painted Faces and Long Hair
The littluns establish routines; Roger throws stones near one child, still held back by remembered social limits. Jack paints his face and successfully hunts. The hunters let the signal fire go out just as a ship passes. Ralph confronts Jack; in the conflict Piggy is struck and one lens of his glasses is broken.

## Teaching point
Avoid reducing each boy to a single fixed symbol: Ralph enjoys the excitement of the island too, and group behaviour changes through interaction.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: draw the island and assembly. 10–20: follow the conch and fire. 20–30: compare shelter and hunting. 30–40: discuss the missing child carefully. 40–50: analyse the missed ship.

## Discussion and revision
Why is the first fire both useful and dangerous? What does the text leave uncertain about the missing boy?

course-35:4.title: Lord of the Flies · Chapters 5–8
course-35:4.text:
# Lord of the Flies · Chapters 5–8
Modern Fiction · Semester 6

## Chapter 5: Beast from Water
Ralph calls a meeting to address shelters, sanitation and the fire, but discussion turns to fear of a beast. Simon struggles to suggest that the danger may be connected to the boys themselves. Jack challenges the assembly’s authority; fear and excitement break up the meeting.

## Chapter 6: Beast from Air
During an aerial battle a dead parachutist comes down on the mountain. Sam and Eric, tending the fire, mistake the wind-moved figure for a beast. The boys search and discover the defensible rocky place later called Castle Rock. Ralph insists on returning to the mountain and the signal fire.

## Chapter 7: Shadows and Tall Trees
On the way Ralph wounds a boar and feels the thrill of hunting. The boys’ imitation hunt becomes frighteningly rough for Robert, who plays the pig. Ralph, Jack and Roger climb the mountain in the dark, see the parachutist’s distorted form and flee.

## Chapter 8: Gift for the Darkness
Jack unsuccessfully tries to remove Ralph as chief and forms a separate group. His hunters kill a sow and leave its head on a stake as an offering.
